title: The Fathers on Romans
rules: Larry Sanger's rules for Deep Dive Bible commentary editions (emails of 8 and 9 Nov 2026): comments of at most 6 adjacent verses (Selected at most 3); cuts marked with an ellipsis; square brackets for editorial additions only; paragraphs added; one-sentence capsule no longer than 40% of the comment. Every word outside brackets is Via Patrum's published translation, checked by script.
scope: Church Fathers (all died by 749) in works published on viapatrum.org as of 9 Nov 2026.

comments.capsule: Paul is consecrated to the gospel as the law consecrates sacrifices.
comments.comment: … being set apart and dedicated to the gospel, just as the law says in a distinction and a separation, that which is separated from the sacrifices to God and to the priests.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Paul is called an apostle directly from heaven, so that he has something more than the other apostles, and his gospel comes by the will of the Father.
comments.comment: As the world is ignorant of the divinity of Christ, he proclaims it. And why does he appropriate the common to himself? Because many, having seen the Lord or not having seen him, believed, but Paul is called from heaven, 'Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?' (Acts 9:4). And there is added to him something more than the other apostles; for the Lord himself had called Peter, James, and John as disciples, and did not immediately make or name them apostles, but he called Paul likewise and led him into apostleship. And that the gospel is proclaimed by the will of the Father.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: If the message about Christ is called God’s own gospel, Christ must be God.
comments.comment:
“Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God, which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy writings concerning his Son, who was born from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was appointed Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness from the resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord.” (Romans 1:1–4)

So then: if the proclamation about Christ is God’s gospel, how is Christ not God? …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: God’s prophets and gospel are his own, not another god’s, for idols have prophets and mortal gospels exist too.
comments.comment: He said of his prophets—since there are also prophets of idols—commanding by his own voice, prophesying prophets and the gospel of gospels; for there are many gospels, but they are mortal and temporary, whereas the one of Christ promises the enjoyment of eternal goods in the holy writings. Therefore, both the prophets and the gospel are of him, and not of another god, but of the Father of Christ.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: A son in the flesh, Christ is revealed as God by the Spirit, so we become children of God.
comments.comment: he became a son in the flesh, sharing our human nature, and through the Spirit and power, the Son is revealed as God, rising from the dead, so that we too might become children of God, receiving adoption and the redemption of our bodies, as the apostle himself said.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ is Son in power and in truth by nature, while we are sons only by grace, and we become sons through him when baptism gives us his Spirit.
comments.comment: “Concerning his Son, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:3). He says that the one born of the seed of David according to the flesh was declared Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by the resurrection from the dead (Romans 1:4). For we too have been declared sons, but not in power; it is rather by way of grace, as those counted worthy of the calling, who gain this by the will of God the Father alone. But with Emmanuel it would not be so; far from it. Even though he was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, and as one of us is reckoned Son of God because of his humanity, he is nonetheless Son in power and in truth, by nature; and through him we too are made sons, since it is indeed true to say that, once we have been enriched with his Spirit through holy baptism, then truly we say without fear of rebuke, “Abba, Father” (Romans 8:15). So, as images stand to their archetype, so we, who are sons by adoption, stand to him whom the Father has attested to be Son by nature, in power, and in truth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains “declared Son of God in power”: Christ is Son by nature, and we are sons by adoption through him.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Because Paul received apostleship for obedience of faith for Christ’s name, faith toward Christ is faith toward God, and so Christ is God.
comments.comment: “Through whom we received grace and apostleship unto obedience of faith among all the nations for his name, among whom you also are called of Jesus Christ.” (Romans 1:5–6) The nations have been called through faith. And Christ was the one proclaimed among them through the holy apostles. So the faith of those being initiated was practiced not as toward a human, but as toward God. For we do not say the nations were called from error into error by receiving the faith toward Christ; rather, having left the falsely named gods, they turned thereafter to the living God. When therefore the initiators say they received apostleship unto obedience of faith for the name of Christ, how would he not be God, if indeed faith toward him is as toward God?
comments.selected_reason: Shows what Paul means by “obedience of faith … for his name”: the nations were called to faith in Christ as in God.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Even the Gentile Romans rightly receive the apostleship’s proclamation.
comments.comment: so that he might show that even the Romans, being of the Gentiles among all those inhabiting the inhabited world, justly receive the proclamation of the apostleship.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Paul says “Father” to show God’s care and “Lord” because the Son is judge and God by nature, so that we remember we are sons only by God’s goodness.
comments.comment: And it is not said simply to the holy ones, but—since many are called and few are chosen; for not all remained in the calling—lest he cast the holy things to the dogs (Matt 7:6). According to the heretics: if Christ is Lord and our God is Father, then the Father will be a slave to Christ; for as the Son is, so is the Father. But it is not so; for our Father said, in order to show grace, and Lord Jesus, in order that, not thinking highly of themselves as being sons of God, they might not bring down the glory of the Son or exalt themselves above nature. He called God Father, because he judges no one; but the Son Lord, because he is the judge. He says Father, so that he might show the care concerning us; but calls the Son Lord, so that we may know that we are called sons by the goodness of God, while Jesus himself, as being God by nature, truly, is our Lord.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul thanks God through Christ and rejoices over the Romans’ faith as heaven rejoices over a repenting sinner.
comments.comment:
they call God, those who approach him uniquely and above all others, the prophets of old, but now the apostles; this shows that there is no thanking God without Christ.

He rejoices, using an angelic disposition, for the holding fast of the faith of Christ in Rome; for joy occurs in heaven also over one sinner repenting, and he rejoices with his co-apostle Peter, having been so strong through grace.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The gospel Paul serves is also Christ’s, so Christ is proclaimed as God, through whom the Father is announced and worshiped.
comments.comment: “For God is my witness, whom I worship in my spirit in the gospel of his Son.” (Romans 1:9) Those who worship God do not worship Christ as another god beside him; and of him, he says, is also the gospel. For he himself is proclaimed as God to the world, although the Father is God by nature and rules over all. So Christ is God—the one through whom and in whom the Father himself is also announced as God and honored with the worship from all.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Paul teaches the unknowing and exhorts the enlightened, and he shows teachers that they too are helped and must not think highly of themselves.
comments.comment:
he teaches indeed, lighting up those not yet knowing, but he exhorts those already enlightened, gladdening them with the word of wisdom, as he himself says, dividing: whether the teacher, in teaching, or the one exhorting, in exhortation.

And he says that he himself will be exhorted together with the Romans, sharing in their exhortation through love, while at the same time being not even himself above the need for the benefit of the word; for the word is an exhortation even to the speaker.

Through this, he instructs the teachers not to think highly of themselves if they should teach, but to know that they do not teach their own things even if they teach, and to be persuaded that they do not only benefit but are also benefited …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says he wants to be strengthened together with the Romans: even teachers are benefited as they teach.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: A spiritual gift is a word of wisdom, a word of knowledge or a similar virtue; wealth or health is a gift of God but not a spiritual one.
comments.comment: … I was saying what even the apostle says: 'that I often intended to come to you' (Romans 1:13). For what reason then? 'That I might impart to you a spiritual gift' (Romans 1:11). And I was saying that not all things given by God are spiritual gifts. Whenever anyone receives a 'word of wisdom,' a 'word of knowledge,' and some other virtue, he has received a spiritual grace; but not if someone receives wealth or health or something of that kind; he has received a gift of God and a grace, but not a spiritual one.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by “a spiritual gift” by separating it from other good things God gives.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The fruit of believing the word is the benefit of its hearers.
comments.comment:
the fruit of those having believed the word is the benefit of those hearing; and the Lord says that the apostles have been appointed to make much fruit.

Indeed, few men are a church that has borne all fruit.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Paul seems to reproach the Romans, perhaps because their faith was becoming a greater exhortation to all.
comments.comment: And again, because many hurried to Rome for certain human reasons, they show their desire, and that this one is pious in his addition. But it appears that he intends to reproach the Romans, perhaps because the faith of the Romans was becoming a greater exhortation to all those under them.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul will not shrink from preaching the saving cross even in the greatest city, since the Son of God bore its shame for us.
comments.comment: even if in the greatest of cities, he says, it is necessary to be mocked by the foolish while preaching the saving cross, I will not shrink back; for if the Son of God bore the shame of the cross instead of us, how is it not incongruous for us to be shamed by the Lord's passion for our sake?
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul is “not ashamed” of the gospel: the Son of God himself bore the shame of the cross for us.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Because the Law condemns rather than justifies, all justification is in Christ, as Paul shows in saying that the righteous shall live from faith.
comments.comment: For if what is under sin is still a slave, and the Law justifies least of all — it condemns rather, and writes down those who transgress — how would it not be clear to everyone that all justification is in Christ, and the perfecting in the Spirit through sanctification, through him and in him? And so the all-wise Paul writes, 'For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and to the Greek. For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith, as it is written, The righteous shall live from faith.' (Habakkuk 2:4) And he writes down the uselessness and weakness of the old Law in this, saying, 'That no one is justified in the Law before God is clear, because the righteous shall live from faith. And the Law is not from faith, but the one who has done them shall live in them.' (Galatians 3:11–12) So in Christ we are justified through faith, and we have been redeemed from the intelligible slavery.
comments.selected_reason: Explains “the righteousness of God … from faith to faith”: the Law cannot justify, but faith in Christ does.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 2

comments.capsule: The gospel and faith free people from evils, so Paul first speaks of the Gentiles, who broke the law written in nature by the Creator, and then of the Jews.
comments.comment:
He teaches how much the gospel and the faith through it free from evils, and having gone through the evils both among the Gentiles and among the Jews, after this he proceeds to bring a word concerning faith, teaching that the presence of Christ had to come about.

And so he discourses about the fall of the Jews, and the last part leads to exhortations; but he begins from the word concerning the Gentiles and says how they unworthily transgressed the law written in nature by the Creator (Rom 1:18), as both the name of God and His reverence were brought into the things of God's creation.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Because the visible creation is enough to show the invisible God, people who made creatures into gods held down the truth in unrighteousness.
comments.comment:
Then he also interprets how: for if the visible creation is sufficient to show the invisible, but men, leaving this, made the creatures into gods, they seized the truth of God in unrighteousness (Romans 1:18), from which it is necessary to know God, having been led astray.

Not being the essence of this working, as he says: it is through the incorruptible, invisible, only wise God (1 Timothy 1:17), but these energies, being invisible in nature and never becoming manifest to anything, are instead indicated through the creation.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christians use created things as a stepping-stone to the intelligible, and those who knew great things but acted impiously have no defence before God.
comments.comment: And the disciples of Jesus look at the things of becoming too, but in such a way as to use them as a kind of stepping-stone to the contemplation of the nature of intelligible things. For “the invisible things” of God, that is, the intelligible things, “from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made” (Romans 1:20); they are seen in being understood. And when they have climbed up from the created things of the world, they do not stop at the invisible things of God; but after exercising themselves enough in these and understanding them, they rise to the eternal power of God and, in a word, to his divinity (Romans 1:20). They know that God in his love for mankind “manifested” “the truth” and “what can be known” of himself (Romans 1:18–19), not only to those devoted to him, but also to some who are outside pure reverence for God and piety toward him; but that some of those who by the providence of God had climbed up to the knowledge of such great things do what is unworthy of that knowledge, act impiously, and “hold down the truth in unrighteousness” (Romans 1:18), and can no longer have even room for a defence before God, since they had knowledge of such great things (Romans 1:20).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul bears witness that some Greek wise men knew God, and that this knowledge came to them from God, yet they did not glorify him.
comments.comment: Paul, as a lover of truth, says of certain wise men among the Greeks, in the points where they speak truly, “that, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks” (Romans 1:21). He bears witness that they had known God; and he says too that this did not come to them without God, where he writes: “for God has shown it to them” (Romans 1:19). He is hinting, I think, at those who ascend from things visible to things intelligible, when he writes that “the invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made, both his eternal power and divinity, so that they are without excuse, because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks” (Romans 1:20–21).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the pagan wise knew God through creation yet did not glorify him.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Since created things perish, their Maker must be imperishable and eternal, leaving people no defense.
comments.comment: “His eternal power and divinity” (Romans 1:20). How is his eternal power known through creation? Because the things brought into being and called into existence in time have a perishable nature, their Maker must surely be imperishable and eternal. So they will find no defense on the day of judgment.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how creation shows God’s eternal power: things that come to be in time must have an eternal Maker.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: All creation keeps its order and shows its ruler, God, so those who ignored him made themselves foolish.
comments.comment: For what of the things around the creation is not done in order? And what of the things that are has not kept its own taxis, and all but cries out the taxiarch? And that it has been yoked under laws it shouts, and is administered by nods of the one strong to rule—I mean God. Therefore also the divine Paul: ‘For his invisible things,’ … he says, ‘from creation of a world are clearly seen being understood by the things made, both his everlasting power and divinity, unto their being without defense; because having known God, they did not glorify him as God, but were made vain, and their unintelligent heart was darkened; saying to be wise they were made foolish.’ (Romans 1:20–22) For how were they not made foolish counseling themselves and indeed also others to think some other things beside what holds rightly?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 6

comments.capsule: Paul shows that the Gentiles cannot excuse their idolatry by ignorance of the law, since reason lets them know God from his works.
comments.comment: Writing to the Romans at the time when the Gentiles had begun to be brought in, and churches were therefore being filled with Jews and Gentiles alike, he calms the disturbances of both peoples. He insists that the Gentiles cannot wash away their impiety—their exchanging God’s glory for a likeness of the image of a human being, birds, four-footed animals, and reptiles (Romans 1:23)—by pleading ignorance of the law. Through their inborn power of reason they could know God from what he had made: God disclosed through his works, though hidden in the depth of his substance, even if they did not know the observance of Jewish ceremonies (Romans 1:20). Each person’s own feeling suggested the rule of the law insofar as it concerns upright living: namely, to inflict on a neighbor nothing of the kind he would be unwilling to suffer himself (compare Matthew 7:12; Luke 6:31; Tobit 4:15). He thus proves that the Gentiles’ impiety can quite rightly be condemned, even if not through the law, then through the justice that established the law.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Paul’s words ask whether anyone would fall into those lusts, passions and a reprobate mind without God handing them over to them.
comments.comment: … what Paul said in Romans, in this way: 'Professing to be wise, they became fools, and changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds and quadrupeds and creeping things. Therefore God handed them over, in the lusts of their hearts, unto uncleanness, to dishonor their bodies among themselves.' (Romans 1:22-24) And after a little: 'For this God handed them over to passions of dishonor' (Romans 1:26); and 'handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is unfitting.' (Romans 1:28) Were those not handed over to them by God not made 'in the lusts of their own hearts'? Would those not handed over by God to 'passions of dishonor' have fallen under them? Would they have collapsed 'into a reprobate mind' without being handed to it by God — those so condemned?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Idols are falsely called gods, and Paul recalls shamelessness he heard of in Rome.
comments.comment: That God truly is God, but the idols with which they worshipped are falsely addressed as gods (Ro 1:25). He does not merely remember such shamelessness, but that he heard in Rome that there was a company of males (Ro 1:27).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul calls the use of the woman natural, showing it is praiseworthy within its bounds.
comments.comment: … Speaking of the ungodly, he says: “Abandoning the natural use of the woman, they burned with desire for one another, males doing what is shameful with males” (Romans 1:27). He therefore shows that the use of the woman is natural and, within its proper bounds, praiseworthy; shameful conduct, however, is committed by a person’s own will against the modesty of the created order.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by the natural use.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum
comments.work: Extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence

comments.capsule: God lets a person go toward a weak mind because we ourselves cause our own suffering by provoking the Master to anger.
comments.comment: … But we ourselves are causes of the suffering to ourselves, whetting the Master of all into angers; for so he lets a man go toward a weak and cowardly mind. Or do you not hear him crying through one of the holy prophets: 'Behold, I give weakness upon this people, and they shall be weak in it, fathers and sons; neighbor and his neighbor shall perish' (Jeremiah 6:21)? And the most wise Paul also writes about some: 'And as they did not approve to have God in knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do the things that are not fitting.' (Romans 1:28) …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God “gave them over” to a reprobate mind: people bring it on themselves.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: The righteousness of God is his just retribution to each according to merit, since people know by reason that those who do such things deserve to be punished.
comments.comment: He says that the righteousness of God is his just retribution, which he gives to each according to his merit (Ro 1:32–2:1). This is what he says: even if men know from their natural reason that those transgressing have deserved to be punished by God, nevertheless they do not desist from the more skillful evaders, and the whole matter is that they also agree with those doing these things. Therefore, the righteousness of God he says is this very thing: that those doing such things are worthy of death, whether through his righteousness simply, or the commandments, or the Mosaic law; for thus he most boldly and decisively commands that those doing such things are judged worthy of death.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The wicked know that a punishment fitting the deed comes from God as Judge, and death overtakes those who do such things.
comments.comment:
There again is God's blamelessness and man's guilt, and the justice of the coming judgment.

For they do these things, not being ignorant that with God the Judge it is a punishment worthy of it; for they are manifest, not being ignorant of such a thing when they judge, and they are overtaken by death, those doing such things.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God's wrath is not a passion in him but something each person prepares for himself through his sins.
comments.comment:
That wrath is not a passion of God, but that each person prepares it for himself through his sins, Paul will make plain where he says: “Or do you despise the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God’s kindness is leading you to repentance? But by your hardness and your unrepentant heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God” (Romans 2:4–5).

How then can each person “store up wrath for himself on the day of wrath” if “wrath” is understood as the passion? And how can a passion of wrath discipline?
comments.selected_reason: Explains that the 'wrath' Paul speaks of is something each person stores up by his own sins.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God does not quickly punish those who stray, so that his goodness may grant time for repentance.
comments.comment: He does not quickly punish those who stray. He does this for no other purpose than that his goodness may grant time for repentance. So the apostle says: ‘Or do you not know that God’s goodness (Romans 2:4) leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you store up wrath for yourself’ (Romans 2:4–5).
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: God's righteous judgment is hidden now, but at the appointed time of reckoning it will shine out and give each person what his life deserves.
comments.comment: They stumble by saying all things thoughtlessly, supposing they cannot see God in human affairs. But when the appointed time of reckoning arrives, then the light of God's righteous judgment is revealed and shines, according to what each one has lived according to his merit (Romans 2:5). Therefore, as an image of a day of wrath, he taught that now is not the time for punishment, nor for wrath, nor for the righteous judgment of God.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: God will render to each according to his works, as the Psalmist and the Savior also say.
comments.comment: Regarding the one discussing about God, he says that He will render according to his works, according to what is said in the Psalmist (Rom 2:1); and the Savior says this about Him, asserting: then He will render to each according to his practice (Rom 2:1).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Both the condemnation and the glory are meant to show God's goodness.
comments.comment: He appointed the condemnation upon the evil, not simply, but upon those working-out; and the glory upon the good, not only upon those working-out, so that through both the good of God might be shown…
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul names the Jew first, as nearer the Master's rebukes and honors.
comments.comment: It is well that here he says first Jew, then Greek; for those closer to the Master and to the reprimands and the honors are deemed more worthy than the others.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The Jew is named first because those closer to the Master are honored above the others.
comments.comment: Well again, he says here, first to the Jew and second to the Greek (Rom 2:10): for those closer to the Master and to the honors are honored above the others and enjoy the honors above the others (Rom 2:10).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says 'first to the Jew and also to the Greek'.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God judges Jew and Gentile alike by their conduct, so descent from Abraham gives no protection.
comments.comment:
The apostle Paul, debating the objections of Jews who swelled with pride in the dignity of their ancestry and disdained believers from the nations being made equal to them, commends both God's justice and his grace. … For there is one Creator of both peoples, who will judge the former through the Law, the latter without the Law, and the former in the Law (Romans 2:12; Romans 3:29–31). He is not the God of Jews alone but also of the nations (Romans 3:29), returning to each what belongs to that person without deceit or favoritism, that is, without partiality toward anyone…

…The Teacher of the Nations therefore restrains Jewish pride and shows that the difference lies not in human seed but in conduct. They must recognize that unless they take care to be faithful, no privilege of circumcised ancestry will defend them. Jacob and Esau, after all, were conceived through one reception of seed and delivered through one act of giving birth, yet experienced very different outcomes because of the difference in what they deserved…
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says God shows no partiality: Jew and Gentile are judged by conduct, not by descent.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Sinning without the law is lawlessness, and sinning after receiving the law is transgression, though the deed is the same.
comments.comment: Transgression is lawlessness, but lawlessness is not always transgression. If one acts outside of the law, he is acting outside of it, and that is lawlessness. But if, having received the law, he violates it, he acts contrary to the law, and that is transgression. … 'As many as sinned in the law' (Romans 2:12), he says; those sinning in the law are transgressors. 'They sin lawlessly' are those not possessing the law. However, the thing being done is one and the same. I take the difference from the volition and the disposition of the one acting, so that at times he is called lawless, and at times he is called a transgressor.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the difference between sinning 'without law' and sinning 'in the law'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Gentiles are condemned apart from the law, and the Jews through the law they sinned against knowingly.
comments.comment: He thus proves that the Gentiles’ impiety can quite rightly be condemned, even if not through the law, then through the justice that established the law. By its judgment, those who sinned without the law will also perish without the law (Romans 2:12). The Jews, however, had even more at stake. They were especially swollen with contempt for the Gentiles, claiming honor for themselves from the law’s purifications. They therefore supposed that Christ’s sin-forgiving grace had not benefited them as it benefited the Gentiles, since they had avoided those sins through the law’s instruction. He shatters this claim with powerful arguments, maintaining that they received all the more through forgiveness precisely because, after the law’s warning, they sinned without any ignorance. By this he proves that they were guilty and could have been severely condemned at justice’s examination, where those who sinned under the law will be judged through the law (Romans 2:12): ‘For it is not hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but doers of the law who will be justified’ (Romans 2:13)…
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Gentiles who follow natural reason have the law in their nature.
comments.comment: If even the hearing of the law is lacking, as he says, the nations (Rom 2:14), but if according to natural reason he fulfills the purposes of the law, he has the law in nature (Rom 2:14).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Gentiles can be said to 'have the law' without having heard it.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God has sown in every soul the moral knowledge he taught through the prophets, so that no one is without excuse.
comments.comment: …for those who teach a just judgment of God, punishment for sins would have been ruled out if all men did not have, by the common notions, a sound preconception about moral matters. It is therefore no wonder that the same God has sown in the souls of all men what he taught through the prophets and the Savior, so that every man may be without excuse at the divine judgment, having the intent “of the law written” in his own heart (Romans 2:15).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that the law is 'written in the heart': God sowed moral knowledge in every soul.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Men judge only what is seen, but God judges the hidden things, since he looks at the heart.
comments.comment: For men alone sit as judges of visible things, but God makes judgment of the hidden things (Rom 2:16); for man, he says, will look at the face, but God at the heart (Rom 2:16); so that as Christ judges, God is to be the Judge.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God's judgment of 'the secrets of men' differs from human judgment.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Law holds the outline of the truth, and the mystery of Christ lies hidden in its shadows.
comments.comment: By righteousness, I think, He means the Law, for the Law is the arbiter of righteousness; and by truth, the teachings of Christ. Yet the outline of the truth is present in the Law (Romans 2:20), and the mystery of Christ lies hidden in its shadows; for Moses wrote about Him (John 5:46). So in speaking righteousness, the power of the truth is also declared along with it, since it is true that the Law was a shadow (Hebrews 10:1), and that in it now lies the outline of the truth.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God is honored through a sound life, so whoever breaks the law dishonours him and whoever keeps it honours him.
comments.comment: See whether we are not taught that honour toward the Son of God, and in the same way honour toward God the Father, is rendered through a sound life, both from the words “You who boast in the law dishonour God by breaking the law” (Romans 2:23), and from these: “How much worse a punishment, do you think, will be deserved by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has counted as common the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and has insulted the Spirit of grace?” (Hebrews 10:29). For if the one who breaks the law dishonours God “by breaking the law” (Romans 2:23), and the one who tramples on the Word tramples underfoot “the Son of God” (Hebrews 10:29), it is plain that the one who keeps the law honours God, and the one who is adorned with the Word of God and with His works reveres God.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The true Jew and true circumcision belong to the Spirit, in mind and heart, not to the flesh.
comments.comment: The spiritual Jerusalem, or Judah, we hold to be the Church, that is, the circumcision in the Spirit: those who have the circumcision made without hands in Christ (Colossians 2:11) in mind and heart. So one of the holy prophets cried out to the Jews: “Be circumcised to God, and circumcise your hardness of heart, men of Judah and you who dwell in Jerusalem” (Jeremiah 4:4). And the divine Paul knows another Jew, not the one according to the flesh but the one in the spirit, for he writes: “For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is circumcision that which is outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter; his praise is not from men but from God” (Romans 2:28–29).
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's 'Jew in secret' as the circumcision of the Spirit in mind and heart.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Circumcision in the flesh is a type of the inward circumcision by which Christ removes all defilement from our thoughts.
comments.comment: For circumcision in the flesh would be a very clear type of the inward circumcision, the circumcision in the spirit (Romans 2:29), by which Christ removes all defilement from our thoughts. For, in the words of the blessed Paul, ‘we have been circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, in the putting off of the flesh’ (Colossians 2:11). For when we have, as it were, stripped off the old self, which is being corrupted by deceitful desires (Ephesians 4:22), and have all but cut away the pleasures of the flesh by the keen edge and the working of the Spirit, we shall already, in some measure, show ourselves fit to be counted worthy even of seeing God, and of becoming a sacred dwelling place of the holy and consubstantial Trinity.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: The unbelief of some does not make God untrue, since the foreknown who received the law and promises became the firstfruits of the saved.
comments.comment: “Will their unbelief nullify the faithfulness of God?” (Romans 3:3). More honored than the rest are those who were foreknown, who received the law as their tutor (Galatians 3:24), who held promises concerning Christ, who indeed received them, and who were called before the others; for the Savior said, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24). They also became the firstfruits of those saved through faith. For if some, out of madness, slipped away from believing, God would not on that account, he says, fail to be true. So then, the Father sent the Son from heaven, yet not all believed in him. Because some have become insolent and unbelieving, will God not be true on that account? By no means!
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's question: the unbelief of some does not make God unfaithful.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God must be thought true because his nature is unchangeable, while human nature can fall into falsehood.
comments.comment: “Let God be true, and every man a liar” (Romans 3:4). That is, let him be thought and spoken of by us as true, and let falsehood be charged, as it were, to every human being. For the divine nature is wholly unchangeable and unalterable, while human nature is badly shaken, and, as far as possibility goes, every man is a liar. For falsehood, as a sin, sometimes overpowers the human mind, and our nature is in some way open to this sickness as well. But of God, who rules over all, it is not right to think or say any such thing. So the charge will be true in this sense: that human nature, that is, the mind, can suffer falsehood. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God is called true and every man a liar: God's nature never changes, ours can fall into falsehood.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The same reasoning applies to righteousness: let God be righteous and every man unrighteous.
comments.comment: …the blessed David: “I said in my alarm, ‘Every man is a liar’” (Psalm 116:11). The same reasoning would apply to God and to us in all other matters too; for example, in the matter of righteousness. For one could say, and not unreasonably, “Let God be righteous, and every man unrighteous.”
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God's word is firm and true, and men are shown to be unstable liars.
comments.comment: Let God's word be confessed, he says, as firm and true everywhere (Romans 3:4), and let men be reproved as unstable and lying (Romans 3:4), so that God may overcome with benefits beyond the value of men, freely bestowing from himself.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The slander behind Paul's question began when Israelites after the exile, chastened for slackness, called the foreigners happy and said it was vain to serve God.
comments.comment: “But if our unrighteousness shows the righteousness of God” (Romans 3:5). The occasion for this slander arose in this way. After the return from Babylon, the sons of Israel, ordered by Cyrus to rebuild the temple, to pay their vows and to offer sacrifices, grew slack, pleading poverty and the hardship left by the captivity. For this they were corrected by measured chastisements: failed harvests and lack of rain (Haggai 1:9–11). Chafing at such blows, they called the foreigners and those who did not serve God happy, as living in good cheer, and said that those people were better off than they were. And so the prophet Malachi said to them: “You have made your words heavy against me, says the Lord. And you said, ‘How have we spoken against you?’ You said,” he says, “‘It is vain to serve God. What more have we gained because we kept his charges, and because we walked as suppliants before the Lord Almighty? And now we call strangers happy, and those who do lawless deeds are built up; they opposed God and were saved.’ This is how those who feared the Lord spoke against him, each to his neighbor; and the Lord gave heed and heard” (Malachi 3:13–16).
comments.selected_reason: Gives the setting of the objection Paul answers: Israel's complaint after the exile.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The condemnation falls on those who pinned 'Let us do evil so that good may come' on the Jews, or said it themselves.
comments.comment: For this reason, he says, some thought that the Jews were saying, “Let us do evil so that good may come” (Romans 3:8). But when he says that their condemnation is just, he means those who pinned those words on the Jews, or rather those who dared to say, “Let us do evil so that good may come.”
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Law was useful as a tutor, but it names sins rather than bringing the knowledge of virtue.
comments.comment: As far as tutoring goes, and knowing what is a fault, and needing to take first principles and elements of the oracles of God, how would it not be thought useful? But it is slower toward the washing-off of sin, and toward being able to perfect into sanctification. And so divine Paul said to us, 'We know that whatever the Law says, it speaks to those in the Law, so that every mouth may be stopped and all the world may become accountable to God, because from works of Law no flesh will be justified before him; for through Law is knowledge of sins.' (Romans 3:19-20) So the Law is a shower of sin, not a bringer of boasts toward virtue. For to say, You shall not fornicate, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not swear falsely, and whatever is fitted to such things, belonged to one marking the kinds of worthlessness and putting people out of uncleanness — not bringing in a knowledge of virtue, nor making the knowledge of the unadulterated life most clear to the hearers.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 2

comments.capsule: The law condemns transgressors, and since it holds so many commandments even its careful keeper must stumble in some.
comments.comment: Again, the law condemns those who transgress; that is why he says elsewhere, “For if there was glory in the ministry of condemnation, much more does the ministry of righteousness abound in glory” (2 Corinthians 3:9). And since the law contains a great many commandments, even the careful keeper of the law must surely stumble in some of them and become a transgressor of the law. The inspired disciples plainly admitted that it is truly burdensome, for they said: “Now therefore, why are you putting God to the test by placing on the neck of the disciples a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?” (Acts 15:10).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why righteousness comes apart from the law: even a careful keeper of the law stumbles.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Even one blameless in the law, like Paul himself, has not yet done the deeds that make a man illustrious, and Paul counted all in the law as loss for the knowledge of Christ.
comments.comment: “But now the righteousness of God has been made manifest apart from the law” (Romans 3:21). I know that it is written of certain people that “they were both righteous, walking blameless in the commandments and ordinances of Christ” (Luke 1:6); and the blessed Paul too said that he himself had become “blameless as to the righteousness that is in the law” (Philippians 3:6). But one who is blameless in these things has not yet done the deeds that will make him illustrious and renowned. Indeed, the blessed Paul himself said again that he counted everything in the law as loss and reckoned it as so much refuse, and that he would seek instead “the surpassing excellence of the knowledge of Christ” (Philippians 3:7–8).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God's righteousness is a free gift added to the law, so we are perfected by it, not judged by human righteousness.
comments.comment: Not in opposition to the law, but according to the addition of good and the free gift of God, so that we might no longer be judged by human righteousness which is altogether convicted, but might be perfected by the righteousness from God (Rom 3:21); and this is the one who rests through the faith of Christ, passing into all the believing ones and to all.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Savior came when all had sinned and no righteous person remained on earth, to taste death for everyone.
comments.comment: …For since the Savior came to take away the sin of the world, it was not fitting that so great a one should come and suffer for few sinners. When the time stood apart in which it is said, “All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23), and there was no longer a righteous person on earth who understood and sought after God, he came who by the grace of God tastes death for everyone on behalf of all of them.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Because all have sinned, Christ justifies Jew and Greek freely by his grace, and his blood is the price that saved the world.
comments.comment: When, then, the Greeks were under sin for not knowing the Creator, and the Jews as guilty of transgressing the law, those on the earth necessarily had need of Christ, who justifies. For we have been justified “not by works of righteousness that we have done, but according to his great mercy” (Titus 3:5). For it was he who long ago said through the voice of the prophets, “I am he who blots out your transgressions, and I will not remember them” (Isaiah 43:25). Justifying grace passes to all alike, I mean to Jews and Greeks, because “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). The glory of God may fittingly be understood as this: neither to know how to do wrong nor to be of a nature that can do wrong. And the whole created order surely falls short of the glories of the Godhead, for even some of the angels slipped. Yet God the Father was pleased “to sum up all things in Christ” (Ephesians 1:10), who justifies freely by his grace (Romans 3:24). For he has been set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood (Romans 3:25). Since he made his own blood the price given in exchange for the life of all, he has saved the world under heaven and made the Father and God in heaven merciful and kindly toward us.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Christ justifies all freely: his blood is the price given for the life of all.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ is the mercy seat, since through him the Father is gracious to us and every prayer reaches its end.
comments.comment: But we say that the mercy seat, if it is understood spiritually, is he who became man for our sake, ‘whom God put forward as a mercy seat through faith, in his blood, to show his righteousness’ (Romans 3:25). For so Paul says. And John, the wisest disciple, also writes to us: ‘Little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the whole world’ (1 John 2:1–2). For through him come propitiation, every prayer, and the asking of good things. …So he himself is the mercy seat. For through him the Father is gracious to us; in him every prayer reaches its end; and through him we draw near, since in no other way are we acceptable.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by calling Christ the 'mercy seat' or propitiation.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: God held back to show his own righteousness, and the righteousness that justifies me is his gift, not from my works.
comments.comment: He who lacks, having something lacking, seeks what is left out; the Jews had the law, but the completion of grace was lacking for them. For God was holding back, so as to show his own righteousness (Ro+m3,25). If it had been released, it would have certainly removed sin; but if it were not holding back, the one being saved would not be. Since he was holding back and adding to the sins, he showed that desiring not only to rid man of sins, but also to justify what was previously held back. Having forgiven, therefore, he granted the remission of sins without end. And we call God just, that is, one who reciprocates or one who grants righteousness as a gift. That by which I am justified is the righteousness of God, since it is not from my works, but from the grace of the one justifying.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Boasting is excluded because all have turned aside and are justified freely, by mercy and grace, in Christ.
comments.comment: “Where then is boasting? It is excluded” (Romans 3:27). For who at all will boast, or in what, when all have become worthless and turned aside from the straight way, and there is no one at all who does good (Psalm 14:3; Romans 3:12)? So, he says, boasting is excluded; that is, it has been thrown out and done away with, and has no place at all among us. And how was it excluded? We have been enriched with the forgiveness of sins committed before (Romans 3:25), being justified freely, by mercy and grace, in Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why boasting is excluded: all have gone astray and are justified freely in Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We uphold the law through faith, because the law was in shadows and the truth does not abolish the types but makes them clearer.
comments.comment: “Do we then nullify the law through faith?” (Romans 3:31). The God of all said to the inspired Moses: “I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers, and I will put my word in his mouth, and he will speak to them whatever I command him. And the man who does not listen to his words, whatever the prophet speaks in my name, I will take vengeance on him” (Deuteronomy 18:18–19). How then do we not uphold the law through faith, when we receive the word that comes from him? Emmanuel has been called a prophet because of his humanity, standing, as it were, in the place of Moses as mediator between God and men (1 Timothy 2:5). And again, the law was in shadows, yet it is seen to be in labor with the form of the truth; and the truth does not abolish the types but makes them clearer.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The law has not been overthrown but turned toward showing the truth, since it tutors us toward the mystery of Christ.
comments.comment: And yet, my friend, you are carried a long way from what is fitting. For you think the Law has been overthrown, as if we had no profit from what is his, and as if it were wholly useless for showing anything of the things we need — not rather that it has been turned toward a showing of the truth, though the blessed Paul writes: 'Do we then abolish the Law through faith? By no means! Rather we establish the Law.' (Romans 3:31) For the Law tutors, and carries us well toward the mystery that is in Christ (Galatians 3:24). And we say that the things of old decreed through Moses to the more ancient people are the first elements of the oracles of God (Hebrews 5:12). And if we push aside the tutor, who will still convey us to the mystery of Christ?
comments.selected_reason: Explains how faith establishes the law: the law is a tutor leading us to Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: Abraham is father of the Israelites by flesh, and they became sons by the Spirit through grace.
comments.comment: But he calls him father according to the flesh of the Israelites, those having become sons according to the Spirit of God; to whom Christ, having been made like them in the fleshly generation, made them like himself through the spiritual generation through grace.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Abraham was justified by faith and not by works, and this is given to the uncircumcised as well as to those in the law.
comments.comment: Abraham demonstrates faith by the pattern according to Abraham (Rom 4:1), not given to those in law and circumcision only for justification but also to those in uncircumcision; for Abraham indeed was justified not from works—for his boasting was not bright, being imperfect and unable to stand before God, by which righteousness limping, it is not able to have a boast—but from faith is the justification of our father Abraham.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Those who look closely at Abraham may point out that James says faith without works is dead.
comments.comment: “For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God” (Romans 4:2). I think, someone has said, that those who look closely into the account of our forefather Abraham ought to say this: it has been said somewhere by one of the holy disciples that faith without works is dead (James 2:26). And to this he adds: “Do you want to know, you empty man, that faith without works is dead (James 2:20)? …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Abraham was justified by honoring God who promised, and offering Isaac was a clear proof of his firm faith.
comments.comment: [Paul's account of Abraham seems to conflict with James 2:21.] Do the Spirit-bearing writers, then, say things contrary to one another? What, then, do we say to this? To him, when he was already far on in years, the God of all promised a son, quite beyond all expectation, and said that the offspring to come from him would rival the countless multitude of the stars (Genesis 15:5). And because he honored the one who promised, bearing witness to God by this that he can accomplish all things, he was justified before him (Genesis 15:6), and received, as a reward worthy of so God-loving a mind, the forgetting of his former offences. In due course God made the oracle concerning Isaac a trial for the righteous man (Genesis 22:1–2); but in this too he was faithful and loved God, as one who put nothing ahead of his love for God. Yet, as the Savior's disciple says, “Faith was working together with the works, and by the works faith was made firm” (James 2:22). …So even if it should perhaps be said that he was justified by works because, when tested, he offered up Isaac, this too was for him a clear proof of the firmest faith.
comments.selected_reason: Reconciles Paul and James: Abraham was justified by honoring God's promise, and offering Isaac proved that faith.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Abraham was justified by faith while uncircumcised, so circumcision is a sign of that faith and not a work that justifies.
comments.comment: …God was promising to Abraham the grace through faith, and, as in a firstfruits of those shown mercy, he was making in him the forgiveness from gentleness older than the Law. For it is written that 'Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness.' (Genesis 15:6) And Paul adds his witness, saying, 'How then was it counted? In circumcision or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, he says, but in uncircumcision; and he received a sign, circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which was in uncircumcision.' (Romans 4:10–11) … Circumcision, then, is a sign of the faith in uncircumcision, and he has been justified not from works of Law, and the boasts through faith appear older than the circumcision in the flesh.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why circumcision came after faith: it was a sign of a righteousness Abraham already had as an uncircumcised man.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 2

comments.capsule: Circumcision was given as a seal and sign of Abraham's righteousness from faith, not as something that makes righteous.
comments.comment: Circumcision was given for these three reasons, so as to be a sign of faith, and a demonstrator and symbol and enigma of a pure and sober citizenship (Ro+m4,11); so that it was not given as a maker of righteousness, but as a seal and sign of the righteousness from faith of Abraham.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Abraham's heirs will inherit the whole renewed world, with the heavenly and earthly goods, after the ungodly are removed to punishment.
comments.comment: He says that you shall be heirs of the world (Ro+m4,13), because the ungodly, having been taken from the midst and handed over to punishment in the day of judgment, the whole remaining world shall belong to the righteous after it has been renewed, and the heavenly goods and the earthly goods shall be theirs.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the promise that Abraham would be 'heir of the world'.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The promise to Abraham was not given by law but by faith, as the books of Moses show.
comments.comment:
God did not ordain the promise to Abraham and to his seed by law, but having justified him by faith (Rom 4:13).

And the promise given to Abraham was, as we have learned from Moses, the one saying: I will give to you and to your seed all this land.

For which reason, that the promise might be a world of inheritance, the apostle says, a promise of land.

And in the letter to the Corinthians, bringing to us, the heirs of Abraham in the Spirit, all of us, he says, whether it be a world, whether existing, or about to be.

And it is evident to those reading the things of Moses, that Abraham did not hold such a promise upon these having received the commands of the law; and indeed Paul in the present matters also gives the reason, through which God did not give the promise upon law, but upon faith.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The promise came to Abraham through faith, so the nations are justified by following in his steps and believing in God.
comments.comment: …And Paul made it clear for us, saying: “For the promise to Abraham or to his seed, that he should be heir of the world, was not through law, but through righteousness of faith,” (Romans 4:13) and again: “so that those from faith are blessed with faithful Abraham.” (Galatians 3:9) … For blessed Abraham was justified having believed toward God; so also the nations would be justified in him, having followed in his steps and believing in God—that is, in Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Paul means that those of the law are not the only heirs, or the uncircumcised who believe would be shut out.
comments.comment: Earlier, then, he had worked to make us understand that the Gentiles could not be excluded from the fellowship of righteousness, but through the same faith are counted in Abraham’s family with the children of circumcision. Now he has added that none of the circumcised belongs to the promise given to Abraham. Unless properly understood, this is a complete contradiction. Therefore, when he says, ‘For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith is emptied and the promise destroyed’ (Romans 4:14), he did not declare that no Jew can be believed to become an heir of the ancient promise through faith. Rather, a word is missing, whose place understanding supplies: those of the law are not the only heirs. It is as though he had said, ‘For if those who are of the law alone are heirs, faith is emptied.’ The uncircumcised would indeed seem excluded if the inheritance of blessing reached none beyond the circumcised.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's hard saying that if those of the law are heirs, faith is emptied.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: The law brings wrath through the wickedness of those who prefer sins to virtues, and where there is no law there is no transgression.
comments.comment: Sinners under the law deserved punishment, and before the law righteousness and faith were not deprived of their reward’s fruits. Clearly, then, the glory of that promise belongs not to flesh cut with a blade, but to minds distinguished by uprightness. What follows is a thunderbolt against inherited transmission: ‘For the law,’ he says, ‘produces wrath; but where there is no law, neither is there transgression’ (Romans 4:15). … This law produces wrath not through its own fault but through the wickedness of those who prefer sins to virtues.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the law produces wrath, and why there is no transgression without law.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Abraham believed with his hope in the power of the one who promised, not in his own nature.
comments.comment: Contrary to him in whom he believed (Ro+m4,17); instead of the face before whom he believed God. Not by the hope of one's own nature, but on the hope of the power of the one promised (Ro+m4,18). And 'thus shall your seed be' (Ro+m4,18) not only in multitude, but also in brightness.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Abraham was strengthened by giving glory to God, believing at once as though he had already received what was promised.
comments.comment: Having said this, he was strengthened; he shows him having been made steadfast in faith with much labor and power of soul and through toil. And how was he strengthened? By giving glory, he says, to God; that is, not having worked out how this comes to be, but immediately believing and blessing God as a benefactor, as one who has already given what he promised.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Abraham was 'strengthened in faith': he believed at once and gave glory to God as a benefactor.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Abraham was promised as father of many nations, so the reward of belief is shared by all who believe as he did.
comments.comment: For now, observe that the promise made to Abraham as a reward for his faith, saying that he would be established as the father of many nations, showed two things. He should not be maintained to be the progenitor of only one people, since he was foretold as the father of many nations. Nor did he receive the reward of belief so exclusively that others who believe in the same way should be thought excluded from sharing the reward. ‘But it was not written only for his sake,’ Paul says, ‘that it was reckoned to him, but also for ours, to whom it will be reckoned as we believe in the one who raised Jesus Christ our Lord from the dead, who was handed over because of our offenses and rose because of our justification’ (Romans 4:23–25).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says Abraham's reckoning was written also for us.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Christ raises his own temple, and the Father also raised him.
comments.comment: For the Lord raises up his own temple (John 2:19); and the Father raised him up from the dead, just as he worked all things through the Son, so also this he worked.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Those who see that justification was given them through forgiveness of sins should hold to harmony, since by the Mediator's gift they have entered this grace and may glory in hope.
comments.comment: ‘Therefore, justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we also have access to this grace in which we stand, and we glory in the hope of God’s glory’ (Romans 5:1–2). You who see that justification has been conferred on you through the forgiveness of sins, he says, hold firmly to harmony, and with united minds praise the Mediator’s gifts. By his gift we have been granted entrance into this grace. Those whom justice held guilty—because it was will, not nature, that made us guilty—he restored to freedom and snatched from retribution. He granted that we who expected eternal punishments should now glory in the hope of God’s glory.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what peace with God and access to grace mean for the justified.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Christian teaching lets believers rejoice even now in distress, since affliction trains endurance, and they count refraining from sin as its own reward.
comments.comment: To express more fully the power and assurance of this teaching, he goes on to describe what Christian philosophy confers on believers: ‘And not only that, but we also glory in afflictions, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance proven character, proven character hope; and hope does not put us to shame, because God’s love has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us’ (Romans 5:3–5). That is: these benefits have not merely enabled us to rejoice someday in the abundance of gifts. Even now, placed amid the burning heat of distress, we are cheerful in the possession of virtue itself. We laugh at the fury of persecutors, judging the wicked’s cruelty a training in endurance rather than a disruption of joy. Thus we do not merely refrain from sin because of rewards; we regard refraining from sin as itself a reward.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: The earnest man bears hardship bravely through hope of the crown, as athletes endure blows for the prize, because hope prepares joy in his soul.
comments.comment: For I think that the noble athlete, once he has stripped for the contest of godliness, must bear the blows of his opponents bravely through hope of the glory that comes from the crowns. In athletic contests, those who have trained their bodies in the wrestling schools are not cowed by the pain of a blow, but they go straight at their opponents out of desire for the proclamation, despising the immediate pains. In the same way, for the earnest man, even if something harsh is present, it will not overshadow his joy. For affliction produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope, and hope does not put us to shame (Romans 5:3-5). Therefore elsewhere we have been commanded by the same Apostle to endure in affliction and rejoice in hope. So it is hope that prepares joy to dwell in the soul of the earnest man.
comments.selected_reason: Shows in a plain picture how affliction leads to hope and joy.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Trials make us better and wiser, for affliction produces endurance, testedness and hope, so we gain a soul that is more tested and freed from cowardice even before the resurrection.
comments.comment: Paul therefore gave us no small comfort even before the resurrection: that we become better and more philosophical through trials. That is why he says: “Affliction produces endurance, and endurance produces testedness, and testedness produces hope, and hope does not put to shame” (Romans 5:3-5). And again someone else says: “An untested man is unapproved, and the unapproved man is worthy of no account.” So we reap no small fruit from affliction even before the resurrection: having a soul that is more tested, wiser, and more understanding, and freed from all cowardice.
comments.author: John Chrysostom
comments.work: On the Resurrection of the Dead

comments.capsule: We judge God's promises by the greatness of his love, and our hope will not be refuted because that love, poured out through the Holy Spirit's gifts, guarantees future blessedness.
comments.comment: Then, when we see the promises of the Testaments being fulfilled, we count absolutely all the good and evil things of present life among trifles. We judge the trustworthiness of God’s promise from the greatness of his love toward us. The disappointment of eternal benefits will not refute our hope, because we hold God’s love as a guarantor of future blessedness. It ‘has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us’ (Romans 5:5): that is, through the Holy Spirit’s gifts God has proved his love for the human race.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: The outpouring of the Holy Spirit is his unconstrained and abundant bestowal, so the love of God poured into our hearts is a fruit of the Spirit.
comments.comment: [On God's gift of the Spirit to the Gentiles:] That is to say: the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, as one might say, is the unconstrained and abundant bestowal of Him, the cause of prophecy and renewal and heavenly goods and of understanding the beauty of the divine truth. For as it seems to the apostle: 'the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace' (Galatians 5:22). Therefore he writes again: 'for the love of God has been poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit' (Romans 5:5).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To pour out signifies a bountiful gift and rich provision, as oil poured from its vessel sends out its fragrance to the utmost.
comments.comment: To pour out signifies always, as if it says: 'I will pour out from my Spirit upon all flesh' (Joel 2:28); it signifies a bountiful gift and a rich provision through the word. 'The love of God is poured out in our hearts' (Romans 5:5). And again: 'Your name poured out as oil'. The poured out oil goes out from the containing vessel and sends out its fragrance to the utmost.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by love being 'poured out' in our hearts.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ's love stands at an unmatched height because others who die for a good cause are helped by the worth of the cause, while Christ died for the ungodly, so we may despair of nothing from his generosity.
comments.comment: Lest examples like these [of people who died for great causes] obscure the uniqueness of Christ’s virtue, the apostle added something to show that Christ’s love and courage stand at an unmatched height. I too agree that some people, though rarely and scarcely, have chosen to die for just and good causes. But the worthiness of their affairs—that is, the nobility of the causes for which they fought—softened the pain of their dangers. Christ, however, had nothing to love in the activities of the ungodly, and did not disdain to expend himself for those made ugly by their own will. Plainly he excels everyone’s virtues: even if he can have a few companions in endurance, he can have none in the cause for which he endured. Let us therefore despair of nothing from his generosity. If he died for us while we were still sinners, much more, now justified in his blood, shall we be saved through him from wrath (Romans 5:8–9).
comments.selected_reason: Shows how Paul's words set Christ's death apart from the noblest human sacrifice.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Boasting in God rests on his love, shown when the Son came and died in the flesh to triumph over Satan, remove sin and the curse of Adam, and bring human nature back to what it was in the beginning.
comments.comment: “Not only that, but we also boast in God” (Romans 5:11). Our Lord Jesus Christ, making plain the truly admirable love of God the Father which he showed toward us, brought forward as proof the goal of his work in the flesh and his suffering on the cross, saying somewhere: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:16). For he truly gave his own Son for us; and we have been redeemed, set free from death and sin. For the Word “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14) for no other reason than this: that by enduring the death of the flesh he might triumph over the rulers and authorities (Colossians 2:15) and destroy “the one who has the power of death, that is,” Satan (Hebrews 2:14); that he might do away with corruption and, with it, remove the sin that had tyrannized over us; and that he might thus make powerless from then on that ancient curse which human nature underwent in Adam, as in the firstfruits of the race and as in its first root. For Adam, by transgressing the commandment, offended his Creator; that is why he became both accursed and subject to death. But the Master of all took pity again on those who were utterly lost. For the Son came down from heaven, forgiving offences, justifying the ungodly by faith (Romans 4:5), and, as God, reforging human nature into incorruption and bringing it back to what it was in the beginning.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why believers boast in God: his love shown in the Son's saving death.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Death slipped in through sin in the first man and then overran the whole race, because all became imitators of Adam's transgression and came under the same penalties.
comments.comment: So he [Paul] says: “As through one man sin entered the world, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men, because all sinned” (Romans 5:12). For, as I said, death slipped in through sin in the first-formed man, at the beginning of the race; then it overran the whole race in turn. Moreover the dragon, the inventor of sin, having prevailed in Adam by the ways of wickedness, made the human mind a road he could tread: “For all have turned aside, together they have become worthless” (Psalm 14:3; Romans 3:12). So, having gone out from the presence of the all-holy God, because the human mind is intently set “on evil from youth” (Genesis 8:21), we lived a life more like that of brute beasts. And “death, having grown strong, swallowed up,” as the prophet says (Isaiah 25:8), and “Hades enlarged its appetite and opened its mouth without ceasing” (Isaiah 5:14). For since we became imitators of the transgression in Adam, in that all sinned, we came under the same penalties as he did.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a clear account of how death spread to all through sin.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Sin has grown with us from our first origin, for through one man it entered the world and is passed on through childbirth, more fittingly said of the mother though it also comes through the father.
comments.comment: This is a request for pardon, because sin has grown together with us from our first origin, passed on to us from the mothers who conceive us (Psalm 51:5). For “through one man sin entered the world” (Romans 5:12), and evil was rooted in the first woman, and from her it passes through childbirth to those who are born. This is said more fittingly of the mother, even though sin also comes through the father, because we are brought forth from the father in seed, but from mothers completely, and we come into the light through childbirth.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Paul traces sinners back to the first man, who led the way in wrongdoing, to humble Jewish pride, and death passed to descendants by imitation, not generation.
comments.comment: ‘Therefore, just as through one man sin entered this world, and death through sin, and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned’ (Romans 5:12). To tame the Jews’ pride—they thought they needed forgiveness of sins less than the Gentiles did, claiming holiness for their race through the law’s privilege—he attacks the disease of human conduct and traces the multitude of sinners backward. The authority of antiquity itself would thus reveal how great a dominion wickedness had seized in this world. He would show how many long-established crimes Christ’s grace had removed: crimes passed from the indecency of predecessors to descendants through the hands of mutual imitation. For this reason he recalls the first man, not as the one with whom sin began—it is established that the woman sinned first—but as the one who, through the privilege of his sex, had assumed leadership in wrongdoing. Through him, then, sin entered, and through sin death—undoubtedly the death foretold for sinners, namely eternal death. ‘And so,’ he says, ‘death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned.’ He has made perfectly clear how this death passed to descendants: by imitation, not generation.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: 'In whom all sinned' means 'because all sinned', as 'in what does a young man correct his way' means 'how', so death passed on in the fact that all sinned by their own will.
comments.comment: For after saying, ‘It passed into all human beings,’ he immediately added, ‘in whom all sinned’ (Romans 5:12). This phrase, ‘in whom all sinned,’ indicates nothing other than ‘because all sinned,’ in accordance with David’s words: ‘In what does a young man correct his way?’ … That is, ‘How does he correct his way?’ ‘By keeping your words’ (Psalm 119:9; LXX/Vulgate 118:9). He is thus said to be corrected ‘in’ that through which he is corrected. Likewise, the apostle said death passed on ‘in’ the fact that all sinned by their own will. The phrase ‘in whom’ should not be taken to indicate either Adam or sin; it should be understood as expressing the fact that all sinned.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the phrase 'in whom all sinned' from the usage of Scripture.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Sin entered through one man who was seen to be guilty, and death passed to later people because the same judgment covers all who imitate his transgression.
comments.comment: According to the apostle, then, sin entered this world through one man, and death through sin, because the world saw that man guilty and destined for condemnation to everlasting death (Romans 5:12). Death passed into all human beings because the same form of judgment encompasses transgressors in later ages too. Yet this death is not permitted to rage against any holy or innocent people: it invades those whom it finds imitating the transgression …
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: By naming and counting one man, Paul shows that what is accused is imitation, not generation, which cannot take place except through two.
