comments.comment: The apostle showed that he was not saying sin passed on by generation when, naming a human being, he added ‘one.’ One is the beginning of number. Explaining through whom he said sin had entered, he not only named him but also counted him: ‘Through one man sin entered this world’ (Romans 5:12). This one person is sufficient to supply an example for imitation but insufficient to accomplish generation. Sin passed on, but through one. Clearly, then, what is accused here is imitation, not generation, which cannot take place except through two.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Sin was imputed to people before Moses, because the natural law, by which we tell the better from the worse, already existed.
comments.comment:
Having foretold that upon the sin of Adam and upon the decree of death all the rest sinned (Romans 5:12), he confirms that they sinned from what he adds; for until law, sin was in the world. For do not think, he says, that sin was not until the law of Moses, nor was sin imputed to men; for it was indeed imputed, since law also was.

What then law does he show? The natural one, according to which we move, distinguishing the better and the worse, concerning which law he already spoke; for when Gentiles, not having the law, do the things of the law by nature, these, not having the law, are a law to themselves. Thus also before the Mosaic law was the law of nature.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Death passed to all because all sinned, but it seized only those who persist in their sins, and that is why Paul speaks of the many.
comments.comment:
This seems to have the opposite to the aforementioned, that death passed to all men (Romans 5:12); for having spoken earlier concerning all, now he speaks concerning many (Rom 5:15).

But it must be known that death passed to all because all have sinned, but it passed to all while searching and testing, seizing not those who sin simply, but those who persist in their own sins, which he makes clear by saying the following: that many were made sinners, through which the unchangeable nature of their wickedness is shown. Thus death passed to all searching, seeing them sin, but it killed not all.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Sin held sway as long as the law stood, since the law exposed and charged transgression, but now that the law is inactive the charge has ceased, and death will cease with sin.
comments.comment: “For until the law sin was in the world” (Romans 5:13). The law given through Moses was, as I said, an exposure of the weakness of those who stumble, not a release from sin; rather, it brought about wrath (Romans 4:15). For those who transgressed had to come under the penalties set down in the law; and wherever there is any form of transgression at all, there sin surely is too. And if sin brings about death, we must surely say that the death which sprang from it shares its strength, and that when sin is pulled down death is shaken down with it and perishes together with it, as with its own mother. So, he says, sin was in the world until the law: for while the law still stood, the charges of transgression held firm against those who stumbled; but now that it has become inactive, the indictment for transgressing has ceased along with it. And once sin has ceased, as I said, death too will cease with it.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Transgressions existed before the law, and the law showed more of them than people had thought.
comments.comment: Having said so that grace might abound, he showed that even before the law there were transgressions, and men knew they were stumbling (Rom 5:13-14). Not indeed all things which they stumbled in, but he perceived them as stumbles; rather, the law being given, it stripped bare and showed more things to be existing than they used to consider.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Paul distinguishes sin from transgression, since those between Adam and Moses sinned without a written law, and transgression adds to the odium of sin.
comments.comment: ‘For until the law, sin was in this world; but sin was not imputed when there was no law. Yet death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is a figure of the one to come’ (Romans 5:13–14). Through different terms he distinguishes kinds of sin, showing that sin is one thing and transgression another. At least in this passage, he intends every transgression to be regarded as sin, but not every sin as transgression. The term ‘transgression’ increases the odium of sin, so that those who crossed a command appear more guilty than those who sinned without the law’s warning by disregarding their inborn reason. Therefore, before the law given through Moses and committed to writing—whose enactment prescribed a pattern of conduct that people living under it were not permitted to ignore—the apostle accuses mortals stained with various forms of corrupt activity of sin, not transgression: those living in the interval between Adam and Moses.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul separates sin from transgression in these verses.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Death reigned from Adam over those who broke the law of nature, and Adam is a type of Christ because death was distributed to all from him as life is distributed to all from Christ.
comments.comment: But as being sinners and living as aliens, death reigned from Adam until the setting of the law, and over those not having sinned, nor having transgressed a commandment of God according to Adam, but having violated the law of nature. And 'who is a type of the one to come,' that is, a type of Christ—Adam—is not according to the sin or the righteousness—for contrary to these things he held—but according to the preceding; for just as from Adam death was distributed to all, so from Christ life was distributed to all.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Adam is also a type of Christ because, as Adam is head of Eve, Christ is head of the church, whose bridegroom he is.
comments.comment: And there is a type also according to another reason; for just as Adam was the head of Eve according to being a man, so also Christ is the head of the church according to which he is proclaimed her bridegroom, as also the apostle says: 'for this reason a man shall leave his father and his mother and shall be joined to his wife' (Gen 2:24). This mystery is great (Eph 5:32), but I speak concerning Christ and the church.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Christ is called 'the one to come' because, though foreordained by the Father, he appeared at his own proper time, at the end of the age.
comments.comment: How, then, does he call him “the one to come” (Romans 5:14)? someone might perhaps ask. For having set before us the first man and recalled the times of the transgression, he named Christ the one who would be present after those times, and the last Adam (1 Corinthians 15:45). He had indeed been foreordained as Saviour and Redeemer in the will and forethought of God the Father, but he appeared at his own proper times, those the Sovereign willed (1 Timothy 6:15); and these are the times at the end, at the sunset, as it were, of the present age.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul calls Christ 'the one to come'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Death reigned even before the law because the whole race that came from Adam came under corruption in his likeness, as shoots wither when a plant is harmed at its root.
comments.comment: “Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses,” and so on (Romans 5:14). But if so, someone might ask, how did death gain the mastery over those on earth even before the law? For even if some were not liable for transgressions of the law, since the law had not yet been given, they too still came under corruption after the likeness of Adam's transgression. It is as if he were saying: death overran the whole race that came from Adam, in the likeness of Adam; just as, when a plant has been harmed at its root, the shoots that grew from it must all wither. Yet he says that Adam is a type of the one who was to come (Romans 5:14), that is, of Christ …
comments.selected_reason: Explains how death reigned over people who had not been given the law.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who sinned under the law sinned in the likeness of Adam's transgression, since Adam too received a law, while those between Adam and Moses sinned without such a law.
comments.comment: The apostle’s words, ‘But death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression’ (Romans 5:14), make his meaning shine through. He defines Jews who sin under the law as having transgressed like Adam. For the first man too had received a law, though delivered to his ears rather than in books: to abstain from tasting the tree, which tested obedience. By eating from it against the command, he incurred the crime of transgression (Genesis 2:16–17; Genesis 3:6). Thus the people who sinned after the law was given through Moses’ ministry are proved to have sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, because, like him, they sinned by transgressing a law. But in the age between the two laws—the first given but not written, the second both promulgated and committed to writing—those who sinned are not shown to be free from sin. Rather, they are said to have erred without the likeness of Adam’s transgression, because they had not received a law (Genesis 3:6).
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Adam is a figure of Christ by contrast, one a model of sin and the other of righteousness, though Christ was the greatest and not the first model of righteousness.
comments.comment: Adam is called a figure of the one to come, that is, Christ (Romans 5:14), but a figure by contrast: as the former is understood as a model of sin, so the latter is a model of righteousness. Yet Christ’s incarnation was not the first model of righteousness but the greatest. Even before the Word became flesh, virtues shone in the prophets and many other holy people through their faith in God (John 1:14). When the fullness of time arrived, however, the exact standard of righteousness shone out in Christ (Galatians 4:4). The one foretold as ‘Father of the age to come’ stood forth as the rewarder both of the saints who preceded him and of those who followed (Isaiah 9:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains in what sense Adam is a figure of Christ.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: The divine word speaks of Adam not so much of one man as of the whole race, so that the curse of Adam is common to all.
comments.comment: For “in Adam,” as the word says, “all die” (1 Corinthians 15:22), and they were condemned “in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Romans 5:14), the divine word saying these things not so much of one particular man as of the whole race. Indeed, in the sequence of what is said as though of one man, the curse of Adam is common to all (Genesis 3:17–19); and as for what is said against the woman, there is no woman of whom it is not said (Genesis 3:16).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: As we were condemned in Adam and come to life in Christ, the grace of God must rise above the trespass, since the Creator will not let death prevail through one man while life through one man accomplishes nothing.
comments.comment: So, having made the second correspond to the type of the first, he all but questions his hearer, speaking the next words with a pause, as a question: “But is it not so with the free gift as with the trespass?” (Romans 5:15). It is as if he were saying: We were condemned to death through the transgression in Adam, since the whole of human nature suffered this in him, for he was the firstfruits of the race; but in Christ we blossomed again into life. And Adam was a type of the one to come (Romans 5:14), that is, of Christ, who brings in for us a grace equal in measure to the perversity of those who went before. Have I, then, he says, missed the truth in saying this? Am I carried beyond what is reasonable? Is it not so with the free gift as with the trespass? Or did death prevail through one, while life through one will be powerless? And yet how is it not true to say this: “For if by the trespass of the one the many died, much more have the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abounded for the many” (Romans 5:15)? For the Creator, since he loves mankind, will by no means allow death to prevail through the one, and the life that comes through one man to accomplish nothing. Grace will rise above what comes from wrath.
comments.selected_reason: Shows why Paul says the free gift is not merely like the trespass but greater.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul declared that the Savior's grace works more effectively, and for more people, than Adam's sin works against it.
comments.comment: The apostle, whose meaning we are disputing, certainly declared that the Savior’s grace works more effectively and abundantly to confer salvation than Adam’s sin works against it. He thus showed that Christ helped far more powerfully, and helped more people—his grace, to use the apostle’s own expression, ‘abounded to more people’—than were harmed by the first man’s transgression, which you say bound sin into human seed.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: The gift of the Lord was greater than Adam's one sin, because it freed people from many transgressions and also led them into righteousness.
comments.comment: He strives, however, to show that even if the evil one fashioned the transgression of Adam, discussing for himself the beginning of the kingship over men, the Lord, having granted a greater gift, bestowed grace. … For he wants to say that Adam's sin was one, but nevertheless, being one from one sin, he condemned the many because of imitating Adam, but the gift of the Lord was not measured against the one sin, but against the many things existing of all. Thus, having freed them from many transgressions, he led them into righteousness; for in this is the abundance of grace, that he not only freed from the transgressions, but also led into righteousness.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Since condemnation passed from the first Adam to all, it is fitting that justification in Christ, the second Adam, should reach many.
comments.comment: “And the gift is not as it was through the one who sinned” (Romans 5:16). He refers, as it were, the nature of the matter and the force of the thought to what most befits God. For if, he says, the condemnation that came from one, that is, through one, Adam, passed on to all after his likeness (for, as I said, he was the root of the race and suffered corruption), how could it not be both acceptable to faith and dear to God that many should be justified from many trespasses by one act of righteousness (Romans 5:16)? Or is saving not what God prefers to destroying? Just as, then, Adam was condemned, and the power of the curse prevailed over Moses, making those on earth subject to corruption, so, since Christ, the second Adam, has been justified, justification will surely travel to us as well along the same road as the first. We say that Christ has been justified, not as though he had once been unrighteous and then advanced to justification by progress toward better things, but because he himself, first and alone of men on earth, “committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul names one sin of Adam to stay true to the history, and adds 'from many offenses' to commend the generosity and abundance of grace.
comments.comment: Wisely, therefore, when speaking of Adam, he named one sin, which he intended to be understood as a model of transgression. He mentioned one, I repeat, and not many, because he knew that only one sin of Adam is recorded in the law’s history. But he praised grace for sending those it initiates out into justification from many offenses, to prevent any suspicion of a meager benefit. If he had said, ‘Grace is from one offense to justification,’ it might have seemed to abolish individual sins rather than all sins. Thus, by first mentioning one sin he remained faithful to the history; by adding, ‘Grace is from many offenses to justification,’ he commended the sacrament’s generosity and abundance (Romans 5:16).
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Grace is poured in once and wipes away many crimes in one action, so Paul sets 'one' and 'many' side by side only to praise grace.
comments.comment: Grace, however, is not conferred in the same way, repeatedly applied to each sin individually. Instead, poured in once, it wipes away many different crimes in a single concentrated action of its power. That is why he says, ‘From many offenses to justification’ (Romans 5:16): it leads human beings freed from many offenses to the glory of justification bestowed on them. … He uses the numbers one and many solely to praise grace: grace need not be repeated as often as each mortal person has sinned, as though individual baptisms could heal only individual sins.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul sets 'one' against 'many' in speaking of grace.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Paul counts the grace that justifies stronger than the curse that condemns.
comments.comment: “For if, by the trespass of the one, death reigned through the one,” and so on (Romans 5:17). See again how he reckons the grace that justifies stronger than the curse that condemns.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who receive Christ's grace will shake off death and reign with him.
comments.comment: For much more will those who have the grace that comes through Christ and the gift of righteousness from the bounty above shake off the power of death and reign together with Christ, who gives life to all things (Romans 5:17).
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what believers gain in Christ beyond what was lost in Adam.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Death reigns through one who was a model of sin, and those who receive abundant grace reign in life through one, so no one is driven to death unless he has embraced the sinner's example.
comments.comment: ‘For if through one man’s offense death reigned through one, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one Jesus Christ’ (Romans 5:17). He consistently confirms what he began. He has set down two statements, intending what he added at the end to apply to both. He declares that death reigns through one who was a model of sin, and in whose likeness those who sin under the law transgress. He also declares that those who have obtained abundant grace reign in life through one—a grace which benefits those who imitate virtue. No question about the ‘one’ therefore remains. The added statement that those who receive abundant grace reign in life also resolves the first statement: no one is driven to death unless he has embraced the sinner’s example.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Adam's transgression, which was disobedience, condemned and killed men, but the righteous act gave them life.
comments.comment: Having examined and having stripped bare both the harm through Adam which was pressed upon men and the benefit bestowed by the Lord (Rom 5:18), he proceeds then teaching more decisively, that the transgression of Adam condemned and killed men, but the righteous act gave life. And what is the transgression of Adam? Disobedience.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: By setting 'all' on both sides, Paul sends us to scriptural usage, in which 'all' is commonly said for 'many'.
comments.comment: What the apostle added—‘As through one man’s offense it came upon all to condemnation, so through one man’s righteousness it came upon all human beings to justification’ (Romans 5:18)—gives us as much support as it brings crashing destruction on your doctrine. By placing ‘all’ on opposite sides, in statements that cannot be combined, he sends us back to scriptural usage, so that we understand that ‘all’ is commonly said for ‘many.’ For on the surface of the words there is a great incongruity. Who are the ‘all’ who come to justification if all have gone to condemnation? Or who are the ‘all’ who go to punishment if all are swept into glory? Making one side universal excludes the other.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: The righteousness of the Lord is the obedience he showed the Father in becoming man and suffering for men, and this obedience removed Adam's disobedience.
comments.comment: But what is the righteousness of the Lord? It is the obedience which he obeyed to the Father, according to the becoming-man and suffering on behalf of men, just as the apostle says in other places: having been found in form as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient even unto death, even the death of a cross. Thus, obedience removed the disobedience and, regarding the best thing, it overcame the worst.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Paul concludes that we were condemned in Adam and death passed into all who sprang from him, but we have been justified and sprouted again into life because Christ was justified on our behalf.
comments.comment: “Therefore, as through one trespass there came condemnation for all people,” and so on (Romans 5:18). To the thoughts already set out the inspired Paul adds, as it were, the conclusion, saying, “Therefore, as through one trespass,” and what follows. For we were condemned in Adam, as I said before, and death, which came from the curse, passed as from the first root into all that sprang from it. But we have been justified and have sprouted again into life, since Christ was justified on our behalf. For our forefather disregarded the commandment given to him, offended God, and underwent what comes from divine wrath, for he slid into corruption. Then sin also burst into human nature; and so the many were made sinners (Romans 5:19), that is, those throughout the whole earth.
comments.selected_reason: Gives the plain sense of Paul's conclusion about Adam and Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Human nature, condemned through the first man's disobedience, had to rise again by a full showing of obedience, so God sent his Son to take a body like ours and justify human nature in himself.
comments.comment: So since human nature was condemned by the sentence of death through the first-formed one’s disobedience, it had to rise again toward its original blamelessness by making a full showing of obedience. But this was already much and far beyond humanity’s measures — for no one is clean from sins… So the God and Father, summing up all things in Christ (Ephesians 1:10)… “sent forth his Son, born from a woman,” (Galatians 4:4) so that taking a body like ours and making it his own, he might be found as a human on earth not knowing sin, and thus having become wholly obedient to God the Father, justify human nature in himself and free it from death’s bonds …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: We became sinners through Adam not by sinning with him but because his disobedience brought corruption and passion into human nature, which we share, and Christ has set that nature free by his obedience.
comments.comment:
But someone might say: Yes, Adam slipped, and because he disregarded the divine commandment he was condemned to corruption and death. But then how were the many made sinners because of him? What are his failings to us? And how at all were we, who had not yet been born, condemned along with him? And this although God says, “Fathers shall not die for their children” (Deuteronomy 24:16), nor children for their fathers; “the soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezekiel 18:20). What, then, would be the way of our defence? Certainly, “the soul that sins, it shall die”; but we became sinners through Adam's disobedience in the following way.

He had been made for incorruption and life, and in the paradise of delight he lived a life fit for the holy. His mind was wholly and constantly taken up with the vision of God, and his body was in calm and stillness, with every shameful pleasure at rest, for there was no tumult of unruly impulses in him. But when he fell under sin and slid into corruption, from then on pleasures and impurities rushed into the nature of the flesh, and the law that rages in our members sprang up (Romans 7:23). So nature caught the sickness of sin through the disobedience of the one, that is, Adam. In this way the many were made sinners (Romans 5:19): not as having transgressed together with Adam, for they did not yet exist at all, but as being of his nature, which fell under the law of sin.

Just as, then, human nature fell sick with corruption in Adam through disobedience, and so the passions slipped into it, so it has been set free again in Christ; for he became obedient to God the Father (Philippians 2:8) and committed no sin (1 Peter 2:22).
comments.selected_reason: Answers the natural question how many were made sinners by one man's disobedience.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A man had to conquer death for us, so the Word became man, that what came under death through transgression might overcome it through obedience, and as we were condemned in Adam we might be justified in Christ.
comments.comment: For it was needful, truly needful, he says, that a man should conquer death for us. For this reason God the Word, who shone forth from God, did not take hold of angels, as Paul himself says, but of the seed of Abraham, so that he might be made like his brothers in every way (Hebrews 2:16–17). For, as I said, what had fallen sick had to be healed, and what had fallen had to rise. What had come under death through transgression and sin had to overcome death through obedience and righteousness. That is why the Only-begotten Word of God, who knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21), became man: so that, as in Adam we have all been condemned, when human nature suffered death, so also, justified in Christ, we might strip off, together with sin, the death that sprang from it. The inspired Paul himself will bear witness, saying, “For as by the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners” (Romans 5:19).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Just as no one earns virtue's rewards without imitating Christ, no one is held a transgressor in Adam unless he has sinned in imitation of the first man.
comments.comment: He untangled the whole argument by saying: ‘For just as through one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so through one man’s obedience many will be made righteous’ (Romans 5:19). Thus, just as no one earns virtue’s rewards unless, after Christ’s incarnation, he strives toward them by imitating Christ’s holiness, so no one is held as a transgressor in Adam unless he has sinned in imitation of the first man, transgressing the law through which knowledge of sin came (allusion to Romans 3:20).
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: In Paul's words 'many' signifies all, both those who disobey and those who obey, so there is no contradiction.
comments.comment: And the apostle writes this: 'just as through the obedience of one man many will be made righteous, so also through the disobedience of one man many will be made sinners' (Rom 5:19). And here 'all' are signified by the 'many': all those who disobey, all those who obey. It is not a contradiction.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Grace abounded where sin abounded, among the Jews, from whom came the apostles and Christ.
comments.comment: And accurately he said that which entered in: for between the disobedience of Adam and the arrival of the Savior, the law took a passage into life. And where sin abounded, grace super-abounded (Rom 5:20). Where then did sin abound? Where the law was. And if the law was among the Jews, there also grace super-abounded; for from there came evangelists and apostles and the head of salvation, Christ.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Paul raises the objection that, since Adam was a type of Christ, the justification in Christ should have come with nothing in between.
comments.comment: “The law came in, so that the trespass might increase” (Romans 5:20). Someone, he says, will reasonably argue along these lines and say: Adam “was a type of the one to come” (Romans 5:14), and just as we were made sinners in him through the transgression, so in Christ we have been justified through obedience. Then, he says, the justification in Christ should have appeared to those on earth with nothing coming in between.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The law came in to prove the weakness of all, so that people would see their need of the healing that comes through Christ alone, and grace had to be great enough to surpass the law that condemns.
comments.comment:
What need, then, was there, as a matter of necessity, for the laws given through Moses? Against such thoughts the inspired Paul all but rises up again, saying, “The law came in, so that the trespass might increase” (Romans 5:20). The words “came in” mean that the law was brought in between the condemnation in Adam and the righteousness in Christ. And if one asks again what need there was for the law’s coming in, he will hear Paul say plainly, “So that the trespass might increase.” What are you saying, Paul? Was the law, then, also a promoter of sin, and has the trespass multiplied through it? By no means.

We must, then, open out more fully the way this sacred teaching works. David said, accordingly, “All have turned aside, together they have become worthless; there was none who did good, there was not even one” (Psalm 14:3). For after the transgression in Adam all who were on the earth had corrupted their way (Genesis 6:12). That is why they were punished: all of them together underwent a common penalty, the flood, and they were also punished in particular ways, at certain times and in certain lands and cities. For even though there was no law, human nature was still being trained by God, through its inborn impulses, toward the knowledge of what is good.

So God took pity on those on earth, who were faring wretchedly, and in his love of goodness he planned to set them free in Christ from the sin that tyrannized them. But he judged, and very rightly, that those on earth must first be shown to be gravely sick, so that the justification in Christ might then be seen to make its entry into the world as something most needed. For we say that it is not the one already righteous who is justified, but whoever is liable for sins. How, then, were those on earth to be shown beforehand as needing the grace that is in Christ? “The law came in, so that the trespass might increase” (Romans 5:20); that is, so that among those under the law the trespass might appear great, since plainly no one could be justified because of the weakness of nature, and all, as it were, fell under the charges that arise from transgression. The law, then, was laid down as a kind of proof of the weakness of all, so that human affairs might be seen to need the healing that comes through Christ alone. That is why he says, “But where sin increased, grace overflowed all the more” (Romans 5:20). For grace had to be so great that it would be seen to surpass the law that condemns.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the law came in so that the trespass might increase.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: However many your sins, grace increased all the more, if you accept it.
comments.comment: If your sins are many, do not be discouraged by their number. For where sin increased, grace increased all the more (Romans 5:20), if you accept the grace. The one who owes much will have much forgiven, so that he may love more (Luke 7:47).
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Sin abounded after the law because the same evil will that sinned before the law now also transgressed a command, adding the weight of transgression.
comments.comment: In this sense, then, the offense is rightly said to have abounded: each person’s will committed it both before and after the law, but before the law the will was sinful, while after the law it was also transgressive. Something grows and abounds when it gains increase within its own kind, just as after Moses the additional weight of transgression was added to the sin of free will.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Paul rejects the idea of staying in sin so that grace may abound.
comments.comment: What then shall we say? It says, shall we remain in sin so that grace might abound? (Rom 6:1) May it never be! He safely led to the 'may it never be'; for not those sinning unskillfully are worthy of forgiveness, but those receiving the methods of the devil through laziness and inattentiveness—these are deserving to be pitied by God.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Paul foresees people claiming that abundant mercy means they should persist in sin, and he answers that those baptized into Christ's death must walk in newness of life.
comments.comment: As he proceeds, the apostle explains himself more clearly. He teaches that, when human salvation was being lost, God, moved by the abundance of his compassion, brought a medicine more effective than usual to a desperate situation. Those whom he had not corrected by commands he would bind to himself by benefits, requiring devotion for the future while not imputing past deeds. People should then strive to preserve the righteousness they had obtained by the direct path of belief. The abundance of preceding sins therefore called for the help of such abundant mercy: unless the forgiver’s generosity had been so great, no other discipline could have helped diseases so serious. But in commending this divine benefit, the apostle saw room for an objection from people who might say: ‘If we rightly assess the worth of causes by their effects, and the abundance of sins obtained an outpouring of God’s mercy, we should persist in sins so that grace’s abundance does not fail.’ Anticipating such an opinion, he says: ‘What, then, shall we say? Shall we remain in sin so that grace may abound? Far from it! For we who died to sin, how shall we still live in it? Or do you not know that all of us baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were therefore buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose in the Father’s glory, we too might walk in newness of life’ (Romans 6:4).
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: We die to sin, not in the flesh, by making sin idle in us through putting to death our earthly members.
comments.comment: Christ died according to the flesh, so that he might undo the sin of the world. We, however, do not die according to the flesh—how could we?—but to sin, as it is written (Romans 6:2); that is, we render sin idle and ineffective in ourselves by putting to death “the members that are on the earth: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and greed” (Colossians 3:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'dead to sin' means in practice.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Baptism is our confession that we have died to the world and to sin.
comments.comment: Since we died to sin, how shall we live in it any longer? (Rom 6:2) Because being baptized we confess to have died to the world and to separate ourselves from sin and the devil (Rom 6:4).
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Paul can say baptized into Christ because naming the Son also names the Father and the Spirit, who are in him.
comments.comment: “Or do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus…?” (Romans 6:3). As all agree, we have been baptized into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19). Yet if he should say that we have been baptized into Christ Jesus, he will not be speaking beyond what is reasonable. It is quite true that by names, by hypostases [the distinct persons], and by the differences of the persons, the Father stands apart from the Son in a certain particular otherness, and the Spirit from both. For the Father is the Father and not the Son; again, the one who is from him by nature is the Son and not the Father; and the Holy Spirit is, in his own proper way, the Spirit. But since the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son (John 14:10), and the Holy Spirit is in both because the substance is the same, then even if someone names only one, by the force of the ideas involved, …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul names Christ because he must name the one who suffered, yet naming him does not leave out the Father or the Spirit.
comments.comment: So the one who names Christ will not leave the Father or the Spirit unremembered. But since Jesus, having become man, endured death for the life of all, the blessed Paul had to go on to what was most needful for the sacred teaching at hand, for he had to name the one who suffered. That is why he says, “All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death” (Romans 6:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says baptized into Christ and into his death.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: In baptism we die to sin with Christ and are buried with him, so that we may rise with him spiritually, which means living in righteousness.
comments.comment: For having first given, as it were, the good pledge of an upright conscience toward Christ (1 Peter 3:21), and having accepted by faith that he died for us, was buried, and came to life again, we have received the forgiveness of sins through holy baptism. We undergo the deadening of sin, and as it were die together with him who died for us, by putting to death our members that are on the earth (Colossians 3:5). For Christ “died to sin once for all, but the life he lives, he lives to God” (Romans 6:10). We undergo a death equal to his and are all but buried with him, carrying about his dying in our own bodies (2 Corinthians 4:10); and we were buried with Christ (Romans 6:4). What we gain from this he will make clear himself, saying, “so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:4). For since we have been buried with him, we must also rise with him spiritually. And if being buried with Christ is having died to sin, then surely it is clear that rising with him can rightly be understood as nothing other than living in righteousness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what being buried and raised with Christ means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Baptism is a confession of dying to the world and sin, and living in newness is a fresh life with the old cast off.
comments.comment: Since being baptized we confess to have died to the world (Ro 6:3) and to separate ourselves from sin and the devil. To live in newness is to begin a certain new and fresh life, having cast off the old, the one in sins; for the rebirth of a certain kind of life and a new citizenship is promised (Ro 6:4).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Christ is said to be raised through the Father's glory because Christ ascribes what exceeds human nature to the glory of the supreme nature, not because he lacked strength.
comments.comment: He affirms, indeed, that Christ was raised through the glory of the Father, not as though Christ lacked strength, for he himself is the Lord of hosts (Psalm 24:10), but because it is the custom of Christ himself and of his own to ascribe what is beyond human nature to the glory of the supreme nature. So even if God the Father is said to accomplish something, he does not shut the Son out of his activity over all things. For if all things came into being through him (John 1:3), how could anyone doubt that he worked through the Son the resurrection of that holy body as well? Indeed the Son, showing himself active in this, said to the Jews, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). See, then, how he promises to raise his own temple himself, although God the Father is said to have raised it. For since he is himself the life-giving power of God the Father, he gave life to his own temple.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the wording raised through the glory of the Father.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: As human nature fell sick in Adam, so we are raised with Christ and the power of the ancient curse is broken.
comments.comment:
…just as in Adam too, when he came under the curse, the whole of human nature fell sick with that curse.

So too we are said to have been raised with Christ and to be seated with him in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6).

For even though Emmanuel is above us as God, yet since he became like us as one of us, he has been raised and sits beside God the Father.

So our old self was crucified with him (Romans 6:6), for through the resurrection the power of that ancient curse has been broken.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those buried with Christ should expect to rise with him, though we are united with the likeness of his death and not with his death in the flesh.
comments.comment: “For if we have been united with the likeness of his death,” and so on (Romans 6:5). The inspired Paul says that those who have been buried with Christ ought also to expect to rise with him. The word “united” would suggest, in a spiritual sense, something like “conformed” and “of the same form.” But this point must be examined closely. Emmanuel laid down his own life for us (1 John 3:16) and died according to the flesh. In what way, then, have we who are baptized been buried with him? Was it by enduring with him the death of the flesh? Not at all. How, then, have we been united with the likeness of his death? …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those baptized are united to Christ through faith, as grafted things grow into one.
comments.comment: Precisely the grafted-together has established this; for of those grafted-together, nature often becomes one through adhesion. Thus also those having been sincerely baptized into the death of Christ are united to him through faith (Rom 6:5).
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Being united with the likeness of Christ's death means that, as he died for the world's sin, we shall share his form in the resurrection.
comments.comment: We have been united, then, not merely with Christ’s death according to the flesh, but with the likeness of his death. And this would be understood as dying for sin, and not for his own sin—far from it! For God is blameless and utterly far from being able to do wrong. Rather, as I said, it was for the sin of the world: “For the death he died to sin, he died once for all” (Romans 6:10). So we have been united with him in the likeness of his death (Romans 6:5). And we shall certainly be united with him and share the same form in his resurrection as well, for we shall live in Christ. The flesh will come back to life, and we shall also live in another way, having dedicated our own souls to him and being transformed toward holiness and into a glorious way of life in the Holy Spirit.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The old self and body of sin mean the earthly body, condemned in Adam and sick with love of pleasure, which the Only-begotten took on.
comments.comment:
“Knowing this, that our old self…,” and so on (Romans 6:6). Who is our old self, what is the body of sin that is done away with, and in what way was it crucified with Christ? We must look into this closely. …

By “body of sin” and “our old self,” then, he means the earthly body, which, from the old condition in Adam, must waste away into corruption; for we were condemned in him, the first man. Besides this, it is also sick with the love of pleasure, for that is how the flesh is by nature, because of its inborn impulses. How, then, was it crucified with Christ? The Only-begotten became man and clothed himself with the earthly flesh, which, as I said, had fallen sick with death because of the old condition in Adam, and which carried within itself, as if in labour, the tendency to be sharpened toward sin by its inborn impulses.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the old self and the body of sin are.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's flesh was no different in nature from ours, so when it was crucified we were crucified with him.
comments.comment: Yet the law of sin lies still in the holy and all-pure flesh of Christ. We certainly do not say that the more unseemly of the human passions were stirred in him, except those whose movement is blameless—I mean hunger and thirst and weariness, and whatever else the law of nature has kept free of blame even in us. Still, even though the law of sin was not stirred in Christ, because it was lulled to sleep by the power and working of the Word who carried out the dispensation, yet when the nature of the flesh is examined by itself, even if it is considered as it is in Christ, we shall find that it is no different from ours. So we were crucified with him when his flesh was crucified, flesh that held, as it were, the whole nature within itself; …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The body of sin done away with is the inborn savagery of the impulses, not the flesh itself, and it was condemned in Christ's flesh first and then for us.
comments.comment:
The body of sin has also been done away with (Romans 6:6). This does not mean the flesh itself, but the inborn savagery of the impulses within it, which always drags the mind down toward what is more shameful and sinks it, as it were, into the mud and marshes of earthier pleasures.

That this too has been accomplished for human nature in Christ, who could doubt, when Paul says plainly, “For what was impossible for the law, in that it was weak through the flesh, God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh” (Romans 8:3)?

Do you see, then, how the body of sin has been done away with? For the sting of sin has been condemned in the flesh. It was put to death first in Christ, and the grace has passed from him and through him to us as well.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the body of sin done away with means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those living by the old man have a body of sin, while those living by the new, Christ, have a body of righteousness and are set free from sin.
comments.comment: Those living according to the old man have a body of sin, lying in wait for the devil for ambushes; but those according to the new, our Lord Jesus, a body of righteousness, since they also are members of the Lord (Ro 6:6–7). Surely, the evil one, having been cast out and those willing are being set free, because he was making men sin, having been defeated through Christ and by the cross the flesh of the Word having been crucified; for the one having died according to the word of baptism, died to the world and has been justified and has been removed from punishment, being freed from sin (Ro 6:6-7).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Since Christ died only once and there is no second baptism, we who were buried and raised with him should not run back to old habits of sin.
comments.comment: If it were possible, he says, for Christ to die for the sinners a second and third time, perhaps it would have been harmless to run back to the old habit of sins, which always had a hope of philanthropy. But if, having died once, he no longer dies, so also we, having been buried with him and having been raised, no longer die to sins (Romans 6:9); for there is no second baptism, nor a second death of Christ, for which reason it is more secure to live.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: As Christ died to sin once and lives to God, so we who reckon ourselves dead to sin should live and serve virtues alone.
comments.comment: …knowing that Christ, raised from the dead, dies no more; death will no longer rule over him. For the death he died to sin, he died once, but the life he lives, he lives to God. So you too reckon yourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus’ (Romans 6:11). Just as Christ, he says, died to sin once—that is, died because of our sins once—and dies no more, but lives in God’s glory, so you too, reckoning yourselves dead to sin, should live and serve virtues alone.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the parallel between Christ's death to sin and ours.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Christ died to sin in that he died for the sin of the world.
comments.comment: Yet “He died to sin once for all” (Romans 6:10), that is, for the sin of the world, for He has been set forth as a propitiation through faith (Romans 3:25); “but the life He lives, He lives to God” (Romans 6:10).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ lives to God forever, so we too die to sins and live to God, and the sin that reigned before baptism is forgiven by grace, which the law could not do.
comments.comment:
…but he who lives, lives to God, that is, to live forever, since he is God. In this way, therefore, you also die to your sins, but live to God, through whom you live (Romans 6:11). Do not let your members be presented as weapons of unrighteousness to sin, instead of you not giving weapons to the evil one and strength by sinning yourselves (Romans 6:11). For sin shall not rule over you; for you are not under law but under grace (Rom 6:14).

What sin shall not rule? The one before baptism, which the grace of Christ forgives. But the law was not able to do this. …
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Paul urges the baptized to long for the grace that comes through faith, so that sin may not reign in their members, and to leave the shadow of the law.
comments.comment:
Everywhere he shows that to seek to be under the law is dangerous.

He urges us rather to long for, and with our whole mind to thirst after, the grace that comes through faith, that is, justification in Christ. He firmly declared that the baptized have been buried with Christ (Romans 6:4), so that, having been put to death to sin, they might live to God in righteousness (Romans 6:11).

That is why he said, “So do not let sin reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its desires. Do not present your members to sin as weapons of unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as alive from the dead, and your members to God as weapons of righteousness. For sin will no longer have dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace” (Romans 6:12–14).

See, then, how he commands them to leave the shadow of the law (Hebrews 10:1) and instead to take shelter under the grace that is in Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: That Paul tells them not to let sin reign shows he means sins of will, since natural evils could not be avoided by admonition.
comments.comment: ‘Therefore,’ he says, ‘do not let sin reign in your mortal body so that you obey it’ (Romans 6:12). I could already say here that the exhortation proves he is treating sins of will. For if evils were natural, they could be defended on grounds of justice or, at least, lamented out of pity; but in no way could people be admonished to avoid them. Greater than any natural evil, if such an evil could exist, would be the evil of the madness possessing anyone who demanded devotion in avoiding natural things. But the apostle enacted nothing that could justly be criticized. He therefore indicates a sin of will when he insists that it must be avoided.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul can command that sin not reign.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Because grace has lifted the weight of guilt, those once ruled by sin should serve God more faithfully and gratefully.
comments.comment: ‘Do not present your members as weapons of injustice to sin, but present yourselves to God as people alive from the dead, and your members as weapons of righteousness to God. For sin does not rule over you: you are not under law but under grace’ (Romans 6:13–14). You should, he says, serve God more faithfully because you do so more freely. Sin ruled over you when punishment for guilt hung over you. But after you received the benefits of God’s grace and breathed freely with the weight of your guilt laid down, a free person’s sense of honor should prompt you to show gratitude to your healer.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why freedom under grace calls for greater service.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Sin no longer masters us because the Law, which gave sin its power by condemning sinners, no longer holds us, as we are under grace.
comments.comment: For the sting of death has been destroyed, since sin has been taken away and no longer has the Law as its power. For the Law condemns those who sin; that is why the inspired Paul says that the Law is the power of sin. But this too has been undone in Christ: for sin will not be master over us, because we are not under the Law but under grace (Romans 6:14); and apart from the Law sin is dead (Romans 7:8).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Some might say that people freed from the law may safely sin under grace, and Paul answers that we are slaves of whomever we obey, whether sin or righteousness.
comments.comment: But this gave occasion for the same question he had explained above: someone might object that people freed from the law, which threatened wrath, could safely sin under the kindness of God’s grace. He therefore immediately added: ‘What then? Shall we sin because we are not under law but under grace? Far from it! Or do you not know that when you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one you obey, whether of sin or of obedience to righteousness?’ (Romans 6:16). Do we now believe him about the kind of sin he has been discussing? When you present yourselves, he says, as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of that one, whether of sin or righteousness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why grace is no licence to sin.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Paul holds back greater things because of fleshly weakness.
comments.comment: I am able, he says, to say something more excellent and greater, worthy of surpassing benefit, but I say this much, being weak in the flesh (Rom 6:19).
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Paul says free from righteousness but could not say freed, a word used only of being delivered from evil.
comments.comment: The apostle says: “When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness” (Romans 6:20). He certainly could not have said “freed”. The language of liberation is fittingly and properly used when a person is freed from harmful things. Those who resolve to owe nothing to the virtues, however, can be called free from virtues. A person can therefore be called free either from good or from evil when, serving one, he aims to owe nothing to the other. But a person can be called freed only from evil, because the word “liberation” contains a sign of the distress that is driven away. What difficulty, then, could be raised here about the apostle's words when, following ordinary human usage, he called them free from good and freed from evil?
comments.selected_reason: Explains the wording 'free from righteousness'.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Sinners are supplied by the devil, trading away self-control and kindness for intemperance and coarseness and so giving themselves to death.
comments.comment: Those who sin are being provisioned by the devil in this way: selling up self-control and buying intemperance, selling kindness and seizing coarseness. Those, therefore, having become the own property as it were of sin, submit themselves to death; for the wages of sin is death (Rom 6:23). Or perhaps he says this, that the things being provisioned from the enemy are the things of death (Rom 6:23).
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: The law holds sway only over the living, since a person who has left the body has put off its authority.
comments.comment:
For laws define, for all who live under the sceptres of kings, what must be done and what must not; but they have force only among those who are still alive.

If someone who is under law departs from life in the body, he has put off, together with his life, the authority of the laws as well. For if he has ceased from wrongdoing, the law too will surely have nothing more to do with him.

It is true, then, that the law has dominion over a person for as long as he lives (Romans 7:1).
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why the law has dominion only as long as a person lives.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul foresaw the objection that the fathers under the law had strayed, so he seems to speak for them while turning the argument toward faith.
comments.comment:
Yet the Spirit-bearer was well aware that some would surely say, or at least reason to themselves, that in that case the fathers had strayed from the straight road and from life, that the law had done them no good, and that the glories of their way of life had somehow already come to nothing.

For if it is absurd to seek to be under the law, and this was the aim of life for the people of old, how could it not be true to say that they missed what was fitting?

So he who has Christ within him takes up the contest. He skilfully gives the impression that he wishes to speak on behalf of those who lived under the law, but in many ways he turns the argument toward the view that, when the time calls to faith, one must not be too eager to linger over the ancient customs.

This is why he says, “Or do you not know, brothers, for I am speaking to those who know the law, that the law has dominion over a person for as long as he lives?” (Romans 7:1).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God, who gave laws and fixed penalties, knew that people live with a free mind, so the law's dominion over the living does not make the mind subject to others.
comments.comment:
Either let our opponents say that God did not know this; or, if they have chosen to think rightly and are deeply afraid to pour ignorance over his ineffable glory, they say that he gave laws, and indeed they will plainly confess that he fixed the penalties for wrongdoers. Then surely he knows that man lives with a free mind and is able to move by voluntary inclination toward whatever he wishes, with nothing to hinder him.

That is why the inspired Paul said that the law has dominion over a person for as long as he lives (Romans 7:1). He does not say such things, then, as though the human mind were subject to the nod of others.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: If Fate ruled us, the law that has dominion over the living would be pointless and the Lawgiver could not justly punish those compelled to sin.
comments.comment:
If someone should insist on it, and choose to think that Paul has assigned to Fate and Fortune the authority over our affairs, how could one not rightly put this question to the apostle: “If we are caught in harsh and unyielding necessities and are in no way masters of what we do or leave undone, but rather yield to others as our rulers and are kept from acting by our own judgment, how did you yourself write to us, ‘Or do you not know, brothers (for I am speaking to those who know the law), that the law has dominion over a person for as long as he lives?’ (Romans 7:1)”

So the law has dominion over the living in a certain way. For it will surely be idle among the dead; it does not set its bounds for them (how could it?), but for those who still spend their life in the body. It crowns with praise the one who habitually does well, and it votes punishment against the profane. How then will the Lawgiver be a holy judge, if he punishes as sinners those whom Fortune compelled to fall into sin against their will? Or rather, why did he lay down the law at all?

For those who have it in their power to do whatever they wish, the law sets a holy penalty if, when they could have won approval by giving their mind to good deeds, they have themselves preferred the more shameful things and exchanged the better for what the law condemns. But for those who have the yoke of necessity hanging over them, and who always turn whichever way their rulers please, the decree is, I think, superfluous.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: While the law prevailed before Christ no one could be bound to another, but now that the law has in a way died, the remnant can be joined to the heavenly Bridegroom.
comments.comment: From this he constructs, that while the law was prevailing before Christ, it was not permitted for another to be bound, that is, to be bound to grace; but when the law has ceased and in a way has died, it is possible for the remnant to be joined to the heavenly Bridegroom (Rom 7:1–3). For he places both the law and Christ in the domain of a man; the one for the church, since just as the man is head of the woman, so Christ is of the church, and the law once of the assembly (Rom 7:1–3). The law, he says, rules over the man for as long as he lives. Who lives? The law. And just as it discourses about a man and his cohabitant, so it is about him (Rom 7:1–3).
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Those who lived before Christ were under the law as the living are, like a wife bound to her husband, but those who died to sin in Christ have died to the law and may live outside it without blame.
comments.comment:
We must also say what the aim of the passage is. He brings two useful points into it.

We, he says, who have been buried with Christ through baptism (Romans 6:4), who have died to sin (Romans 6:2), have passed outside the authority of the law, for we have been remade for another life.

But those who lived before his coming, not yet having undergone the death that is understood in Christ, were still living to sin.

So the law ruled over them as over the living, just as a husband rules over his wife.

For as a married woman, while the man lawfully joined to her is still alive, cannot unite with another man without answering for it, yet if he dies, he says, she will be free of penalty even if she chooses to do this, since she does it lawfully (Romans 7:2–3), in the same way, I think, those who did not yet have the deadening of sin in Christ, but were living, as it were, in sin, were rightly under law as well; for the law has dominion over a person for as long as he lives.

But those who have already come under the grace that is in Christ, through which they have died to sin and been put to death to the flesh, that is, to the passions of the flesh, may lead a life outside the law without blame, if they are no longer reckoned as people living in the world (Colossians 2:20).

For, as I said, they have been put to death through the body of Christ, and they died to the law (Romans 7:4), being justified through faith.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's marriage illustration and what it means to die to the law.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To be put to death to the law is to leave its worship and belong to Christ, following his gospel decrees, chief of which is faith in him.
comments.comment: “So, my brothers, you also were put to death to the law through the body of Christ, so that you might belong to another, the one raised from the dead, in order that we might bear fruit for God.” (Romans 7:4) We are put to death to the law by leaving its worship; we belong to another, the one raised from the dead — that is, to Christ — eager to follow his gospel decrees, so that we may bear fruit for God. The chief of the gospel decrees is faith toward him, and this fruit of ours is offered to Christ as to God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in a few plain words what dying to the law means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Those buried with Christ are dead to sin, so the law that was decreed because of sin ceases to act, and they serve in the newness of the Spirit.
comments.comment:
What then does Paul say? He speaks to those who have been buried with Christ through baptism (Romans 6:4) as to people who are dead to sin, and as to people already rich in the deadening of the passions. It would be fitting for them to go outside the law, since they have been freed from the passions that the law condemned.

So, he says, while we still remained in the mind of the flesh, the passions that the law denounced and named were at work in us; and at that time we were also answerable to the law, because sin was still alive in us.

“But now we have been released from the law, having died to that in which we were held captive” (Romans 7:6).

We were liable to the law, he says, because sin had made us subject to it. But if we have died to that in which we were held captive, that is, to sin, then the law too will surely cease to act, together with sin; for the law was decreed because of sin, to convict those who transgress.

So those who have been put to death to sin no longer need the law. For we have come to belong to another (Romans 7:4), and let us serve him in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the letter (Romans 7:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why believers are released from the law.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The passions of the flesh were not stirred by the law but arise from inborn pleasure, and they even rise up against the will of the law.
comments.comment:
“For while we were in the flesh, the passions of sins, which were through the law, were at work,” and so on (Romans 7:5).

By “flesh” he means the fleshly mind, as he says elsewhere too: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God” (Romans 8:8).

And yet who would deny that he gives such instructions to those he was initiating into the mystery as to people who had not left the body?

What he means to show must be examined closely.

When we lived in a fleshly way, he says, and the earthly mind ruled in us, then the passions of the flesh were at work in us through the law, to bear fruit for death (Romans 7:5).

“What then?” someone might say. “Were the passions of the flesh brought in through the law? Then how shall we clear the law of the charges against it?”

What do we say to this? The passions of the flesh were not stirred in us through the law. Rather, they are born from inborn pleasure and they plunder the weak mind.

He makes this plain to us when he says, “The flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to each other” (Galatians 5:17).

Here, leaving this aside, he says that the flesh is set in battle against the Spirit, with nothing placed between them.

So the passions of the flesh are not stirred in us through the law, but rather by nature; and, strange to say, they rise up against the will of the law …
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the passions were at work through the law without the law causing them.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Giving a pretext to the passions was not the purpose of the law, which was heavy and could not accomplish what it intended or prevent what it did not want.
comments.comment: It was not the law that provided the stumbling, the one standing against not sinning, but through forgiving the pleasure by the sufferings (Ro 7:5). So, to provide a pretext for the sufferings was not the purpose of the law, but what was happening was the economy [God's plan of salvation] that was to be given then. I say indeed that eating and drinking was active in our members—for desire also moves even in those fasting—but it is not active unto bearing fruit for death. Thus a ministry of death has been written by Moses, since the law was heavy, and what he intended was not accomplished, and what he did not want was not prevented (Ro 7:5).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Scripture can call the devil flesh, law, sin and death, so Paul's phrase attacks not our own flesh but the flesh that shares the name, from which baptism has set us free.
comments.comment: Just as divine Scripture knows how to call people by their actions—fleshly, soulish, spiritual, and countless other names—so too it knows how to call the devil not only Satan, the Adversary, the devil, the serpent, the lion, and Beliar, but also flesh, law, sin, and death. For we were enslaved to these through disobedience, and not to Christ. That is why Paul says, “When we were in the flesh” (Romans 7:5), making clear that they are no longer in the flesh, even though they are in the flesh—so he is not slandering the flesh we wear, but the flesh that bears the same name, from which we have been set free because we died in Christ by being buried with him through baptism.
comments.author: Eusebius of Emesa

comments.capsule: Paul said through the law, not from the law, because the law did not provide for sinning but, by giving indulgence, gave the passions a pretext.
comments.comment: For when we were in the flesh, he says, instead of being in the law; for those in law were giving indulgence to the flesh (Rom 7:5). He spoke accurately, 'through the law', not 'from the law'; for the law did not provide for sinning, even though it commanded not to sin (Rom 7:7). He said therefore 'through the law', because by forgiving, it gave indulgence to the passions as a pretext, so that the law was constructing not what it wanted, but what it did not want (Rom 7:7). But the sin, he says, I did not know except through law (Rom 7:7).
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Paul says we are truly released from the flesh and the law that held us, and then begins an assumed voice that runs from the question about the law to the cry of the wretched man.
comments.comment: We have truly been set free from this flesh. For Paul goes on to say, “But now we have been released from the law of sin, having died to that which held us captive, so that we serve in newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the letter” (Romans 7:6). Then he began again the assumed voice by way of hypothesis, starting from “What then shall we say? Is the law sin? By no means!” (Romans 7:7) up to “Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?” (Romans 7:24).
comments.author: Eusebius of Emesa

comments.capsule: Paul denies that the law is the source of sin: he would not have known sin except through the law, which points sin out so that people may turn to better things.
comments.comment:
“What then shall we say? Is the law sin?” (Romans 7:7).

See how wisely he frames what he says about the law. He had said, “When we were in the flesh, the passions of sins, which were through the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death” (Romans 7:5).

But that statement would by no means have been free from suspicion. Someone would at once have replied, “Is the law, then, the director and author of sin? For if it is true that the passions of the flesh are at work in us through the law, how could it not be thought the very origin of sin?”

What, then, does the teacher of the mysteries do? He meets the objection sharply. He denies that the law is the father of sin, and instead lays the blame on human nature, as weak and, through the law, falling under penalties.

This is why he says, “What then shall we say? Is the law sin? By no means! Yet I would not have known sin except through the law” (Romans 7:7).

Notice his sober care. He did not say, “I would not have had sin except through the law,” but rather that he would not have known it.

So the law is not the occasion of sin, but rather points it out, making it plain to those who did not know it. It does this not so that, having learned of it, they might commit it, for even before they knew it they were surely committing it anyway, “for there was none righteous, not even one,” as the Psalmist says (Psalm 14:3; Romans 3:10), but so that, knowing what is wrong, they might turn to better things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says he would not have known sin except through the law.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The law is not sin but only shows it, as a light that reveals what lies in the road does travellers the greatest good.
comments.comment:
[The law is compared to a light set up at a crossroads to show travellers what lies in their path:] Did the light, then, do them wrong because it showed them what was hurting them? Or shall we say instead that it did them the greatest possible good and made them safer? This, I think, is clear to everyone.

So when we, who were sinners and stumbled into a great many offenses, came to know sin through the law, the law could not reasonably be thought or called sin, far from it. Rather, as I said, it is what points sin out.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The law, given for our benefit, became an occasion of desire for the weak because people desire what is forbidden, so the blame lies on our weakness and not on the law.
comments.comment:
“For I would not have known covetous desire if the law had not said, ‘You shall not covet.’ But sin, seizing an occasion through the commandment, produced in me every kind of covetous desire” (Romans 7:7–8; Exodus 20:17). Here he also brings in the weakness of our nature: the law, given for our benefit, turned against us when no one expected it, as the light of the sun does to those whose eyes are weak. So when he says that the commandment in a way became an occasion for desires, let no one suppose that he is accusing the law. He is rather crying out against the weakness in us, since we, who ought to have been held back by the law, are spurred on by these very things toward what is worse.

For the human mind is always sick with a love of empty things that draws it toward desires. The one who carries out his desires lives as he pleases and is left untroubled; but the one who checks them meets a fiercer onslaught of the passions. No one desires what lies ready to hand; what a person is forbidden, that he desires. So when the law forbade what does harm, it became for the weaker an occasion to desire that very thing all the more.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how a good commandment became an occasion for covetous desire.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The law is the cause not of sin but of discerning it, and since peoples differ on what is lawful, the giving of the law is needed to define right and wrong actions.
comments.comment: "I did not do it except through the law," he said, but he did not know, so that the law is the cause not of doing, but of discerning sin. Therefore the law is a pedagogue, not permitting through ignorance a fall into the nature of the irrational. However, that must be sought: how having said this here, he did not know the sin except through the law, while in other places he shows that we have within ourselves the faculty of discernment, in which he says: for when the nations, not having the law, do by nature the things of the law, these, not having the law, are a law to themselves. Through these things he establishes that even without law, the necessary things were being observed. But let it be considered, that even if they were, it was not all things. In this same way even now there are some things among other nations that are lived as good and lawful, among others as lawless and ill-treated. Therefore the giving of the law is necessary, defining for us both the practical things and the non-practical, and dividing for us and illuminating the life of the righteous.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: The law is not bad: it made sin known but could not turn it away, which showed sin's greatness so that the excess of grace could be shown.
comments.comment: Not bad, he says, is the law, nor sin, but to make known the sin, while not having the power to turn it away, it provided an opportunity for it (Ro 7:7–8). But why this, he says? Showing the greatness of sin, so that he might demonstrate the excess of grace. Thus, he says, sin was strong, because through the forbidding things it rather prevailed and more strongly exerted itself; just as a flame, having begun, they extinguish whatever it touches, but once it has spread further, they pour more and more extinguishing water, so the law reproved sin, having held it over the whole inhabited world and having watched over all, but it was not able to extinguish it. Because it is not even able to condemn the one who has sinned in ignorance, the law, having been given and having shown the sin, gave power to the sin.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Sin is dead when no law condemns it, because the law provokes evil into strength, and where nothing resists, the urge to contend lies idle.
comments.comment: “For apart from the law sin is dead” (Romans 7:8). If no law were laid down, he says, to condemn the way of wickedness, evil would become powerless. For through the law it is all but provoked into strength. In some people the sting of pleasure will press with less force when no one rebukes it; it is all but blunted, charmed by the wide freedom it is given. For where there is nothing at all to resist, there the urge to contend surely lies idle as well. Sin, then, is dead when the law does not declare what must be done.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by sin being dead apart from the law.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul calls the devil sin, as Scripture calls the Savior life, since the devil turned the commandments into material for his art, and Paul indicates the common man through himself.
comments.comment: It seems the devil says "sin" (Rom 7:8). Just as the Scripture calls the Savior "life" and calls him the cause of life and righteousness, so also he calls the opposite power, through its own energy, sometimes sin, sometimes falsehood, sometimes death; so also having said the following: "sin lived," he names the devil sin. Taking its starting point through the commandment. How then did the devil take a starting point through the commandment? Because having made the commands of the law like a certain material for his own art, he turned the man toward the opposite of the commandments. And it is clear that through himself the apostle indicates the common man.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus
