comments.capsule: Paul speaks of himself as living without the law and dying when the commandment came, but sinning with knowledge brings a heavier punishment than sinning in ignorance.
comments.comment: The guide into the mysteries says that he once lived without the law, and then, when the commandment came, he insists that sin came back to life, while he himself died (Romans 7:9–10). In these words he frames the argument in his own person, but I think he wishes to show something like this. It is agreed that even sinning in ignorance is liable to judgment. But that the punishment will be heavier for those who know, the Savior has made fully certain when he says, “The one who knows his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten with many blows; but the one who does not know and does not do it will be beaten with few” (Luke 12:47–48). It is agreed, then, that it is better to sin in ignorance than with knowledge of the laws.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Sin was as if dead when no law condemned it, but when the commandment came into the open it came back to life, and penalty was made ready for those who fall in weakness.
comments.comment: For if sin is truly dead apart from the law, is it not reasonable to think that sin is in a way brought to life through the law? For the law makes it manifest and, as it were, puts breath into it, though it was not known before, even if it was in us. For we were not righteous; but since sin was, as it were, dead, perhaps because there was no law to condemn it, we lived, and our ignorance gave us a ready plea for excuse. “For where there is no law, there is no transgression either,” as he himself says (Romans 4:15). So when the commandment came forward into the open, sin, as it were, came back to life, and death and curse and penalty were made ready for those who fall into transgressions out of weakness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how sin came back to life when the commandment came.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: When the commandment came, knowledge came with it, so sin gained strength and the man is judged according to knowledge, since without the law sin could not be sin or condemn to death.
comments.comment:
So understand this for me, he says, lest the law had been placed first, as now it is not possible for those who are still infants to understand, and there is no condemnation there (Rom 7,10); for ignorance is not subject to punishment.

After these things, behold the commandment coming; there sin is astonished against us, the knowledge having come and the anger no longer dismissing itself against those things happening.

In this way, sin indeed lives, gaining power and strength, but the man dies, being judged according to knowledge, and the command of the law, which gives life, stands around as a pretext for death; for without it, it is not possible for sin to be sin, nor to condemn man with death, because of this, the guilt of wickedness and the penalty of punishment are established.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Sin lived again when Adam, having received the commandment, was deceived, whereas the law was given to discipline those about to do right and not to prevent sin.
comments.comment:
He says, "But when the commandment came, sin lived, and I died" (Rom 7:9–11). If it lived, it is clear that, having died, it lived again. When then did it live? When having received the commandment, Adam was deceived by the perilous transgression and the devil accused him. … Since therefore there was neither a commandment nor a law in between, sin was dead through the ignorance of those sinning; for the most part they were ignorant while stumbling, so that they were not even judged by the conscience.

What then is the result of these things? It is not that the law was given to prevent sin, but rather that those about to do right were being disciplined. Yet it is absurd for the slothful and pleasure-loving to undermine the hypothesis of salvation which belongs to the diligent and earnest.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: The commandment given for life led to death through human sickness and not through any fault in it, as sunlight harms sick eyes, so that sin took occasion from it and deceived.
comments.comment: And what came of this? Something beyond all hope and expectation happened in our case. For the commandment, he says, which was given for life, was found to lead to death (Romans 7:10). Just as the light of the sun’s ray somehow harms those whose sight is sick, though by nature it is sweet and greatly longed for, and it is not the light itself at all that does the wrong, but the harm they receive from it should rather be laid to the charge of the sufferers’ sickness, so in the same way, I think, he says that the commandment gave sin an occasion, and that he was deceived through it and brought down even to death (Romans 7:11).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how a commandment meant for life ended in death.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Because the love of pleasure fights against the law's purposes, sin took occasion from the commandment and in effect killed by sharpening the pleasures within us to resist.
comments.comment: One might also put it another way: the love of pleasure is always very prone, in one way or another, to fight against the purposes of the law. The ways of wickedness, when they are checked by decency, march out against it the more stoutly. At times they plunder the mind, overturning it into transgression and bringing it under the penalties of the law, though it was the law that gave them the occasion for this war. This is why Paul, wise as he is, says that he was deceived through the commandment and died through it (Romans 7:11). For in effect it killed, by sharpening the pleasures within us to resist, in the ways already described.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul calls the devil sin, the first inventor of sin, who used the commandment given to Adam to deceive him with a greater promise.
comments.comment:
Let me now attempt to speak briefly, in passing, about the very words spoken in an assumed voice, beginning from: "But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me" (Romans 7:11). The name "sin" does not indicate an existing substance, but rather a manner and way of life in which someone has missed the mark of what is reasonable and correct. For "sin" is a most general name, predicated of many different things. Every sin comes about neither by reason nor by a commanding law. For if it came about according to law and right reason, it would no longer be a sin, since it would have a defined and ordered principle of origin. But since the divine apostle does not mention mere sins, but a most general sin that has a mind, that has a law, that is able to deceive and to procure opportunities for the preparation of evil, he is not naming anyone else as sin in the most general sense except the originator and father of sins himself, the devil. For this reason the apostle also declared that he reigns over sins: "Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body" (Romans 6:12). For just as we call people by the craft they practice, so also he calls the devil himself "sin," since he was the first inventor of sin.

So then, through the commandment given to Adam he deceived the man, and through it he deceived Adam, procuring opportunities through the commandment. This is what he said: "Why did God say, 'You shall not eat from every tree in the garden'?" (Genesis 3:1). "And on the day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil" (Genesis 3:5). He deceives them by hiding the deception under a greater promise. He promises more, so that he might cast down the keepers of the commandment from the foundations of virtue by a fall like his own. For having goaded the man to want to become equal to God, he procured the opportunity for his deceitful conversation from the commandment that had been given. This is why Paul said, "But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me" (Romans 7:11).
comments.author: Eusebius of Emesa

comments.capsule: The law is holy because it makes holy those who keep it, but keeping it was in some way beyond reach, for who can understand his offenses?
comments.comment: “So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good” (Romans 7:12). The law is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good, for it makes holy and just and good those who choose to keep it, so that they may in no way be caught by the charges that arise from transgressions. But this was, in some way, beyond reach; for “who will understand his offenses?” as it is written (Psalm 19:12).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul calls the law holy and just and good.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The law is holy because it calls its hearers to the knowledge of God and, read spiritually, its types proclaim Christ, the true Holy of Holies.
comments.comment: For the law also is holy: it calls its hearers to the knowledge of him who is God by nature, plants in them an understanding of righteousness, and carries those it instructs on to the beginnings of goodness. ‘For the beginning of a good way,’ it says, ‘is to do what is right’ (Proverbs 16:7, Septuagint). And the inspired Paul writes somewhere: ‘So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good’ (Romans 7:12). The law is holy of holies, not in its shadow, but because, if it is turned to spiritual contemplation, its types proclaim aloud to us Christ himself, who is truly the Holy of Holies.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The commandment is holy, righteous in judging transgressors, and good in favoring those who keep it.
comments.comment: Regarding Romans 7:12, he speaks of the Mosaic law, but of the commandment given to Adam in Paradise, he teaches it as holy as is fitting, just as he teaches it as righteous because it rightly brings a verdict upon transgressors, and as good because it makes life favorable to those guarding it.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: By law Paul means the law that admonishes beforehand and punishes sinners, not the law warring against the law of our mind, and so he calls it holy and just and good.
comments.comment:
He set down an unshakable foundation in his prologue, making his defense by saying: “What then? Is the law sin? By no means!” and that “the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good” (Romans 7:12).

Here by “law” he does not mean the law warring against the law of our mind, but the law that admonishes beforehand, the law that punishes those who sin. That is why he voted with it as holy and just and good.
comments.author: Eusebius of Emesa

comments.capsule: Because the devil called sin is not sin by substance, which admits no more or less, Paul can say that sin becomes sinful beyond measure.
comments.comment: But so that no one would blame the commandment or the God who gave it, he used a neighboring and kindred word, saying: "We know that the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good" (Romans 7:12). Since sin itself—that is, the devil—is not sin by nature or substance, he brings in the next statement: "so that sin might become sinful beyond measure through the commandment" (Romans 7:13). For what exists as a substance will not admit the more and the less; it is what it is, always being what it is in its substance.
comments.author: Eusebius of Emesa

comments.capsule: A good law is not evil because sin is harmed through it, just as the sun is not evil because gazing at it harms the eyes.
comments.comment: But if they should say: How could the commandment and the law be good and just? How could they be holy, when through the occasion they provided sin became sinful beyond measure? Let them hear in response that it is not the case that if something is harmed, the occasion through which it is harmed is already base and evil. For it is not because those who gaze at the sun immoderately and without measure are harmed in their eyes that we call the sun evil; nor is it because the devil became sinful beyond measure by having plotted against the Son of God that we say the Son of God is base and evil.
comments.selected_reason: Answers how a good law can be the occasion of sin, with the example of the sun.
comments.author: Eusebius of Emesa

comments.capsule: The law indicts the devil's wickedness, who through the good law brought death, and Paul's calling sin sinful shows he means the devil.
comments.comment: Regarding Romans 7:13, he says the law is an indictment of the devil's wickedness; but he said the law was good. Thus the evil one appears to be a skilled evil-doer when, through the good which was given, he has brought death to those receiving the good law. Regarding 'sin is sinful', he says; now it has most clearly shown that he was calling the devil sin, and now has named him a sinner; for the one who makes sin is a sinner.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Because those under the law cannot plead ignorance, their sin is reckless folly and not innocent error, which is how sin becomes sinful beyond measure.
comments.comment:
How, and in what way? If penalty always follows those who break the law, and we have now sunk so far into weakness that we are always being caught in transgressions, it is already fairly plain that in this way the law that saves, holy and good as it is, seems somehow to have become the sinews of sin and a road to death for those who are under sin.

And perhaps, he says, it was “so that sin might become sinful beyond measure through the commandment” (Romans 7:13). Those who did not know what the Master wills will certainly be caught by penalties, for they have acted lawlessly, even if they did not know it. Yet they have, I think, a plea in their defense that is not unconvincing, for they will likely put forward their ignorance. But for those under the law, to say that they did not know the Master’s will is surely empty. So if such a person is seen to have chosen to live an unholy life, the charge against him will be not ignorance but reckless folly, and, beyond that, the utmost lack of love for God. In this way sin might be called sinful beyond measure. For the one who has done wrong as in ignorance is also a sinner, but he is by no means called, nor is he, a sinner beyond measure.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by sin becoming sinful beyond measure.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul answers that the good law did not bring death, for in saying so he accuses sin, not the law.
comments.comment: “Did that which is good, then, become death to me?” (Romans 7:13). The law is holy, and the commandment too is holy and good. How, then, did he say, “And the commandment meant for life was found, for me, to lead to death” (Romans 7:10)? Tell me, then: has the good become the bringer of ruin? “By no means,” he says (Romans 7:13). “In these words I am least of all blaming the law; I stand, as it were, as the accuser of sin. …
comments.selected_reason: Answers whether the good law became death: Paul blames sin, not the law.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The law is spiritual because keeping it made a person spiritual and because the Holy Spirit's energy lay behind its giving.
comments.comment: Regarding Romans 7:14, 'likewise it is said the law is spiritual'; for the commandments contained therein, having been kept, made the man spiritual, or also because, he says, it was legislated by the energy of the Holy Spirit, so that those obeying it might be able to be receptive to the Holy Spirit, having been purified by the pedagogy of the law.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: The law is called spiritual because it makes spiritual those who follow it, just as the Psalm calls the law blameless because it makes people blameless.
comments.comment: “For we know that the law is spiritual” (Romans 7:14). He calls the law spiritual because it makes spiritual those who follow it. And a person is understood to be spiritual who does not live according to the flesh, but has turned rather toward the wish to follow the will of the Spirit. The blessed David also said, “The law of the Lord is blameless, turning souls back; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, making infants wise. The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever and ever” (Psalm 19:7, 9). Just as he says that the law is blameless, because it knows how to make people blameless, and the testimony faithful, because it makes them faithful, and the fear pure, because it makes pure, so you will take it here too that the law is called spiritual because it makes spiritual those who follow it. For even if it is in shadows, it still holds the form of the truth (Romans 2:20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul calls the law spiritual.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Because the law is spiritual and man is of the flesh, the two wills are opposed, so the law is most burdensome to a nature so sick with sin.
comments.comment: What, then, does Paul do? He insists that the law is spiritual, but he blames human nature as gravely sick with sin. And he tries to convince us that, because the law is spiritual, for that very reason it is most burdensome to human nature. For what, tell me, he says, if “the law is spiritual, but I am of the flesh” (Romans 7:14), that is, ruled as by a tyrant by the mind of the flesh? Do you see how great an opposition of wills his words set before us? For the will of the Spirit is one thing, and the will of the flesh must be understood as another. They are opposed to each other (Galatians 5:17), and they cannot possibly come together into one. When, then, man is of the flesh and the law is spiritual, how could the law even be bearable to those so sick with sin?
comments.selected_reason: Explains the contrast between the spiritual law and Paul being of the flesh.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The one who knows the law is spiritual, a statement made of the saints in general, is not himself the flesh sold under sin, for Paul separates himself from such things.
comments.comment: 'We know that the law is spiritual' (Rom 7:14)—we, the perfect, the disciples of the Spirit, those having received the divine and spiritual law. 'But I am flesh, sold under sin' (Rom 7:14). It is not the one knowing that the law is spiritual who is flesh, sold under sin; for he was separating himself from those things. 'We know that the law is spiritual,' he says generally concerning the saints. 'But I am flesh, sold under sin.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul does not teach that Fate rules us, since that would leave no one to blame, so his words about not understanding what he does are no confession of necessity.
comments.comment:
“For what I am doing, I do not understand” (Romans 7:15).

Some of the more ignorant Greeks, as one might expect, suppose that he means to confirm a myth, one which, I do not know how, they have decided to champion, deceiving and being deceived (2 Timothy 3:13). For they invent a Fate and a Fortune to suit their own opinion, then hand control of our affairs to things that do not exist, and so they rob man of what most befits him: I mean that he should live freely, with an unhindered and voluntary inclination toward whatever course of action he chooses.

By subjecting him, as it were, to necessity and to the limits and decrees laid down by those powers, they do no small wrong to those who live this life. For if, on their view, someone goes on to do what is unlawful, since he cannot escape the nod of Fate even if he should wish to, no one in his right mind would blame him at all, even if he were seen doing wrong. What he had to do by necessity and not by choice would surely leave him beyond blame and punishment, if he were caught having done it. And it would not be very sensible to praise the gentle and well-ordered man either. For what if he became such a man not by his own will, but carried into it by another’s nod, or rather because Fortune rose up against him with a necessity he could not fight?

It is therefore wholly out of tune to say that the teacher of the noblest things is swept along with the quibbles of the Greeks, or to think that the one who became steward of the divine mysteries for us trails behind their folly, if he says, “For what I am doing, I do not understand; for I do not practice what I want, but I do what I hate” (Romans 7:15).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul reasons as a philosopher and takes on the part of one still sick with love of the flesh, speaking for the weakness of those not yet like him.
comments.comment:
Rather, he reasons as a philosopher and examines closely the passions of human nature. He all but digs out with precision the sicknesses that reach inward to the mind, and he brings a charge against the body for its inborn love of pleasure, very fittingly taking on himself the part of one who is still sick with love of the flesh.

For though he himself had been crucified to the world, and the world to him (Galatians 6:14), and was truly worthy of admiration, he still thought it wise not to look to his own gift, but to make the weakness of those not yet like him the necessary subject of his discourse.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul speaks as one who is weak though he is not.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Not understanding what one does fits great sinners who take pride in their pleasures, as drunkards do not know what they do, and it shows a disease of the human heart.
comments.comment:
So when you hear him say, “For what I am doing, I do not understand” (Romans 7:15), think of certain exceedingly great sinners who suppose that they are living the truly best life, and that nothing could equal the luxury and the fleeting things of this world. They loathe the ways of decency, but they take pride in their own pleasures and wallow in them without restraint. It is of them, I think, that Paul says, “Those who set their minds on earthly things, whose god is the belly, and whose glory is in their shame” (Philippians 3:19). These people, carrying out what is base as though it were something highly praised, might fittingly say, “For what I am doing, I do not understand.”

Let them hear, then: “Wake up, you drunkards, from your wine” (Joel 1:5). For just as lovers of drink and the drunken, their clear thinking impaired by the passion, would not know what they were doing while they were drunk, so those whose minds have grown sick from love of the flesh and the most shameful pleasures would not know what they are doing at all. So Paul is explaining to us a disease of the human heart when he says, “For what I am doing, I do not understand.”
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Someone with a tender conscience who is grieved at doing wrong yet overpowered by pleasure might say that he does what he hates, as many who admire self-control are overcome.
comments.comment: But suppose there is someone who offers a tenderer heart, as it were, to the reproofs of conscience, who is grieved that he does wrong, yet is still overpowered by the pleasures that lead to sin, and goes toward wrongdoing as if against his will. He might fittingly say, “For I do not practice what I want, but I do what I hate” (Romans 7:15). How many people, how many times, have admired self-control, and even begun the practice of it, and then been overcome by the goads of loathsome pleasure …
comments.selected_reason: Explains who might truthfully say I do what I hate.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul is not accusing himself but writing the common condition of men into himself, for all under law desire virtue yet are defeated by pleasure, but not those under grace.
comments.comment: Regarding Romans 7:15, he says, 'not that I am unaware that sin is sin, but instead I do not perceive how I do it and how I am being stolen away,' such as often, judging I would prevail, I was defeated by myself. It is necessary, however, to know that he is not accusing himself, but is inscribing the common condition of men within himself, declining to place the burden on another; for he shows that we desire virtue, but are defeated by pleasure, all of us who are under law, but certainly not those who are under grace, who even outside of sin have become righteous through grace.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Paul turns to the nature of the body, whose appetites and faults of a pleasure-loving life have their source in the flesh.
comments.comment:
“Now if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law that it is good” (Romans 7:16).

Again he turns the precision of his inquiry to the nature of the body, and examines the power of the sicknesses that are in it by nature. For the appetites that carry us off toward every kind of passion, and the faults of a pleasure-loving life, have their source in the flesh. The Savior’s disciple confirms us in this when he says, “Where do wars and where do quarrels among you come from? Do they not come from here, from your pleasures that wage war in your members?” (James 4:1).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The sin dwelling in us is not the flesh but the devil, who works out the form of evil beforehand in our thoughts while the soul that receives him cooperates.
comments.comment: “But now it is no longer I who work it out, but the sin dwelling in me” (Romans 7:17). Through this saying he made his defense: the flesh is not evil by nature. For it is not the flesh we are clothed in that dwells in us, but the devil who dwells in the lawless. For in the same way that I say Christ dwells in every righteous person who works the good, I think the devil dwells in every evildoer. Therefore we are not wicked insofar as we have flesh, but the sin dwelling in us is—and it is something other than the flesh and the soul of the human being. For the devil is said to make his home especially in the soul, according to “Satan entered into the heart of Judas” (John 13:27), and according to “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart?” (Acts 5:3). And it was well said: “no longer I work it out, but the sin dwelling in me.” For there is a great distance between a work and a working-out, because the working-out precedes the work—as, for example, with a house or a ship: the working-out is the advance preparation of the material. So the sin dwelling in sinners—that is, Satan—admittedly works out beforehand in our thoughts the form of the evil to come, its construction, while the soul that has received him cooperates with him in the wickedness, just as the womb of a woman cooperates with those who sow, so that what is sown may be brought to maturity. … Just as the Holy Spirit is said to labor together with virtue-loving souls, according to “I labored more abundantly than all of them—not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Corinthians 15:10), so when a careless soul is persuaded by the devil's promptings, it has the devil himself as its coworker for evil. For he himself worked out beforehand in the soul the pattern of the sin to come. This is why it is said: “no longer I work it out, but the sin dwelling in me” (Romans 7:17).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by the sin dwelling in him.
comments.author: Eusebius of Emesa

comments.capsule: Paul says nothing good dwells in his flesh in the person of Adam, who lost God within him and fell under the reigning death, a kingdom that has a beginning.
comments.comment: "I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh" (Romans 7:18). Now he interprets this into the person of Adam. And because he was deprived of having God in himself, he exchanged death for true life—for not only did the common death of his members seize him, but also the death of disobedience entered against his soul. For the ruling death reigned especially before the coming of Christ, holding disobedience as the law and scepter of its kingdom over all. But the kingdom of death is not without beginning or unbegotten; for dying comes from the living, and one person's disobedience comes from the obedience of those who obey.
comments.author: Eusebius of Emesa

comments.capsule: If we only will the good but cannot work it out, God sent souls into bodies in vain.
comments.comment: …"For the willing lies beside me, but the working out of the good does not" (Romans 7:18). "For the good I want, this I do not do, but what I hate, this I practice" (Romans 7:19). If the willing alone is in us, and the working out of the good that is willed is not in us, then the good God sent the souls of the same substance as himself into bodies in vain. For what is dear to him and to them they do not do; they do not enact it, but only will it …
comments.author: Eusebius of Emesa

comments.capsule: Willing the good lies close at hand but the power to do it does not, because the flesh forces the mind aside, so the blame falls on what overpowers the mind.
comments.comment: “For willing,” he says, “lies close at hand for me, but accomplishing the good does not,” and so on. To show that the flesh stands accused, since it is in terrible labor with sin within itself, he wisely grants that the good lies close at hand for us, but not also the power to carry it through. For the flesh forces the mind, against its will, to turn aside where it does not wish to go. So as far as the mind’s own choice went, it would be free even of sin. But since it suffers an overpowering that is hard to escape, the blame would rightly belong not so much to the mind as to what overpowers it. That is why he says, “Now if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me” (Romans 7:20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul can will the good and yet not do it.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul, an image of good works, is not speaking of himself in these words but playing a part in an inserted persona to refute those who love sin.
comments.comment: The divine apostle became an unblemished image of good works for his disciples, which is why he cried out, “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1). So what he said is not literally about himself: “I know that nothing good dwells in my flesh” (Romans 7:18), nor “Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?” (Romans 7:24). Rather, he says these things and others like them playing a part in an inserted persona, to refute those who love sin.
comments.author: Eusebius of Emesa

comments.capsule: The upright mind, ashamed of its weakness, cannot throw off the burden of passions, and the law gives no help.
comments.comment: He [Paul] insisted that the mind of the more upright is at times distressed when it is tyrannized by the passions of the flesh, that it is deeply troubled and ashamed of its weakness; yet it has no means at all of throwing off the burden of the sin it does not want, since pleasure falls upon it so fiercely. That is why it is too weak to resist, receiving no help whatever toward this, at least from the law.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: If Paul's words abolished the good in everyone, virtue would never have existed, so the cause of good not coming to be lies in softness of soul and not in the flesh.
comments.comment: But if this is true, I will speak as the impious do: then the good never was and never will be in human life, and no one ever enacted it—if they take the words “the good I want, this I do not do, but what I hate, this I practice” (Romans 7:19) as the abolition of the good and beautiful for every human being. And from where did the names of virtues ever appear in human life? But if there are people who enact the good—even if those who do it are few—will not all of them say, “We know that good does not dwell in us; for the good they wanted, this they practice”? If those who enact the good do so while they are in the flesh, and those who do not do this but do evil are also in the flesh, then the cause of the good not coming to be should not be attached to the flesh, but to their softness of soul. For if evil lies beside those who want to do the good, and likewise the good does not lie beside those who want to do evil, but they deliberate and choose beforehand and only then come to action—are our bodies then evil by nature and substance? For deliberation and willing lead the way before our actions, and these belong to a soul that has a self-determining mind, able to incline toward whatever actions it wishes.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why 'the good I want I do not do' cannot mean that no one does good.
comments.author: Eusebius of Emesa

comments.capsule: Like captives who serve their conquerors by necessity, the mind overpowered by the flesh should not be blamed for the sicknesses of the flesh, even if it holds the reins of its will.
comments.comment:
But someone might say: suppose some wicked barbarians laid waste a city or a country, then took some of its inhabitants as captives of the spear and laid on them the yoke of slavery, and those who suffered this yielded by necessity to the bonds and laws of their masters. Would they deserve blame and indictment because they are not stronger than necessity, and do not strive to carry out what pleases themselves in defiance of the authority of those who have seized power over them? No one, I think, could fairly find fault with them. For they serve as slaves because they cannot be set free, and they yield, as I said, to misfortunes they did not want. They are distressed that they have been robbed of freedom, but, overcome by necessity by those who are stronger, they serve against their will. Now if this is not far from reason, let the human mind be acquitted of any charge over the sicknesses of the flesh.

“But it was in its power,” someone says, “not to choose to do it; for it holds the reins of its own will.” Then let it be stronger than that overpowering and free from the tyranny of sins. But if the nature of the flesh is hard to bear and hard to resist, stirring up untamed pleasure against the mind, and the law is too slow to help (for it does not have the power to put sins to death), no one could justly accuse the mind of failing to do the better thing and let go of the more shameful, even if it does perhaps hold the reins of the will within us.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The law instructs the mind in what is beneficial but cannot put sin to death, so it is a counselor and not a redeemer, whereas Christ's grace both teaches and strengthens.
comments.comment:
“…to do what is good, evil lies close at hand for me” (Romans 7:21). Notice again how wisely and skillfully he approves of the law: not as able to blunt the sting of sin, nor as capable of putting to death the sin within us, but only as instilling into the mind the knowledge of what is beneficial. For if, he says, evil lies close at hand for me as something that dwells in the flesh, the law nonetheless exposes it as counterfeit; it grants its help and is understood as a counselor, but not also as a redeemer.

Yet those who are sick with sin surely need not only to know clearly that they ought to do what is better, but also to be able to accomplish whatever is good and seems right to the law. So too, of course, for those who wish to win distinction in battle, bare knowledge of tactics alone is not enough; only if strength is added to it would such men then, and scarcely then, be brilliant and admired. If, then, the law teaches skill in what is good, but in no way helps those who are overpowered by cutting the sinews of sin, it is good because it is also a teacher; but it could not fairly be counted equal to the grace that comes through Christ, who is able both to make us wise and to make us stronger than evil.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the law can and cannot do for a person sick with sin.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Under the law the common man sees what is necessary with the mind but is turned to the worse, whereas the one who believes in Christ acts with the mind by the Spirit's help.
comments.comment: Regarding Romans 7:21, 'I find the law, there remains the thing that is difficult to do right'; for he says that from which things, even when willing to do something good, I am not able, but I am turned toward the worse. 'I find the law difficult to do right, desiring to do the good'; for the evils, being more ready, lie before me for the doing. And through this 'lie before,' he shows that it is not toilsome to pursue evil. Regarding Romans 7:22–23, he describes the common man in these things; for the common man is one who sees the necessary things with the mind but does not always do right, whereas the one having believed into Christ does the things with the mind through the assistance of the Spirit; therefore such a one is also called spiritual.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: The word man can mean especially the soul, and Paul's inner man is the mind, the soul.
comments.comment: The word 'man' signifies also the composite living thing which is composed of soul and body, and especially the soul. Therefore, the wise Peter the apostle calls the hidden part of the heart 'man', and the blessed Paul: 'For I consent according to the law of God according to the inner man' (Rom 7:22), that is, according to the mind, according to the soul.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by the inner man.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The mind longs to be free and honors the law, but the flesh forces it toward disordered pleasures, for the law of sin is the inborn impulse and the law of the mind is its will toward the good.
comments.comment: “For I delight in the law of God in my inner self” (Romans 7:22). As I have already said, the mind thirsts for freedom, longs to be rid of what stands condemned, and crowns the law with the highest honors as the guide to what is noblest; but the nature of the flesh forces it toward disordered pleasures, while the law of sin wages war and presses hard upon it (Romans 7:23). By the law of sin he means the inborn impulse, and whatever one might suppose the passion of love for the flesh to be, just as he called the law of the mind its inclination and will toward the good.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by the law of sin and the law of the mind.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Sin's law is in the members, and the soul dislikes the body's passions.
comments.comment: … For the law of sin, he says very guardedly, is in the members, showing that the soul is not pleased with the sufferings of the body, even though it is often dragged down together with it.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Paul meant by the law in his members an evil habit that rebels against holy intentions, as habit is called a second nature.
comments.comment: But at present we are not asking whether the apostle said this. We are asking with what belief, meaning, and reasoning he said it. By the law in his members he meant an evil habit that, through the practice of shameful deeds, rebels against holy intentions, at least in the beginning of amendment. Even learned people of this world commonly call habit a second nature.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: By body of death Paul meant sins and not flesh, for had he meant bodily misery he would have said the death of the body, and Scripture commonly calls sins members.
comments.comment: By “body of death” he [Paul] therefore meant sins, not flesh. Had he been speaking of the misery of our bodily members, which you think resulted from sin, he would more rightly have called it the death of the body rather than the body of death. To see that Scripture commonly calls sins “members”, read what this same apostle says to the Colossians: “Put to death your members that are on earth: fornication, impurity, and greed, which is the service of idols. Because of these things God's wrath comes upon the sons of unbelief. In these things you too once walked, when you lived in them” (Colossians 3:5–7). See how he calls “members” the things he identifies as sins.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Paul prays to be released not from the body but from the death that holds it through sin, in order to show how the Savior brought peace to soul and body.
comments.comment: It must be noted that this is not simply from this body, but from the death of the body; for it does not pray to be released from the body, but from the death that holds the body through sin (Rom 7:24). He remains, exposing the old man's warfare against himself, not being at peace with the soul of the body. He argues these things in order to demonstrate the achievements of the Savior's arrival and the union and peace of soul and body that has come through the rebirth of the washing. Thus he brought together what he intended, and came to what he was preparing, saying: 'Therefore there is now no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus' (Rom 7:25–8:1).
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Paul calls the pleasure-loving body a body of death because the law of sin is a sickness in it, and Christ redeems us not from the flesh but from the death in our members.
comments.comment: “Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death? I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:24–25). For now he laments and cries out against the flesh; and he calls the earthly, pleasure-loving body a “body of death,” because in it the law of sin is a sickness. He says that he seeks the one who is able to free us from such evils, and he does so in order to bring in the Redeemer for us at a fitting moment, that is, Christ, to whom he also gives all thanks. For through him we have been redeemed, not from the flesh but from the death of the flesh; not by dying, but by being set free from the death in our members, that is, from the savage pleasure in our members. For Christ has made us stronger than pleasure and sin.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul asks to be rescued from.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul asks to be delivered not from the body itself but from what has seized it through the sin of death, so that his body may become a body of life.
comments.comment: Regarding Romans 7:24–25, having perceived with the mind the war occurring through the body against the soul, and through it the man being taken captive, he seeks a refuge of salvation and looks to the one delivering, so that this very body of death might be transformed into a body of life. Then, having found the one delivering and being ready, he sends up to God through Jesus Christ a thanksgiving appropriate to the grace of salvation, through whom it also became possible for him to be delivered from the enemy. He does not say simply or pray merely to be delivered from the body, but from that which has seized the body of death through the sin of death; for he wants his own body to be a body of life, not a body of death nor a body of sin.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The body of death makes the soul wretched, and Paul gives thanks through Jesus Christ, who frees him from it.
comments.comment: And the body itself indeed makes the one burdened wretched. This concept is submitted by the apostolic word which has it thus: 'Wretched am I, man; who will rescue me from the body of this death?' (Romans 7:24). Since indeed I am in the body of death, I am wretched, and not by chance will the Savior make me out of such wretchedness; for he immediately brought forward: 'I give thanks through Jesus Christ' (Romans 7:25), who freed me from the body. We say, therefore, that wretchedness comes to the soul from the body of death.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: With the mind we served God's law, but the flesh forced us toward sin, so those who wished the good but could not were condemned until Christ ended the domination of the fleshly impulses.
comments.comment: So the inspired Paul speaks the truth when he insists that with the mind he serves the divine law, but with the flesh the law of sin (Romans 7:25); and this, I think, is what he meant when he said, “For willing lies close at hand for me, but accomplishing the good does not” (Romans 7:18). Formerly, then, as I said, so far as the mind and the will within it were concerned, we had the choice to serve the divine law; but the flesh forced us toward sin, raising up its own will in opposition, as it were. So there was, then, condemnation for those who wished to accomplish the good but were not able, because they were tyrannized by the passions; but in Christ what condemned has come to an end, that is, the domination of the fleshly impulses.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul cannot be divided between Christ and Beliar, with sin living in him, so his question about serving two laws shows he is not describing himself.
comments.comment:
Then he began again to explain in sequence what he had said earlier, prefacing it with a word of thanksgiving: “I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:25).

Then, to condemn those who seize on this as a pretext and abuse the flesh we wear, he asks interrogatively: “So then, do I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin?” (Romans 7:25). Am I, Paul, divided—serving the law of God in one part and the law of sin in another? Do I hold Christ and Beliar in myself at the same time and in the same place? Am I the one who said, “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20)—and have I lied, having living sin within me? I who proclaimed to others, “Do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit within you?” (1 Corinthians 6:19) and “Glorify God in your members” (1 Corinthians 6:20)—do I myself have nothing good in my body? But he is not like that; he is not. By no means! For a child of wrath and a vessel of wrath before, he changed his manner, not his nature, and became a precious vessel of election.
comments.author: Eusebius of Emesa

comments.capsule: Paul's mind is the spirit and his flesh is the soul that still desires fleshly goods and resists the spirit by the habit of sins, a habit that has become nature through mortal generation.
comments.comment: For this spirit is also called mind, about which the apostle says: “With my mind I serve the law of God” (Romans 7:25). He also says in another place: “For God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit” (Romans 1:9). But the soul, when it still desires fleshly goods, is called flesh and resists the spirit—not by nature, but by the habit of sins. Hence it is said: “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin” (Romans 7:25). This habit has been turned into nature through the mortal generation brought about by the sin of the first human being.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by serving God's law with the mind and sin's law with the flesh.
comments.author: Augustine of Hippo

comments.capsule: People buried with Christ are no longer condemned for Adam's disobedience, and Paul confirms this by saying there is now no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus.
comments.comment:
…For such people [those buried with Christ] have been freed from what is called the flesh. They will no longer be condemned because of Adam's disobedience. Sin no longer reigns over them, nor does the death that came through sin. For they were buried with the life of Christ, who wiped out disobedience by his obedience and drove out the death that came upon us from it by his voluntary death. He willingly placed himself under the law of disobedience so that he might redeem us who were under the law of condemnation. This is why every redeemed person says, "Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord" (Romans 7:25). For what the law could not do, weakened as it was through the flesh, God did: by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, he condemned sin in the flesh (Romans 8:3).

That these things have been rightly observed, the divine apostle shows by adding: "There is therefore now no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free from the law of sin and death" (Romans 8:1-2), and what follows.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why there is no condemnation for those in Christ.
comments.author: Eusebius of Emesa

comments.capsule: Those under the law live by the flesh and are condemned, while those in Christ are not, because the flesh, not the law, was unable to meet the law's requirement.
comments.comment: For having shown that those under the law, as they live according to the flesh, are under sin and condemnation, he led to the conclusion that those under Christ are not under condemnation, because they do not walk according to the flesh. He [Paul] spoke of the law of the spirit, contrasting it with the law of the letter (Rom 8:2), instead of the life-giving grace from Christ. For that which was impossible for the law, in which it was weak through the flesh (Rom 8:3–4), it was not the law, he says, that commanded the impossible, but the flesh was unable to fulfill the legal requirement because of the hindering evil, which Christ condemned through his own flesh.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: The law of the spirit of life is the mind's will toward the good, which, enriched by Christ's grace and freed from its weakness, wins freedom from the law of the flesh and so brings life instead of death.
comments.comment:
“For the law of the spirit of life in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:2). To make the ideas in these words perfectly clear, I think it necessary to say this: just as he calls the fleshly way of thinking, which carries us off toward every kind of wickedness, the law of sin and death, so he calls the spiritual will, that is, the mind’s inclination toward the good, the law of the spirit of life. But “the one who sows to the flesh will reap corruption from the flesh, while the one who sows to the spirit will reap eternal life from the spirit” (Galatians 6:8).

So the law of the spirit of life, that is, the will of the mind that carries us toward life, was in us even before, for with the mind we served the law of God; but, as I said, it was sick, powerless to resist, and, overcome by the desires of the flesh, it was condemned by the law. But since it has cast off its sickness and been made strong through Christ — for through him we have been sealed with the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13) and have been clothed with “power from on high” (Luke 24:49) — for this reason we have been redeemed and are no longer yoked to evil, but, as I said, we have been called to the dignity of freedom.

So the law of the spirit of life, that is, the will of the mind, which inclines toward doing good and carries us toward life, once it has been enriched with the grace that comes through Christ and set free from its ancient weakness, then, disregarding the evils that come from sin and prevailing over the law of the flesh, “has set me free,” he says (Romans 8:2). Not that it gives the freedom by itself, of course; rather, it has become for us the one who procures the freedom that comes through Christ. And just as those under the law of sin must, by every necessity, also be bound in the snares of death, so those who have come out from sin and been set free through Christ must in turn be beyond death, be seen to be above corruption, and live in holiness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'the law of the Spirit of life' means in Paul's argument.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The law's inability, whether of the written law or of the inborn law, ended through Christ, because once the flesh is put to death the law of the mind is no longer weak.
comments.comment:
He approves, then, as able to help, both the law of God (I mean the written law) and the law of the spirit, by which we have come to will the good, even if the power to do it may not lie close at hand. For he said, “For willing lies close at hand for me, but accomplishing the good does not” (Romans 7:18), clearly because sin gains the upper hand and the law of the flesh turns the mind, against its will, toward its own ends. In this same way, I think, one may rightly understand the law’s inability: both of the law that is written and given through Moses, as I said just now, and also of the law that is inborn and within us, by which even the Gentiles, though they do not have the written law, are seen to do by nature what the law requires and are a law to themselves (Romans 2:14); “for they show the work of the law written in their hearts” (Romans 2:15), as it is written.

Now is the time to examine what the inability in both consists of. The written law was a teacher of good order and a guide to what is best, but it justified no one at all; while the inborn law within us, which he also calls the law of the spirit, inclines toward the good but is thoroughly defeated by the law that calls us toward what is more shameful. So the inability, that is, the weakness, whether of the written law or of the inborn law, has come to an end through Christ. For once the flesh has in a certain way been put to death, and the pleasure within us has been, as it were, destroyed, the law of the spirit, or of the mind, will in no way be weak.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's body was the same nature as ours but was not flesh of sin, only the likeness of sinful flesh, so that he could condemn sin in the flesh.
comments.comment: How the sin within us has been put to death, let us say as far as we can. The Word of God, by the good pleasure of God the Father, came to be in the likeness of sinful flesh, so that he might condemn sin in the flesh (Romans 8:3). For he became man, lowering himself into self-emptying (Philippians 2:7); and that his body was of the same form and the same nature as our bodies, how could anyone doubt? Yet the bodies of all others might be called flesh of sin, because by nature they suffer the rise of disordered pleasures; but one would say that the body of Christ is not flesh of sin, by no means, but rather the likeness of sinful flesh…
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'the likeness of sinful flesh' means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God sent his Son in the likeness of flesh, not of an angel, so flesh could conquer the evil one.
comments.comment: He [Paul] says that God sent his Son not in the likeness of an angel or of any such power, but in the likeness of flesh, so that flesh, having been defeated over Adam, might conquer the evil one in the Lord's person. He says that the Lord was sent because of the prevailing sin of men;…
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Christ's flesh condemned the power of sin so that this victory passes to us, and the law's requirement is fulfilled in those who live by the Spirit.
comments.comment:
But since the Word who sanctifies the whole creation made his dwelling in it [Christ's flesh], the power of sin has been condemned, so that what was achieved might pass over to us as well.

For we have shared in him both spiritually and bodily: when Christ comes to dwell in us too, through the Holy Spirit and through the mystical blessing, then surely the law of sin is condemned in us as well.

It is true, then, that the law’s inability, in that it was weak through the flesh, has ceased through Christ, who condemned and abolished sin in the flesh, so that the just requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us (Romans 8:3-4).

For the just requirement of the law has been fulfilled, that is, the force of what the law decreed, namely the will that looks toward virtue, since the law within us is, as I said, in no way weak any longer through being tyrannized by innate pleasures.

So the just requirement of the law has been fulfilled in us who do not walk according to the flesh (Romans 8:4) but wish rather to live spiritually.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the 'just requirement of the law' fulfilled in us means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The mind set on the flesh brings death and opposes God, while the mind set on the Spirit brings life and peace with God.
comments.comment:
For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace (Romans 8:6).

He says, and quite rightly, that the mind of the flesh is death, while that of the spirit is life and peace. For love of the flesh truly brings about death, whereas the choice to live one’s life spiritually brings about life everlasting and the good things from above.

For if the mind of the flesh is enmity toward God (Romans 8:7), since it does not bear to yield to the divine laws—indeed it cannot, for how could a foul and profane pleasure please God?—then surely the mind that is clean of filth and passions is at peace with God, so far as human nature allows.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the mind of the flesh is death and the mind of the Spirit is life and peace.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Because the mind of the flesh opposes the law, it is senseless to think the law stirs up the passions.
comments.comment:
…Paul says, “The mind of the flesh is hostility toward God, for it does not submit to the law of God, nor indeed can it” (Romans 8:7).

If the mind of the flesh fights against the law, how is it not senseless to think that things so opposed to the law are stirred into action through it?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The flesh that cannot please God is not the visible body, since the saints pleased God while still living in it.
comments.comment: …For He does not speak of the immediate flesh; otherwise, it would happen that no man could partake of the Spirit of God. But that there is another flesh besides this visible one in which we are surrounded, Paul writes: 'For the mind of the flesh is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can it be: for they that are in the flesh cannot please God' (Romans 8:7); for if someone were to take the visible flesh, many would have pleased God with it, all the saints. And again saying, 'But ye are not in the flesh, but in the spirit' (Romans 8:9), he signifies the false flesh; for they were still in the flesh, having this life.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To be in the flesh is to let earthly pleasure rule the mind, which cannot please God, while a mind enriched by grace is in the spirit and does what pleases him.
comments.comment:
Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh but in the spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you (Romans 8:8-9).

When earthly pleasure prevails over a person’s understanding, he is in the flesh, as one who sets his mind on the things of the flesh; and such a one could not please God.

But when the mind has grown rich in the grace that comes through Christ, is filled with strength from above, is fervent in spirit (Romans 12:11), and hastens toward virtue, such a person is understood to be not in the flesh but in the spirit, and readily does what is pleasing to God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to be 'in the flesh' and 'in the Spirit'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul's 'if the Spirit of God dwells in you' keeps them alert and stops them from pride in thinking they already have the Spirit.
comments.comment: …he says, 'You are not in the flesh but in the Spirit', instead of 'You are not in carnal desires, but live in the Spirit'. If the Spirit of God dwells in you, it stirred them up to keep the mind awake and not to lie back, as if they had achieved perfection, having brought forth the word saying, 'If the Spirit of God dwells in you'. For for them to look haughty and be puffed up as if they already possessed the Spirit of God would have been harmful and sufficient to cut off their zeal.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Anyone in the spirit is in righteousness and life, since the body of sin is nearly dead, and 'spirit' here means the human spirit given life by the Holy Spirit's grace.
comments.comment:
Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9).

If, then, anyone is in the spirit, he will also be in righteousness and in life, since the body of sin is all but dead and every unseemly pleasure has been quenched. For righteousness and unrighteousness, holiness and impurity, cannot exist in the same person at one and the same time.

By “spirit” we mean the human spirit; and in the words “the spirit is life” (Romans 8:10), we mean the spirit given life by the grace of the Holy Spirit and enriched, through its communion with him,…
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Though Christ is said to be raised by the Father, he raised his own temple through the Spirit, and so he will raise our bodies.
comments.comment:
But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you (Romans 8:11).

Our Lord Jesus Christ was raised by the Father, life being worked in his flesh through the Holy Spirit, who is his own.

For he himself gave life to his own temple, as he shows when he says to the Jews, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19).

So even if he is said to have been raised by the Father, it was nonetheless he himself who raised it up through the Holy Spirit; for every work befitting God is worked by the Father through the Son in the Spirit.

Christ, then, will also raise our bodies from the dead.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Christ was raised by the Father and also raised himself.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul shows the Spirit is both Christ's and the Father's, and that the first prize of the struggle is resurrection.
comments.comment: …having foretold the Spirit of Christ, he says again that the Spirit of him who raised Christ dwells in you. Having brought the Spirit back from Christ to the Father, he is clearly teaching nothing else but that the Spirit is also from the Son and is not foreign to the Father's divinity, … Consequently, he says that when the Holy Spirit has come to dwell and sin has been put to death, he says that prizes follow those who struggle, the first and greatest of which was the resurrection from the dead.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Those led by the Spirit are sons of God, freed from the slavery of law and letter and crying 'Abba, Father' in the Spirit of adoption.
comments.comment:
For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God (Romans 8:14).

Those who live by the spirit are the ones who are also led by the Spirit, because they have been sealed with the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13), set free from the slavery that lies in law and letter, and passed over instead into freedom, and because the Spirit of adoption bears them witness that they are sons of God and that in that same Spirit of adoption they have cried out, “Abba, Father” (Romans 8:15-16).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what being led by the Spirit and the Spirit of adoption mean.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The 'spirit of slavery' is not slavery to the evil one but the law and those under it, and the same Spirit worked in both peoples.
comments.comment: …some say it is a spirit of slavery to the evil one, but it is not; for he calls the law here a spirit of slavery and those under the law slaves; therefore, as if being punished, they were afraid if they stumbled, which is a sign of slavery. But the permission to call the Father 'God' promises the hope of adoption through the purity of life; and it is the same Spirit who worked in both peoples, the spirit of slavery and the spirit of adoption, according to what is advantageous and fitting according to the dignity of both.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Israel under the law had a spirit of slavery, but the Holy Spirit was given to those justified by faith after Christ's return to life.
comments.comment: For a spirit of slavery was upon Israel; but to us the gift was granted through Christ after his return to life from the dead. For he breathed on them, saying, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John 20:22). That is why Paul also said to those who had believed: ‘For you did not receive a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba, Father”’ (Romans 8:15). And that the power of the worship under the law was not rich in a share of the Holy Spirit, but that this has been given rather to those justified by faith, the wise John will assure us when he says: ‘For the Holy Spirit was not yet, because Jesus had not yet been glorified’ (John 7:39). For Christ had not yet returned to life; for it was then that human nature was, so to speak, gilded by the Spirit and by fellowship with him.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: Whoever chooses the good for its own sake rather than from fear is a son of God, though the Savior is the source of all such sons.
comments.comment: …everyone who is no longer schooled by fear, but chooses the good for its own sake, is, as Paul named him, a son of God. But the Saviour differs greatly, and by a long way, from everyone who is called a son of God because of virtue, for he is, as it were, a kind of spring and source of all such. Paul’s words run like this: “For you did not receive a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you received a spirit of adoption, in which we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8:15).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Spirit of prayer testifies with our spirit that we are children of God and cries out 'Abba the Father.'
comments.comment: And it [the Spirit] testifies with our spirit, because the one having the gift prayed in the Spirit on behalf of the whole people, while praying, said, 'Our Father in the heavens' (Matt 6:9). Therefore, he says, the Spirit of prayer testifies with our spirit which we have through baptism, that we are children of God; for the Spirit cries out this: it is the gift of prayer, 'Abba the Father.'
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Glory is not won without toil, but the saints' toil rests on great hopes of unmeasured glory, shown when their bodies are changed.
comments.comment:
If indeed we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified with him (Romans 8:17).

The good is not achieved without toil, but for the saints the toil rests on great hopes. For nothing earthly has been promised them, but glory without measure and a share in what lies beyond mind and speech.

For those who disdain the things of earth are worthy of the highest rewards, and those who have first toiled with courage and endurance will enjoy crowns of a preeminence beyond compare; for the toil spent on virtue falls short of the honors that follow.

He speaks of the glory of the saints because in due time the righteous will shine like the sun (Matthew 13:43), having come into honor, glory and incorruption when their bodies are changed, just as Christ was transfigured on the mountain (Matthew 17:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul promises to those who suffer with Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To suffer with Christ is to choose his sufferings, enduring persecution and being ready for death for piety, and so be glorified as God's children and co-heirs.
comments.comment: If we suffer, he says, so that we may also be glorified with him (Rom 8:17-18). To suffer does not mean to be physically joined or to be mixed with the one who has suffered, according to the logic of habit; for Christ did not suffer anything against his will, nor did he grow weak, desiring to defend those who grieved. What then is to suffer with Christ? To choose the same sufferings, to endure what Christ endured, who, representing the truth, was suffering under the Jews. If we endure being persecuted in the same manner, not being dishonored or being distressed, if we are ready for death for the sake of piety, sympathizing with him, we shall be glorified in becoming children of God and co-heirs of Christ.…
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to suffer with Christ.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Paul corrects the idea that glory is a wage by showing God's reward is not measured by our toils but far exceeds them.
comments.comment: That suffering for Christ becomes a cause for us to be glorified with him, and it seemed that such toil was a wage and not a gift of grace, even though the greatest gift is the amnesty granted to those who have overcome sins. Correcting this, he brought forward that the fruit of the citizenship from God is not measured to us according to an analogy of toils, but is manifold and far exceeds the value of those who have labored; for God, being both good and just, preserves the just regarding those who sin, giving to the sinner only what the hypothesis of the sins requires, but the good is shown regarding those who are upright, not only giving to them according to their merit, but also exceeding the analogy of their lives with gifts.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Eager expectation means hope, and creation awaits God's children because it will be changed for the better when they are made glorious and incorruptible.
comments.comment:
For the eager expectation of creation awaits the revealing of the sons of God (Romans 8:19).

“Eager expectation” means hope: the looking for and watching out for how events will turn out.

Creation does await the revealing of the children of God, not because it knows in any way what is to come—how could it, or from where?—but because, by the hidden dispensations of God, who reshapes all things for the better, matters will come to this end.

For when the children of God—that is, those who have achieved a life of good repute—are refashioned, as it were, from dishonor into glory and from corruption into incorruption, creation itself too will surely be changed for the better.

On this point the inspired Peter does not let us doubt, when he says, “We await new heavens and a new earth, and the things he has promised” (2 Peter 3:13).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'eager expectation' means and why creation waits.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The eagerly awaited expectation is the stretching forth of those who hope.
comments.comment: …it is said that the eagerly awaited expectation is the stretching forth of those who hope, who by chance incline the head and strain the eyes, as if they were about to see the thing expected.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Creation's waiting is spoken of the powers God set over creation, not of soulless matter.
comments.comment: He says that we shall be in such a state of God's good gifts, so that the hope and expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God (Rom 8:19), as if their hidden blessedness were to be revealed a little later. The written things give an intention to the many, as if the seen creation is animated and the world has some kind of rational perception. For if it groans and sighs and awaits the revelation, it is clear, he says, that it also perceives and is moved by thought. But it is not so; rather, he speaks of a creation now, not of soulless matter, but of the standing powers that God has established to pervade the creation according to the will of the Creator, according to what is written: when the Most High divided the nations, as he scattered the sons of Adam, he set the boundaries of nations according to the number of the angels of God (Deut 32:8). Thus also, regarding the blessing of cold and heat and again hail and snow and the like, it should be understood as being through the powers standing over these; for one is not exhorted to praise God through unfeeling matter.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Creation waits for the sons of God and follows them as a possession follows its owner, as a slave follows the free man.
comments.comment:
All, he says, creation waits for us, and the time when we shall be seen in the glory due to us, as if nothing were more brilliant than the glory that will be about us (Rom 8).

But it is fitting for creation to follow the sons of God, being God's possession; for the slave follows the free man, and the possession is subject to the son because of his nobility.

And the appropriation toward the Father subjects the slave to the sons.

It is evident, then, that having grace, the sons are of God.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Here 'vanity' means those who live in vanity, in a fleshly mind.
comments.comment:
For creation was subjected to vanity (Romans 8:20).

Here he calls “vanity” those who live in vanity, that is, in a fleshly mind. Of them it might be said quite fittingly, “Man has become like vanity” (Psalm 144:4), and indeed also that…
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Creation was subjected unwillingly, in hope of the freedom it will have under the saints, so that it may serve God's children alone.
comments.comment:
…For the life of such people is truly vanity.

To them creation is subjected, and certainly not willingly (Romans 8:20)—how could it be?

But in what sense do we say even this? The creation that is perceived and seen knows nothing at all of our affairs, for it is not rational.

Yet even if one were to grant that it could understand something, it would not, he says, have endured so shameful a slavery, nor would it have wished to be subjected to and to serve those who have chosen to spend their lives on nothing needful, that is, on nothing good.

Rather, he says, it has been subjected for the time being in hope (Romans 8:20-21), the hope of those who will be saved and of the saints and elect of every age. God yokes it and, as it were, keeps it for the freedom it will have under the saints and those who love him, so that it may serve his children alone and be at hand for the needs of the chosen.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why creation was subjected and what it hopes for.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Creation did not submit to the devil willingly but by God's forbearance and in hope of being set free in the time of the righteous.
comments.comment: He says, however, that she [creation] neither willingly nor by her own impulse submitted to the devil from the beginning, but she submitted through the forbearance of God, and she submitted in hope of what is to come. In what hope? This one: that even the creation itself shall be set free. And when shall she be set free? Into the time of the freedom of the righteous; therefore, it is fitting that the expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the children of God. He says, not only does creation groan and suffer birth-pangs, awaiting freedom through the Spirit (Rom 8:22-23), but also we, although we have already received the firstfruits of the Spirit and have been tested by its goodness, even if we do not yet have the perfection of the…
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Creation groans in labor and believers groan too, waiting for the redemption of the body, which means not laying the body aside but having it become spiritual.
comments.comment:
For it is all but distraught, in labor and in pain (Romans 8:22); and if it could know anything of our affairs, it would perhaps even be wailing aloud.

Yet yielding to the divine will, it waits in its own way for “the revealing,” as I said, “of the sons of God” (Romans 8:19).

And not only so, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, we ourselves also groan within ourselves (Romans 8:23).

He takes as proof of what has been said what naturally happens within us.

For we ourselves, he says, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan within ourselves, weighed down, as we wait for adoption, the redemption of our body (Romans 8:23).

For it is true that “a perishable body weighs down the soul, and this earthly tent burdens the mind with its many cares” (Wisdom of Solomon 9:15).

But once the Spirit has come to be in us and is remaking us toward a longing for virtue, love of the flesh, as it were, leads out its forces against us, and the law that has fastened on our members (Romans 7:23), ever goading us toward unseemly pleasures, rises up against us without mercy.

That is why we groan, counting the redemption of our body as our adoption.

For what we thirst for is not to lay our bodies aside, nor do we say that this is the redemption. Rather, we expect the body to become spiritual (1 Corinthians 15:44), that is, to have cast off entirely the fleshly and earthly mind, and the sting of sin (1 Corinthians 15:56). This is what we call the spiritual body.

If the grace of adoption includes the redemption of our body, then let no one distort the resurrection for us in any way. Nor let anyone come to such folly as to treat the flesh as something to be thrown away, and to say that once it has fallen into the earth it will vanish entirely, while something else rises in its place, something spiritual—thin, I mean, and airy. For that is how they understand “spiritual.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains why believers groan and what 'redemption of our body' means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: If death is not destroyed there is no redemption of the body, since Christ must have made us stronger than death for the adoption we await.
comments.comment: So if death is not destroyed, his design was in vain, and the mystery of the dispensation in the flesh is of no profit to us either; and we have missed the hope of life as well. And how have we been called to adoption, and how are we children of God, as the wise John says (1 John 3:1)? If it is true that “we wait for adoption, the redemption of our body” (Romans 8:23), what redemption is there at all, unless Christ has made us stronger than death? Or how “will he change the body of our lowliness to be conformed to the body of his glory” (Philippians 3:21)? For what time will there be for this at all, unless death is made idle? Or what change will there be for those who will stay as they were, or rather end in a worse state?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Our bodies' freedom from corruption and death is laid up in hope, to come certainly and to be awaited with patient endurance.
comments.comment:
For in hope we were saved (Romans 8:24).

We believe that our bodies too will come to be beyond corruption and death. This is laid up for us in hope, not as something already present, but as something that will certainly come to be in every way; and we wait for it with patience (Romans 8:25), enduring hardship, so that we may obtain so holy a gift.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
