comments.capsule: The spirit that intercedes is our own, groaning when we eagerly make our supplications to God.
comments.comment: “But the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words” (Romans 8:26). It is our own spirit, plainly, that intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words; for at times we groan when we are eager to make our supplications to God. So this too we learn in the Holy Spirit, for the Spirit is wise, just as the Son is.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We know how to pray, but we do not know what the redemption of the body will be, so we groan in the spirit for things we believe will come.
comments.comment:
But since he says, “We do not know what we should pray for as we ought” (Romans 8:26), let us look into this. And yet we have already been taught by Christ how we ought to pray, for he says plainly, “Pray, then, like this: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as in heaven” (Matthew 6:9–10), and all that follows. Since, then, we know the fitting way to make our supplications, tell me, what would be the sense of the apostle’s words? Or at what would the words spoken through Paul’s voice be aimed?

We say, then, that we do pray, seeking to ask for good things, and before all else for what serves the glory of God, and for the things by which we may live rightly and achieve a life that is truly approved. But “having the firstfruits of the Spirit, we ourselves also groan within ourselves, waiting for adoption, the redemption of the body” (Romans 8:23); and it is in this respect, at least, that “we do not know what we should pray for as we ought” (Romans 8:26). For if “no eye has seen and no ear has heard, nor has it entered the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9), what shall we ask for when we draw near? Or how could we know what we have not seen, or rather, things that lie beyond the mind and are not known to human hearts? What the redemption of the body will be, or what its refashioning is, and how it is re-formed into incorruption and glory, only he who is the craftsman of these things would know.

The Savior’s disciple, too, said somewhere to some who did not know how to pray as they ought, “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your pleasures” (James 4:3). It would therefore be quite fitting, and with good reason, for those in such a state to say, “We do not know what we should pray for as we ought” (Romans 8:26). So with groanings too deep for words we ask in the spirit for things that we believe will come to be, though we are wholly ignorant of the manner in which they will come.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says we do not know what to pray for.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Because people often ask for what is not beneficial, someone with the gift of prayer asks God for good things with inexpressible groanings.
comments.comment:
…for what we ought to pray we do not know, but the Spirit itself intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings (Rom 8:26). And this indeed requires interpretation; and there is such a gift of prayer, which is upon the apostles.

Since many times we also ask for things not beneficial, therefore someone standing upon the apostles, the one having the gift of prayer upon the people, asked God for the beneficial things, using inexpressible groanings, in order that he might draw all toward reverence and fear.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Our mind cannot pray unless the Spirit first prays, just as it cannot sing to the Father unless the Spirit first sings.
comments.comment: …attached to 'but what to pray as we ought, we do not know, but the Spirit intercedes with unutterable groanings' (Romans 8:26) is 'I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind also; I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the mind also.' (1 Corinthians 14:15) For our mind cannot pray unless the Spirit first prays, as in accompaniment of it — just as it cannot sing and hymn the Father in Christ rhythmically, melodiously, metrically, harmoniously, unless the Spirit who searches all things, even the depths of God, first praises and hymns him whose depths it has searched and, as far as it could, grasped.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'According to purpose' means according to will, which raises the question whose will, since every longing for righteousness would come from God the Father.
comments.comment: “We know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to purpose” (Romans 8:28). All things do work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to purpose. But according to whose purpose? And what is meant by “according to purpose”? “According to purpose” would mean “according to will.” Then according to whose will have those under discussion been called: that of the one who called them, or also that of those who were called? Now every longing that carries us toward righteousness would come to us from God the Father;…
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Some are called according to the purpose of the caller and their own, but only those foreknown as conformed to Christ's image are chosen.
comments.comment: [Whose purpose is meant by “called according to purpose”:] Yet in this matter one would not miss what is fitting if one said that some have been called according to purpose, both the purpose of the one who called them and their own. “For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed,” and so on (Romans 8:29). Many, he says, are called according to purpose, but not all are chosen (Matthew 22:14); only those have been honored who were also foreknown as those who would be conformed to the image of his Son.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those living spiritually are conformed to the Spirit, which is the image of the Son.
comments.comment: …for just as the Son is the unchanging image of the Father, so also the Spirit is the image of the Son. Therefore, all those who, having been made worthy of the Holy Spirit, live spiritually, these are conformed to the Spirit, which is the image of the Son.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Christ is Only-begotten as God, but called Firstborn because by lowering himself into our condition he came to be among many brothers.
comments.comment: The inspired Paul says somewhere, “And when He again brings the Firstborn into the world, He says, ‘Let all the angels of God worship Him’” (Hebrews 1:6). And yet to which of all beings is it unclear that He is Only-begotten insofar as He is understood to be God? For He alone has been begotten of the Father alone. But when He lowered Himself into our condition and came to be among many brothers (Romans 8:29), then He was set in the first place. So besides being Only-begotten as God, He has also been called Firstborn because of His humanity.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Foreknowledge is seeing what is coming, not causing it, so Paul speaks of being conformed, not of existence.
comments.comment:
Foreknowledge is a theoretical viewing of what is coming to be. But according to kind, foreknowledge and knowledge are the same. They differ in time. For example, suppose I foreknow that tomorrow there will be thunder. When the thunder comes to be in the middle of the day, it is knowledge, no longer foreknowledge. And the knowledge of the thunder does not make it such, but what it is, that becomes the knowledge. Thus the known thing makes the knowledge, which does not receive the knowing from us. …

'Whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son' (Romans 8:29). He does not speak about existence, but about being conformed. Foreknowledge does not lead to existence.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The image of the Son means a holy life of obedience, as opposed to the image of Adam, and those foreknown to imitate it are called, justified and glorified.
comments.comment: What the image of his Son should be understood to be, the blessed Paul himself will make clear again, saying, “For just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, let us also bear the image of the heavenly one” (1 Corinthians 15:49). For those who have paid no heed to fleshly desires are the ones who have imitated the image of Christ, that is, the way of life and conduct that is in holiness. For just as we say that the image of the man of dust, that is, of Adam, is the life lived in disobedience and sins, so too the image of the heavenly one, that is, of Christ, is holiness, justification and obedience. All, then, who were foreknown as those who would, in their own times, be conformed to the life of Christ and be its imitators, so far as human nature allows, these have also been called. “And those whom he predestined he also called; and those whom he called he also justified; and those whom he justified he also glorified” (Romans 8:30).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what being 'conformed to the image of his Son' means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Foreknowledge does wrong to no one, since the called who refuse are left out by their own unwillingness and Christ calls all to himself.
comments.comment:
It is not at all unlikely that some, carried away by ignorance, should make this matter a ready pretext for unbelief and say, “If those whom he foreknew according to purpose and predestined are the ones who have been called, it has nothing to do with us who have not yet believed; for we have not been called, nor have we been predestined.” To them we will say that the one who gave the wedding feast for his son sent his servants to gather those who had been called, but they would not come (Matthew 22:2–3). After them, those who were called according to their own purpose came in, and so the wedding hall was filled with guests (Matthew 22:10). So nothing is seen standing in the way of those who are willing to come. Foreknowledge does no wrong to anyone at all, nor does it give anyone an advantage. Otherwise, let them teach us whether those who in their disobedience outraged the God who called them were not foreknown as well. More than that, some were called and rushed into the wedding, yet they did not become chosen, nor were they justified or glorified. For what reason? Because they were not wearing a garment fit for the wedding (Matthew 22:11–12).

Besides, we shall find our Lord Jesus Christ himself saying openly, “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). See, he was already calling all people to himself, and no one would be without a share in the grace of being called; for in saying “all” he sends no one away at all.
comments.selected_reason: Answers the worry that foreknowledge leaves some people out.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul puts foreknowledge before predestination, and foreknowledge is no necessity, so those predestined are those called by their own purpose.
comments.comment:
…Even in these things, the word does not deny the power of its own accord; for first it said that God foreknows, then that he predestines (Rom 8:29–30). And foreknowledge is clearly not a necessity of the impulse or the intention of those being lived. It would be clearer if we opened up what was said here, starting from the last things toward the first.

Whom then did God glorify here? Those whom he justified. And whom did he predestine? Those whom he foreknew, those being called according to purpose, that is, those being worthy to be called and to be conformed to Christ through their own purpose.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: God's not sparing his Son is the great proof of his love, so no one can hinder the gifts he manages for our sake.
comments.comment: He [Paul] brings forward the great proof of the love of God, having shown through his deeds that all things work together for our good through the love of God toward us, namely, those whom he found to be called according to purpose, which he demonstrated in not sparing the only-begotten (Rom 8:31–32); … Therefore, since God is managing all things for our sake, who will hinder? Who is so strong as to obstruct the gifts of God toward us? For it is fitting that he who did not spare the Son for our sake will manage all other things for our sake and will add grace to the good things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God's giving of his Son shows that nothing can stand against us.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: All things work together for those who choose good, since God shields them.
comments.comment: “What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare his own Son” (Romans 8:31–32). For those who have chosen to do good, all things work together, since God shields them. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul does not let the called fall into helplessness: they will be set free from former sins and justified, for if the Lord of the law forgives, no one can condemn.
comments.comment: …how will he not also, with him, give us all things (Romans 8:32)? “Who will bring a charge against God’s chosen? It is God who justifies; who is the one who condemns?” (Romans 8:33–34). Perhaps Paul, with a wise purpose, does not let the minds of the called fall into helplessness, but teaches that they will be set free from their former sins and will be justified, as God grants it. For although every sin involves a transgression of the divine law and condemns the careless, yet if the Lord of the law himself forgives, who is the one who condemns the sinner?
comments.selected_reason: Explains why no one can condemn those whom God justifies.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ has freed the elect from accusation, so neither the condemning law nor the rulers of this age can stand against us, since he lives at the Father's side and intercedes for us.
comments.comment:
He has unloosed the elect from all accusations, and justification has pre-ordained the condemnation (Rom 8:33-34); so that neither a condemning law, nor the rulers of this age, holding man by sin and drawing him through sin into the slavery of death, shall still be strong against us.

But the terror of the law ceases, being overcome by the grace of Christ, and the wickedness of the rulers of this age is weakened by the goodness of Him who was slaughtered for us and voluntarily gave Himself up by the good pleasure of God and Father, even though a resurrection came upon Him, concealing death, and we no longer see Christ having died, but living and sitting at the Father's side, and interceding for men according to the human, through which also He was joined to men, uniting what was divided.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ acts as ambassador for the Father on our behalf, which shows the Son asking and the Father granting so that the right order of the two persons is kept.
comments.comment: For he was not sufficient to die for us, but he also acts as an ambassador for the Father on our behalf. … What then is the purpose of the ambassadorship and the encounter? The word cuts ahead of the impious doctrine of Sabellius, teaching how, even if the essence is one of the Trinity, it is not one hypostasis [distinct person]; for through the encounter, the one asking and the other being asked are shown. It is not strange that the Son should ask and the Father should grant, so that a fitting order may be preserved regarding both persons.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: One who says 'we more than conquer' is far above such trials.
comments.comment: …For one who says, “In all these things we more than conquer through him who loved us” (Romans 8:37), is far above such things; and that is greater than conquering.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Israel was God's chosen firstborn but, by its pride and its killing of the Lord, was cast out and put behind the nations.
comments.comment: “I am speaking the truth in Christ, I am not lying; my conscience bears witness with me” (Romans 9:1). In the beginning God made Israel his chosen one and even called him firstborn (Exodus 4:22). But they became boastful and insolent, and, what goes beyond even this, slayers of the Lord. That is why they have perished; for they have been sent away and cast out, and, having slipped wholly from their closeness to God, they have been placed behind the nations; and they have shown themselves strangers to the hope of the fathers.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul, who had been sent to the nations and kept saying that Israel had fallen away, swears to his sincerity so that no one will think he gloats over his own kin.
comments.comment: Now the blessed Paul had been appointed a minister of the divine gospel and was proclaiming Jesus to the nations. Again and again he said that those of Israel’s blood had fallen away, and he insisted that those who were once in darkness and served demons had become called according to the purpose and foreknowledge of God. So that none of the less instructed might think he was all but leaping on his own kin as they lay fallen, and smiling over their fall, he makes a necessary defense and says, “I am speaking the truth in Christ, I am not lying,” and what follows (Romans 9:1).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul opens chapter 9 with an oath: he is defending himself against the charge of gloating over Israel's fall.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul calls on God as witness that his sorrow for his kinsmen, who missed the promised good things, is real and constant.
comments.comment: From the hoped-for good things, both extremes have proceeded (Rom 9:1-5): the contention regarding love and the lamentation regarding those who have fallen away. For those being benefited love, but those failing in the benefits lament appropriately. He says, intensifying with divine testimony, that he does not speak only in word but also in disposition and truth, that he has the greatest sorrow continually present for his kinsmen.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: To grieve over the fallen is love, but to wish oneself accursed for them is hyperbole, a proof of the most perfect love.
comments.comment: Over those who have gone so far in perversity as to slip from their love for God, and then to suffer harsh penalties for it, one might well grieve; and to shed a tear for them out of fellow feeling would not be beyond reason; or rather, it is the fullness of love. But to wish even to be accursed from Christ on their behalf (Romans 9:3) goes beyond the measures of love. For no one, if he is in his right mind, would choose to offend God for the sake of the salvation of others, counting his own life as nothing while choosing that others should have it. What, then, does he mean in putting forward his own salvation as the price of the salvation of the Jews? The statement is a hyperbole, and it gives proof of the most perfect love. “For I could wish,” he says, “that I myself were accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers” (Romans 9:3). It is as if he were saying, “If Israel were saved by my offending Christ, I myself would have chosen it.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's startling wish to be accursed as hyperbole that proves his love.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul's sorrow and his wish to suffer for his enemies should not be doubted.
comments.comment: Let no one disbelieve, he says, if I lament concerning the adversaries and persecutors, nor let it be considered paradoxical if I desired to suffer the greatest things on their behalf, being handed over unto death by Christ.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Paul justifies his willingness to be accursed by listing what Israel had, so that its fall is the more dreadful.
comments.comment:
So, he says, I for my part would very gladly choose to be accursed from Christ, if only I could save those of my own blood (Romans 9:3). Then he adds, as if to show that the cause of his grief over them is quite able to work such a disposition in him, so that he might not seem to have said something harsh and jarring in offering his own life in exchange for the life of others: For first, he says, they are Israelites; theirs are the adoption and the glory and the covenants and the giving of the law and the worship and the promises; and from them, according to the flesh, comes Christ himself (Romans 9:4–5).

Now if they had been among those who had not known from ancient times the One who is God by nature and in truth, if the law given through Moses had not become for them the steward of their closeness to him, if they had not sprung from the root of the holy fathers and been made heirs of their good name, if they had not been the first to practice the ways of worshiping God and had not grown rich in the hopes of the promise, then one would have grieved over them more moderately. But since “theirs are the fathers,” and the rest (Romans 9:5), and since, when their affairs were all but running before a fair wind, they have fallen into an end no one expected and have missed their hope, how is what has befallen these wretched people not truly dreadful?
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul lists Israel's privileges: they show why its fall grieves him so.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Israel's condition is pitiable because it was glorified and chosen and kin to the Lord, yet is now cast off and brought low, though God who judged this is still to be blessed.
comments.comment: For how is not their condition pitiable, especially in the eyes of their own people and kin—men called sons of God from the beginning, glorified with glory from God in the world, who received the first covenant concerning bodily ordinances, and now hold in their hands the second one that has come concerning spiritual things, and those chosen for the worship of God and the promises of future good things, the fathers of the saints and God-loving ones, those homogeneous with the flesh of the Lord, these being cast off and despised and having fallen now into the greatest shame and lowliness. But therefore, even if what happened concerning them is worthy of lamentation, it is worthy to bless the God who thus judged, the Master over all, to whom all blessing is justly returned from all and upon all.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God's word has not failed, for it promised Abraham many nations and not only Israel, since all who walk in his faith are his children.
comments.comment:
“But it is not as though the word of God has failed” (Romans 9:6). The statement is exact. For he says that the word of God has by no means proved false, that is, that it cannot fall away from the truth. For the God of all, as everyone agrees, promised Abraham at the beginning that he would be the father of many (Genesis 17:4–5), and again, “I will surely multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven in number” (Genesis 22:17).

Abraham, then, had to be shown to be the father not of those from Israel alone. For the nation that came from him was one, but the nations throughout the whole earth are past counting, and they too have been reckoned as Abraham’s children, if indeed they are of the promise and “walk in the footsteps of the faith” he had “in uncircumcision” (Romans 4:12), as it is written. For as blessed Paul himself says somewhere, “The promise to Abraham that he would be heir of the world did not come through the law, but through the righteousness of faith. For if those who are of the law are heirs,” he says, “faith has been emptied and the promise made void” (Romans 4:13–14).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how God's word to Abraham has not failed even though Israel as a nation has fallen away.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul's "not all are children" and "not all those of Israel are Israel" mean that true Israel is the man without deceit, not Israel according to the flesh.
comments.comment: But as for that which is sometimes declared as not both seed and child, Paul writes: 'not all are children' (Rom 9:7); for not all those of Israel are Israel (Rom 9:6), but rather that one about whom the Savior said: 'Behold a man Israelite in whom there is no deceit' (John 1:47); but not these about whom it has been said: 'See Israel according to the flesh' (1 Corinthians 10:18). These things are regarding the difference between seed and child; let us return to what was explicitly set forth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because Abraham's offspring is reckoned in Isaac, that is by promise, the children of the flesh are not simply children of God; those who come through faith are.
comments.comment: Since, then, the offspring of Abraham has been reckoned as being in Isaac, that is, according to promise (Romans 9:7–8), for this is the word of promise, “About this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son” (Romans 9:9), it would surely be plain that the children of the flesh would not, simply and in every case, be counted as children of God (Romans 9:8). Rather, it is the children of the promise, that is, those who come through faith, who would have that honor for themselves.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who Abraham's true children are: the children of the promise, who come through faith.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God's truthfulness stands, because Scripture meant by Israelites those who show themselves worthy by piety, and God's promise follows foreknowledge in the Gentiles' case as in Isaac's.
comments.comment: Since the things promised to the Israelites were transferred as if to the Gentiles (Rom 9:6-9), which was an accusation against God as if he were falsifying the promises, he shows the truthfulness of God, demonstrating that the Scripture did not signify the Israelites according to the flesh, but those showing through piety that they are worthy to be called Israelites and children of Abraham; for in Isaac, he says, you shall be called seed, and the things following. In Isaac, not through Isaac, which, explaining, he says: that is, not these children of the flesh are these children of God, but the children of the promise are reckoned as seed. But he wishes to say that not those from the flesh of Abraham, these are children of God, but children those from the promise, such as the pious and the righteous, whom God promised as sons to Abraham according to foreknowledge, since Isaac, having come to be from the promise, was shown to be righteous; for he foreknew and promised him righteous; for God would not be permitted to grant an impious son. Thus also he promised Abraham to be a father of nations, foreknowing the piety of the nations that were to come. Therefore he said: in Isaac you shall be called seed, that is, through the promise according to the pattern of Isaac, who was righteous and a pattern of the righteous. And the entire structure of the text is that the promise of God is according to foreknowledge, and the promise is according to the judgment of righteousness, and just as regarding Isaac, so also regarding the Gentiles.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Paul's sentence about Rebecca is left unfinished and needs words added to make it complete, namely that she too serves as a pattern of the calling that comes by election.
comments.comment:
One should note that the aim of this sentence is by no means brought to completion; rather it is left hanging and needs a brief addition, that is, words to be understood, so that it may not appear to limp. What I mean is this. He had already shown, from the fact that Isaac was given to Abraham by promise, that the children of the flesh would not necessarily be counted to him as offspring, and that it would rather befit him to bear the name of father of those who are of faith and promise. Then he takes up Rebecca and what happened in her case, and says, “And not only so,” that is, my argument will not stop at the birth of Isaac alone, “but also Rebecca, having conceived by one, our father Isaac” (Romans 9:10). And he needed to add something like this: “will also be brought in as proof and assurance,” that is, “will serve as a pattern and image of the calling and grace that come by election and foreknowledge.” For had something of that kind been added, his sentence would then have seemed complete.

But I do not know how he came to pass this over and go straight on to what was said and done at the birth of Isaac’s sons.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul teaches that God judges by conduct and not by descent, as Jacob and Esau, born together, had different outcomes according to what they deserved.
comments.comment: Thus he rightly condemns those descended from Abraham when they live wickedly and drives them from his inheritance, just as he does Gentiles found acting similarly. Conversely, he rewards the good wills, true faith, and upright deeds of either people with eternal joys. The Teacher of the Nations therefore restrains Jewish pride and shows that the difference lies not in human seed but in conduct. They must recognize that unless they take care to be faithful, no privilege of circumcised ancestry will defend them. Jacob and Esau, after all, were conceived through one reception of seed and delivered through one act of giving birth, yet experienced very different outcomes because of the difference in what they deserved
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: God used the birth of Isaac's sons to sketch beforehand the mystery of grace by election, assuring Isaac that he would be father of countless nations of faith.
comments.comment: But since the mystery of grace by election and of the gift given in foreknowledge had to be sketched out beforehand, for that very reason God, our supreme craftsman in such things, put the moment to good use and all but seized it. At the birth of the children he assured Isaac that, though he was the one and only son from Abraham, he would be the father of countless nations, those who are of the promise and who would be called in faith.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God spoke of Jacob and Esau at their birth: to foreshadow the calling of the nations by promise.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul speaks of election according to purpose, not purpose according to election, for God loved the one for his virtue and hated the other for the badness of his disposition.
comments.comment: the apostle, for the demonstration of the same matter being before him, having remembered both Esau and Jacob (Rom 9:11), says thus: lest indeed, before they were born or had done anything good or evil, so that the intention of God according to election might remain … the one He loved because of his own virtue, and the other He hated because of the badness of his disposition, from which it is clear that the apostle speaks of an election according to purpose and not a purpose according to election.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Paul answers in advance the charge that God chose by whim, since foreknowledge of Jacob's goodness and Esau's perversity makes the choice just.
comments.comment:
It was likely that some fault-finders would suppose that Jacob and Esau had met with an untested swing of will, and that the one was loved because God nodded assent out of personal favour, while the other was hated (Romans 9:13). So the apostle of necessity does away in advance with this view of the matter as ruinous … For if, he says, even before the infants had done anything, before any testing of them and before any deeds, the one was thought worthy of love and the other was hated, and was even appointed to serve the younger (Romans 9:11–12), then perhaps, he says, God is even unjust.

And then how is this not senseless?

For if Jacob had not become a good man, if Esau had not been wicked, one might reasonably say that the foreknowledge had perhaps gone astray, and that what was determined for both of them was the work of a random impulse and an unsteady will. But since Esau was very perverse and Jacob wise, God’s foreknowledge would do no wrong at all in granting, even ahead of time, to the one who was good in his ways that he should be loved, and to the one who was not such that he should be condemned. For it would have been no hard thing for God to bear with them patiently and wait for the time of their deeds, so that each might be shown plainly by his own actions.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul meets the charge of injustice in God's loving Jacob and hating Esau by denying it, which sends us to look for the answer by another route than foreknowledge.
comments.comment: Again, concerning Esau and Jacob, the apostle, as if speaking in a dilemma, says: 'What then shall we say to this? Is there injustice with God? May it never be!' (Romans 9:14). Because he had refuted injustice, he forced us to seek how there is not injustice with God. If it were so, as those who speak of foreknowledge say, we would rather find injustice in Him. 'I loved Jacob,' He says, 'but I hated Esau' (Romans 9:13). But one is hated or loved according to things done and according to things thought. How then does foreknowledge have room? Is injustice found with God? But he, refuting this, said: 'What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? May it never be!' Since there is no injustice, let the matter be sought in another way, how it has come to pass.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God is not unjust, for he does not fail to give each according to merit.
comments.comment: What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? (Rom 9:14) May it never be! For He says to Moses: I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I will have compassion (Rom 9:15). Therefore, it is not of the one willing nor of the one running, but of the God showing mercy (Rom 9:16). … But it is not so; for God is not unrighteous so as not to give to each according to his merit (Romans 9:14).
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: God is faithful and not unjust in showing mercy to some and not to others, for mercy is not given because of our works but by God's wise authority.
comments.comment: No one should suppose, he says, that those things which do not belong to the logic of justice are to have injustice in God, but rather, those things being administered according to the administration of mercy, have injustice in God; for God is faithful and there is no injustice in Him, nor is it unrighteous to show mercy to those whom He may seem to show mercy to, and others not, whom He may not wish to show mercy to. For he has said, he says, through Moses, and has made known the manner of mercy, not by the counter-measurement of human standards, but according to the wisdom of God which encompasses it, so that it is not of our works that mercy is shown, but of God who has mercy by sovereign authority. For mercy is distinguished from judging, and each man becomes the cause of himself regarding the answers he owes, reaping what he sows, according to the Apostle. But for those given out of mercy, God is the cause, knowing with wisdom and administering to whom He must and must not.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God has pity on those to whom mercy is fitting, as he told Moses, so the matter is beyond all reproach.
comments.comment: [If, in keeping with his foreknowledge,] he, as God, again has pity on those he may choose, or rather on those to whom it is fitting that mercy be shown, for he said somewhere to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion” (Exodus 33:19; Romans 9:15), then how will the matter not be beyond all reproach?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul sets out the objection that arises from ignorance, that if Esau, Jacob and Pharaoh are so treated, everything about us depends on God's nod.
comments.comment: The apostle, I think, clearly foresaw that some would perhaps suppose that it is by God’s nod that some are good and others disobedient. So of necessity he himself puts forward the objection that springs from their ignorance, and says, “So then it depends not on the one who wills, nor on the one who runs, but on God who has mercy” (Romans 9:16). For if Esau was hated even before he had done anything wicked, and Jacob was honoured even before he came into being, and if again God has mercy on whom he has mercy, is it not then right to conclude that the one who runs or wills, that is, the one eager to do something good, gains nothing, and that everything about us hangs on the nods of God? Then he heaps on top of these the words that could fix that opinion still more firmly, and says, “For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, ‘For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you’” (Romans 9:17; Exodus 9:16). To these he adds what is, as it were, the conclusion of the whole problem, and says, “So then he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills” (Romans 9:18).
comments.selected_reason: Shows the objection Paul himself raises against his own teaching on God's mercy and hardening.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Nothing God does is in vain, and the judgment on Pharaoh benefits the whole world, for all who see it are seized with fear and wonder.
comments.comment: And this is not in vain; for nothing is in vain or irrational on the part of God, but each thing is pre-ordained by wonderful words, just as He has made known concerning Pharaoh; for the Scripture says to Pharaoh: 'I raised you up for this very purpose, so that I might show My power in you, and so that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth' (Ex 9:16). Behold, the not showing mercy to Pharaoh. It has been shown that it happens through the benefit of the whole cosmos, so that all, perceiving the judgment against the impious as much as possible, are seized with fear and wonder toward Him who has judged these things and has done them.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God used Pharaoh to display his strength so that his name might be proclaimed, and Pharaoh deserved what he suffered for his earlier sins.
comments.comment: God made use of this man to display the strength that is in himself, so that his name might be proclaimed in all the earth (Romans 9:17), and so that Pharaoh, when he suffered, might be seen to deserve his suffering; for suffering was owed to him for his first sins, even if he had not offended by his later ones.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God raised up Pharaoh only because he foresaw that Pharaoh was stubbornly diseased.
comments.comment: And again the Scripture says to Pharaoh: For this very purpose I raised you up, so that I might show my power in you, and so that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth (Exod 9:16). Is not then Pharaoh not to blame, but the one raising him up for the showing of his own power? But even this is not so; for he would not have raised him, even though through him he was admonishing the others, if he had not foreseen him being stubbornly diseased.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: God could never make anything evil, for all he made was very good, and Pharaoh shared the same nature as the rest of us.
comments.comment:
…he himself, someone says, hardened Pharaoh’s heart (Exodus 9:12); and indeed he said to him, “For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you” (Exodus 9:16; Romans 9:17). If, then, he both hardens some and raises them up, who are vessels of wrath and are said to be prepared for destruction (Romans 9:22), “why does he still find fault? For who has resisted his will?” (Romans 9:19). And how could the one hardened by him have become good?

What, then, could I say to this? To know the truth, it is enough to be settled in the conviction that God could never be the maker of evil things; for all that he made was very good (Genesis 1:31). If, then, they insist that the Egyptian was not a human being and did not share the same nature as we do, let them prove it, and we too will keep silent. But if he was like us, let them either openly accuse the divine voice of not seeing what is good and what is not; or, if they shudder at that, let them confess that the things he brought into existence are good.

In this way they will reject that most rash opinion.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: "I raised you up" does not mean "I created you" but "I called you forth" to resist, so that Pharaoh, idolater and oppressor of Israel, was justly punished as a vessel of wrath.
comments.comment:
The words spoken to Pharaoh, “For this very purpose I raised you up” (Exodus 9:16), do not mean “I created you” or “I made you”, but rather “I called you forth, to the point of choosing to set yourself against me”; and this not at the start of his life, but when Moses was being sent to redeem Israel. On what grounds, and for what reason, the all-wise Paul will make plain to us: “For God,” he says, “desiring to show his wrath,” and the rest (Romans 9:22).

In times long past the whole earth had gone astray. Some worshipped the creation (Romans 1:25); others made an object of reverence of whatever seemed good to them. At length Abraham was called to knowledge, and so the race descended from him sprang up, devoted to the worship of God. But when they too went down into Egypt and then spent a long time there, they slid into deception and worshipped the gods of the land. Yet God remembered what he had promised to the fathers (Exodus 2:24). Moses had been appointed to the mission, to release Israel from slavery; but it was necessary, both for those called to worship him and for all on earth, not only to learn that after long ages the God of the Hebrews had been made manifest, but also to be confirmed by surpassing wonders in faith in him and in the conviction that he is not, like the other gods, voiceless and powerless, but rather himself steers the universe, and that wrath strikes those who act against his will. Yet, on the other hand, God, wishing to work wonders, had to be seen to have good grounds for doing so. So Pharaoh was raised up to resist, by God’s providential ordering, and grew hard against the divine power. For this reason he was punished, and not unjustly: for he was unholy and an idolater, he maltreated Israel with clay and brickmaking (Exodus 1:14), and he made toil their wage. Therefore he was of necessity named a vessel of wrath, and was prepared for destruction (Romans 9:22)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul answers the Jews' boast in the ceremonies by showing that God has power to reject whom he wishes and take whom he wishes among the peoples.
comments.comment: They [the Jews] boasted of observing ceremonies and sacrifices, and therefore supposed that other nations, consecrated by none of the Law's rites, neither could nor should suddenly be admitted to fellowship with them. He would tell them that even if the whole of righteousness had consisted in those observances, God would still have had power to make a change among the peoples, rejecting whom he wished and taking whom he wished. In answer to this meaning, a reply is made in the person of the Jews: nothing should now be demanded from the human will, since God “has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills” (Romans 9:18). To this the apostle replies: “O human being, who are you to answer back to God?” (Romans 9:20). He introduces the prophet Isaiah's testimony: “Does what is molded say to the one who molded it, ‘Why did you make me like this?’” (Isaiah 45:9; Romans 9:20). He adds in his own words: “Does the potter not have power over the clay to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Romans 9:21).
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Paul's answer is obscure, but it assures us that God gives each what befits him, mercy to some and, after long patience, punishment to the wicked.
comments.comment: “You will say to me then, ‘Why does he still find fault? For who has resisted his will?’” (Romans 9:19). What, then, was his way of answering? It is very obscure, and perhaps even seems to support the objections they raise; yet it is enough to assure us that nothing could come from God that lies outside what is fitting. For he gives to each what befits him: he pities and has mercy on those for whom mercy is fitting, and he subjects the wicked to punishment. Yet his wrath does not follow the offences at once and on their heels; rather, a long patience goes before it, so that some even suppose that God has stopped caring about those on earth. So Paul brings out his reply and stands up to those who say such things, directing the force of his words at the persons who had been brought forward, I mean Esau and also Pharaoh. He spoke, then, as though to each of those he had named: “But who indeed are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will what is moulded say to the one who moulded it, ‘Why have you made me like this?’” (Romans 9:20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul answers the objector with the image of the clay: God gives each what befits him.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul rebukes the one who boldly searches out God's will and shows human nature's insignificance by the image of the potter's clay.
comments.comment: For who has opposed his will? For if he himself performs all things through us, we are nothing in authority over what we do. But indeed, O man, who are you, the one answering back to God? Does not the thing formed say to the one who formed it: Why did you make me thus? (Rom 9:19-20). Correcting all the preceding, he reproves indeed as if you were boldly searching out the will of God, but he also shows the insignificance of human nature, taking the clay of the potter as a fitting image.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: The potter image does not strip us of free will, for those who can complain to God must be masters of themselves.
comments.comment: Therefore, if God manages something according to foreknowledge, whether he raised up Pharaoh or hated Esau and loved Jacob, let no one suppose because of these things that nothing is upon us, but rather that our autonomy is being cut away. Some have spoken this, not as a reproach, but to say: 'Nevertheless, O man, who are you to answer back to God?' For they say it is absurd to have sought such great questions, unsettling the listener's mind without resolving any of them, but only rebuking those who seek to simply flee from the things sought, while also appearing to strip us of autonomy by the image of the potter, as if the potter fashions the vessels as he wills, while the rest remains as it has become from the beginning. They say these things unworthy of the apostolic grace and teaching. The word is not spoken as a reproach, but the mind holds it thus: if from which, he says, he raised up Pharaoh and hated Esau and loved Jacob, and before their birth gave all things in the will of God, and nothing is upon us, then in short: who are you, O man, and how do you answer back to God? And how do you have the authority to speak and to accuse him as if he reproaches us unjustly, saying, 'Why is he still reproaching?' … How then do you charge God, if nothing lies in our power as you say? For if nothing is up to us, neither is it in your power to complain or to answer back to God. 'Not the things of the potter,' he says, 'the vessels, since they lack sensation; they complain against the maker even if they become dishonorable, or even if they become honorable according to the maker's power' (Rom 9:21). But you complain, so you have sensation and power, as having a will that is free. And he who has the power to complain, it is evident that he is also master of himself in all other things, to say and to do what he wills. For he is not a master of himself only in complaining to God, but in other things he is deprived of mastery.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Paul cuts down rash curiosity about God's purposes, since a creature can no more know its Creator's mind than clay can, and the Creator may shape each as he sees fit.
comments.comment:
And regarding these things, the apostle moves the word forward to two points: first, to show that it is not fitting for men to search out the depths of God; and second, to preserve the most correct word of salvation, since some are not receiving mercy and some are receiving mercy. For he says, 'the creature does not say to the creator' (Romans 9:20), and the following. This first cuts down the rash curiosity of many, who, seeking to examine the purposes of God subtly, attempt to unearth things unsearchable for men down to the finest detail.

For who are you, he says, that you would judge God? And about what things are you searching so intently? It is impossible for you to know the mind of the Creator, just as it is for a creature to know the mind of its maker; for you differ in nothing from a soulless thing in being able to grasp the purpose of God. Moreover, it also absurdly attempts to cut into the authority of God, as if he were not obligated to have authority to arrange each of those being made in whatever way he would wish and deem beneficial, even if the nature of all is one and all are recipients of mercy. For just as the potter has the authority, with the same single material of clay being present, to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor, so also the Creator of all things, foreknowing the future through the present, brings forth one to be shown mercy and another to be shown wrath.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God, like a potter, has authority to honour whom he wants and to punish whom he wills.
comments.comment: Did God not have authority as He wished? But a potter indeed fashions some for honor and others for dishonor, yet God does not have the authority that the potter has, so as to honor whom He wants and to punish whom He wills? Having said this out of surplus, he subsequently makes the solution.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The clay must not judge the potter's art, and no one should think God shows mercy or hardens at random, for he bestows according to foreknowledge of worth.
comments.comment: For what does he say, why does he question the Creator? The potter knows how to use the clay and what kind of vessels are to be made for dishonor and what kind for honor. But the clay, being clay, must not judge the art of the Creator; for even if you seem to have rational perception, O man, you are left so far removed from the economy and art of God as to be an unfeeling clay to the potter's will. Therefore, do not dare to accuse God, nor suppose that he happens to show mercy to one and harden the other, but rather that according to the power of foreknowledge he bestows upon each according to his worth. Thus, it is not the one foreknowing who is the cause, but those who are foreknown, upon which it is for them to be evil or not. For he teaches that this is in us, through others; for speaking of vessels of gold, silver, and earthenware, he says: if anyone cleanses himself, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified. So we provide the cause, but God bestows according to worth.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: The potter image does not mean that some are made evil by nature, for Jeremiah shows that God moulds each for honour or dishonour according to what they do.
comments.comment: To such arguments one might reply, first of all, that they could not claim that the force of these thoughts hints to us at differences of nature. For he did not say that some were made harsh and hardened, or made into vessels of honour and of dishonour, nor did he assign them such a nature at all. Rather, he leads us to think this: that some are moulded like vessels of clay, some for honour and some for dishonour; and we have been taught the meaning of the illustration from the words of the prophets. In what way, then, some are moulded as if by a potter, some for honour and others for dishonour, and for what causes, anyone may learn by reading the words of Jeremiah. It is written thus: “Arise and go down to the potter’s house, and there you will hear my words. And I went down to the potter’s house, and there he was, making a piece of work on the stones. And the vessel that he was making fell in his hands; and again he made it into another vessel, as it seemed good in his sight to make it. And the word of the Lord came,” he says, “to me, saying: Shall I not be able to make you as this potter does, house of Israel? Look, like the potter’s clay, you are in my hands. At last I will speak against a nation or against a kingdom, to root them out; and that nation will turn from all its evils, and I will relent concerning the evils that I planned to do to them. And at last I will speak concerning a nation and concerning a kingdom, to build it up and to plant it; and they will do evil before me, so as not to hear my voice, and I will relent concerning the good things that I said I would do for them” (Jeremiah 18:2–10). Do you see how some are moulded for honour and for dishonour, not because they were allotted a nature made that way, but because they receive an equal and fitting return for what they do? So if the Maker of all punishes the one who passes from good ways to more shameful ones, and crowns with honours the one who moves from the more shameful to the better, how is it not true to say that some have by no means become evil by nature, or been moulded so by him, but have rather become vessels of dishonour because, though it was open to them to choose to win approval with God, they fell sick with a willing inclination toward evil?
comments.selected_reason: Explains the potter image: people become vessels of honour or dishonour by their own choices, not by a nature given to them.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The demonstration of wrath is forgiven through long-suffering, but vessels of wrath are under death's limit.
comments.comment: He speaks of a demonstration of wrath (Rom 9:22), which He forgives to men through long-suffering, allowing them to do what they want; but he speaks of men as vessels of wrath prepared for destruction (Rom 9:22), who are under the limit of death.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: God bore with the vessels of wrath so as to benefit the vessels of mercy, who are those called through faith from both Jews and Gentiles.
comments.comment: So let every reproach and every idle charge against God be dismissed. For “desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, he endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction” (Romans 9:22), in order to benefit vessels of mercy (Romans 9:23), that is, those who have received mercy through faith; for we have been called not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles (Romans 9:24).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the vessels of mercy are: those who have received mercy through faith, Jews and Gentiles alike.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Vessels of wrath and of mercy receive their lot as the wages of their own will, for Paul says elsewhere that whoever cleanses himself becomes a vessel for honour.
comments.comment: Most consistently, then, Paul adds that vessels made for dishonor and those made for honor receive this as the wages of their own will: “If God, wishing to show his wrath and make his power known with great patience in vessels of wrath completed for destruction, and to make known the riches of his glory in vessels of mercy which he prepared for glory, whom he also called, namely us, not only from Jews but also from the nations” (Romans 9:22–24). Here he certainly clears up what the previous debate had concealed: God brings wrath only upon vessels completed for destruction, while glory is given to those prepared for it. By whom such vessels are prepared to receive the things we have named, the apostle's own words disclose: “In a great house there are not only gold and silver vessels but also wooden and earthenware ones, some for honor and some for dishonor. If, then, anyone cleanses himself from these, he will be a vessel sanctified for honor, useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work” (2 Timothy 2:21).
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: The servants of idols who were not God's people have received mercy through faith and been called, justified and sanctified through Christ.
comments.comment: “As indeed he says in Hosea” (Romans 9:25). We too, the servants of idols, who did not know the one who is God by nature and in truth, were not his people (Hosea 2:23); but we have received mercy through faith, have come under him, have been called through grace, and have been justified and sanctified through Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Even if Israel were as many as the sand, only the remnant justified through faith will be saved, and the gospel is a short, simple word compared with the long circuit of the law and prophets.
comments.comment: “Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea” (Romans 9:27). So even if Israel were as many as the sand, “the remnant will be saved” (Romans 9:27; Isaiah 10:22), that is, those who have been justified through faith in Christ; and this has come about because God had mercy on them. “For he is completing and cutting short the word” (Romans 9:28). He saved, he says, by “completing and cutting short the word”; that is, he declared to us the preaching of the gospel as an apt and concise and, so to speak, cut-short saying. For the law and the prophets, by a long circuit of words, scarcely set before us through the letter the meaning of what they say; but the preaching of the gospel is simple and a word cut short.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by God 'cutting short the word': the gospel is simple and concise.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Jews fell away because they sought to be justified by works of the law, not believing in the law that invited them to faith.
comments.comment: Since it has been said in the things before, that the nation of the Jews is cast off by the part that prevails, while the nations are contending for the status of adoption, it follows by seeking the cause for which those practicing in the law have fallen away, while those who have grasped the law were justified (Rom 9:29-31). He then concludes by explaining that the Jews fell away from running toward faith just as the nations did; for they desired to be justified by works of law, not believing in the law which invited them.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: It is strange that those with no aim of doing good were justified while Israel, trained by the law, missed righteousness, because it would not accept salvation through faith in Christ.
comments.comment: “But Israel, pursuing a law of righteousness” (Romans 9:31). In giving the reasons why not all the Jews have been saved, he at once weaves wonder into his argument and says: What a strange thing! The crowd of those who had gone astray, with no aim at all of doing good, has been justified (Romans 9:30), while Israel, though trained toward righteousness by the law given through Moses, missed its hope and has had no share in the gift that leads to it (Romans 9:31). What the cause is, then, is plain: they did not accept salvation through faith and justification in Christ, but thought that the boasts they had, as in shadows, were enough for them (Romans 9:32).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Israel missed the righteousness it pursued: it rested on the shadows of the law instead of faith in Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ was not set in Israel to make them stumble, but God foretold the stumbling so that, knowing it, they might rise above it, and Christ is ruin to unbelievers and life to believers.
comments.comment: “A stone of stumbling” (Romans 9:33). Surely we do not say that Christ was set in Israel for this purpose; but since this was foreknown to God, he of necessity foretold what was to be: that a cause of slipping would lie in the foundations of Zion, and that some of the foolish would fall upon it and suffer this from their disobedience (Isaiah 8:14; Isaiah 28:16). He made the prediction for their benefit, not that they should stumble, but that, knowing it beforehand, they might rise above the evil. So Christ has been laid as a precious stone (Isaiah 28:16); but for those who stumble out of unbelief the loss was ruin, while for those who have believed the gain is life and justification.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'stone of stumbling': God foretold it for their benefit, and it brings ruin or life depending on faith.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul's saying is gathered from two places in Isaiah, one calling the Lord a stone of stumbling and the other a precious cornerstone.
comments.comment: The stated word lies scattered within the prophecies of Isaiah (Rom 9:33), not as it is now said by the apostle, being gathered together. For concerning the beginning of the book it has been written regarding the Lord according to the edition which Aquila agreed with and the apostolic one: 'He himself is your fear and he himself is your trembling, and he will be for sanctification and for a stone of stumbling, a solid stone of offense (Isa 8:14). And after much it is, that behold, I lay in the foundations of Zion a precious stone, an elect cornerstone, honorable, and he who believes will never be ashamed (Isa 28:16).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ is the stone of stumbling, over which some are shattered through disobedience while those who believe in him escape shame.
comments.comment: A stone of stumbling and a rock of offense (Romans 9:33); and the one who believes upon him will not be put to shame. When righteous Symeon received the divine infant into his arms, he said to God: “Now you release your servant, Master, according to your word in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation which you prepared before the face of all the peoples,” (Luke 2:29–34) and what follows; and he added: “Behold, this one is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign spoken against.” (Luke 2:34) So the same one is the stone of stumbling and the rock of offense; and some, striking against him through disobedience, were shattered, while those who received the faith toward him escaped being put to shame.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: The Jews failed to see that God promised faith through the law, so by setting up the law's constitution as their righteousness they fell from the salvation that comes by faith in Christ.
comments.comment: Regarding the tendency to oppose faith against the law. They did not recognize, he says, that through the law God promised faith, and faith is not contrary to the law as being testified by it (Rom 10:1–3). Therefore, the righteousness of God is Christ and the faith in him, but the righteousness of the Jews is the political constitution of the law. Thus, the Jews, not knowing Christ and setting up the political constitution of the law, appropriately fell away from salvation; for they are saved, those making progress through the faith of Christ. For faith, being a disposition of the soul, is appropriately preferred over the deeds of the flesh, to which it was necessary for the Jews to come, having placed the law as an end.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Paul grants their zeal yet convicts them of straying.
comments.comment: “For I bear them witness” (Romans 10:2). He bears them witness, then, to their zeal for God; yet he convicts them of having gone astray …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The righteousness of God is the righteousness that comes to all who believe through Jesus Christ, and it differs from the human righteousness the Jews sought to establish.
comments.comment: Paul, writing about the difference of these things concerning the Jews, says, 'For I testify to them that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge; for knowing not the righteousness of God, but seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to the righteousness of God' (Romans 10:2-3). By saying the righteousness of God, he means that which comes to all who believe through Jesus Christ, which He Himself also desired. He says all things were sent so that one might be found having the righteousness from God through faith and not his own. Wishing this to be present also for the disciples, Jesus says to them, 'If your righteousness does not exceed that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you will by no means enter the kingdom of heaven' (Matthew 5:20). This distinction between human righteousness and that of God, according to the will of the Lord, is to be judged, knowing how this judgment will lead Him to salvation.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Jews did not know the righteousness from God, which is Christ or the righteousness through faith in him, so they stayed disobedient to the Son who frees and justifies.
comments.comment: Or it may be read in this way: they have not known the righteousness that comes from God (Romans 10:3), that is, Christ, or else the righteousness that comes through faith in him. Supposing that they were fighting side by side with the law given through Moses, they remained disobedient, not seeking the Son who is able to set free (John 8:36), who justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5), and who, in his saving dispensation, cuts short the righteousness of the law, so hard to achieve, to give release from hardship and toil.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'the righteousness that comes from God' means: Christ, or righteousness through faith in him.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ is the end of the law in the sense that he completes it, as the truth fulfils the riddles and as colours added to a sketch bring out its outlines.
comments.comment: “For Christ is the end of the law” (Romans 10:4). The law, then, was brought in beforehand to be a tutor for the people of old, leading them to the mystery of Christ (Galatians 3:24), and to give them glimpses of the truth through riddles. That is how we define Christ as the fulfilment of the law and the prophets, and quite rightly. Or would not the truth reasonably be understood to be the fulfilment of every obscure riddle? And how could anyone doubt it? So the passage from what was in shadows to the truth does not do away with the laws given through Moses; rather, it makes their meaning clearer. Now that things have passed over into truth, and what was in types and riddles has been changed for the better, we do not say that the law has been abolished, but rather that it has been brought to completion at the time when the truth, that is, Christ, shone upon us. For Christ is the end of the law and the prophets, and he would not speak falsely when he says, “I did not come to abolish the law but to fulfil it” (Matthew 5:17). For just as the many colours, added in due time, by no means do away with the shadowy outlines first sketched on painted panels, but rather bring them into clearer view, in the same way we say that the shadows of the law have not been overturned, but rather brought to completion, as in an advance toward the truth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'end of the law' as fulfilment, not abolition.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ is the beginning of another life, and the law has two ends, since he both used it and brought it to a stop.
comments.comment: Christ is not as a part of the law, but as a beginning of another life (Rom 10:4). Therefore it is said that the end of the law, as having become the end of the law, is this: that He stopped it (Rom 10:4). So there are two ends of the law, because He used it and because He stopped it.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Because no one is justified in the law but everyone who believes in Christ is, the law was preparing the way to Christ, who is its fullness and the salvation of men.
comments.comment: For Christ is the end of the law for justification (Rom 10:4). For not being justified, he says, a man in the law, but having believed in Christ he is justified, just as it has been preached in Antioch of Pisidia saying: 'Let it be known to you, brothers, that through this to you the forgiveness of sins is announced, and from all things from which you were not able to be saved in the law, in this everyone who believes is justified (Acts 13:38-39).' If therefore that which was strived for by the law, but because of human weakness was not perfected, this Christ provides to those believing, imparting of the holy righteousness; the end of the law is Christ, and toward Christ the law was preparing, showing this one to be both the fullness of himself and the salvation of men.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Only the one who fulfils the law enjoys what it promised.
comments.comment: The one having fulfilled the law, he says, will alone enjoy the good things promised through the law, that is, a land flowing with milk and honey (Rom 10:4–5).
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: No one could carry out the righteousness of the law blamelessly, so the grace that justifies is better and frees us from the law's indictment.
comments.comment: “For Moses writes of the righteousness that is from the law,” and the rest (Romans 10:5). “For Moses writes,” he says, “of the righteousness that is from the law, that the person who does it shall live by it” (Romans 10:5; Leviticus 18:5). But there was no one at all who could carry it out blamelessly; for “who will understand transgressions?” (Psalm 19:12). So the grace that justifies is better, and it frees us from the indictment that stands in the law.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the righteousness from the law could not save and why grace is better.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Faith must be free of doubt and of prying into what lies beyond reason, because the things God works are beyond words and no eye of the heart can behold God.
comments.comment: “But the righteousness that is from faith speaks thus” (Romans 10:6). He usefully lays down how faith should be practised on our part, if it is to be blameless before God and to seem very well done indeed. For to doubt at all, and to be given to being tossed about into feeble double-mindedness, is utterly to be rejected; and it is perhaps superfluous, and among the most dangerous things of all, to think one must pry into what lies beyond all reason and above our understanding. For how could the things God works in ways beyond words be plain to see? And what eye of the heart could be so great as to be able to behold God? Or rather, who will understand, even if someone chose to speak and set out things that are very far above us?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ showed Nicodemus how far the human mind is from heavenly things, so matters beyond reason call for faith with no idle questioning.
comments.comment:
…our Lord Jesus Christ once set before Nicodemus the words about spiritual rebirth, and he said, “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born from above, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:3, 5). [Then he added to these the words that follow.] But when Nicodemus understood nothing at all, then indeed Christ, showing how far the dullness of the human mind stands from the fineness of these thoughts, says, “If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?” (John 3:12). And to these he added, “Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak of what we know and bear witness to what we have seen, and no one receives our testimony” (John 3:11).

So the things that are beyond us are not to be put to the test. For if it is true that “we find with difficulty the things that are in our hands,” as it is written (Wisdom of Solomon 9:16), how can we not see that, in matters beyond reason at least, faith is of the greatest use, with no inquiry following after it and no idle questioning brought to bear? For it is by understanding that matters of this kind are splendidly honoured.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Believers are to doubt neither the Lord's descent nor the resurrection.
comments.comment: The word teaches those believing not to take up any doubt, neither concerning the descent of the Lord from heaven to us, nor concerning the resurrection of the dead and the ascent into heaven (Rom 10:6–10).
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: God let the ancients travel the long road of the law, with its shadows and riddles, as training, but Christ shows the straight and near road through faith, which gives boldness by the Holy Spirit.
comments.comment: ‘Near you is the word, in your mouth and in your heart—that is, the word of faith which we proclaim, that if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved; for with the heart it is believed unto righteousness, and with the mouth it is confessed unto salvation.’ (Romans 10:8–10) This road then, thus near and contracted, God was not letting those of old step through; but he was devising as it were some circuit not having the straight way—the law in turns of words and in enigmas, having a longer and not untroubled pedagogy—so that, having the things in shadows as a kind of practice of the more perfect, and being catechized beforehand into the mystery, they would not be simply terrified by whatever frights into flight and apostasy from Christ, but having been trained beforehand as it were and learning thoroughly what truly benefits, they would be readier toward desire and eagerness for the truth, and would have love toward God fixed and unshakeable. Through a long and as it were not straight road, then—the worship according to the letter—the law was pedagogue. But Christ is not so. For he showed us the straight and near one—that is, the one through faith—reforging into boldness, and into the need thereafter to play the man against those who stand opposed; and to love most of all to endure hardship for the good, and to set oneself nobly against the devil’s methods, saying perhaps that word in the prophet: ‘Behold the Lord helps me; who will mistreat me?’ (Isaiah 50:9) And what produces in us such admirable boldness would surely be nothing other than the power from on high—that is, the sharing and communion of the Holy Spirit.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 3

comments.capsule: Belief in the heart unto righteousness is not enough without confession of the mouth unto salvation, and the mouth must say what the heart believes.
comments.comment: That is why God is 'believed in the heart' by such 'unto righteousness,' and 'confessed with the mouth' by such 'unto salvation' — who grasp that neither shall they be justified unless they so believe God with their heart so disposed, nor be in salvation unless, as the disposition is, so too the word. For they deceive themselves who think the 'for with the heart is believed unto righteousness' (Romans 10:10) suffices toward obtaining an end in Christ — even if the 'but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation' be not added. One might even say it is rather honoring with lips, with the heart 'far' from God, than honoring him 'with the heart,' when the mouth confesses not 'unto salvation.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul joins confessing with the mouth to believing in the heart.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Israel must not keep salvation through faith as its private good, since the God of all saves without distinction everyone who calls on the Lord.
comments.comment: “Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame” (Romans 10:11), and the rest. Let Israel not make salvation through faith its own private good. For, he says, “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13), whether he is a Jew or a Greek, a slave or free. The God of all saves without distinction, for all things are his. In this sense we say that all things are summed up in Christ (Ephesians 1:10).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'everyone who calls': Paul means Jew and Greek, slave and free alike.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God gives grace to those who ask and entreat, and he even provided a way around ignorance by sending evangelists and preachers to call people to ask.
comments.comment: He has necessarily set forth those calling upon him; for God does not arbitrarily give grace, and he does not refuse to provide even so much as to those willing to ask and entreat the Benefactor (Rom 10:11–13). In order that no one might say that many do not call upon the Lord Jesus not through unbelief and ignorance, but through simple lack of knowledge, he shows through the following: that God even provided a way around their ignorance, having sent evangelists and preachers, exhorting and calling toward the request for the gift. Therefore, he brought forward the following.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: The Jews could not call on the Lord because they did not believe, having an unsuitability even after hearing, as the Lord's own words to them showed.
comments.comment: It is not possible, therefore, for them to call upon Him, he says, because they did not believe. And they were not able to believe, having an unsuitability, even after hearing, just as the Lord was conversing with them in a concealed manner, and showing that there was only a little among them capable of hearing, saying: 'Let him who has ears to hear, hear' (Matthew 13:9). And being present with them, having the transition from them, he had an aim, saying: 'O perverse generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I endure you?' (Mt 17:17) (Matthew 15:24). And because they were unable to hear him and to believe, he said: 'You do not believe, that you are not of my sheep. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me' (John 10:26-27).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Jews' strife deprived them of the universal grace, so that those not calling on the Lord, like the blind or deaf, were deprived of the salvation sent to the nations.
comments.comment:
