… that the salvation of the Lord's calling is for all men, but the previously mentioned strife of the Jews deprived them of the universal grace, having a private unfitness for the common good, because of which the apostleship, the preaching, the hearing, the faith, and the calling stood not toward them, but toward the nations.

Just as light, being common to all by nature, becomes foreign to those darkening themselves, and the sun shines not for the blind nor rises, nor does the one who has cried out speak to the deaf, so indeed the ones sent and preaching do nothing toward the Jews; for it is a prerequisite that they are unable to hear, as if they had fallen into deafness toward the divine preachings, whence they were deprived of salvation by not calling upon Him, just as it was revealed in the prophet: 'For there is not,' he says, 'one who calls upon your name and remembers to take hold of you, because you turned your face away from us.'
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The cause of the Jews' not calling on the Lord is the mystery of God's plan, by which the apostles were sent to the nations and turned to the Gentiles when Israel cast the word aside.
comments.comment: But he does not prove the fault of the Jews, as I said being previously advanced in the present, but rather the mystery of the economy concerning them is the cause of their not calling upon the Lord, namely that the apostles were sent not to them but to the nations, just as the Lordly command has: 'Having gone, make disciples of all nations.' And the apostles did not transgress the command by starting toward the Jews first and later turning to the nations when they were expelled by them, but the one who gave the order knew to whom the preaching was to end, those of the former who were not receiving it graciously. Nor does the apostle now say anything contrary to what he previously practiced, while conversing with the Jews, asserting that the apostleship was not sent to them, but according to the determination and the foreknowledge of God is given to the Gentiles; the aim being rather that the apostles would walk toward the persecution of Israel, just as Moses walked toward Pharaoh: for God knew that they would not believe and had said previously, 'I know that you will not persuade Pharaoh' (Exod 3:19). And there, too, the end of Pharaoh's opposition was the showing of the signs for the benefit of the world; but here, the end of the Jews' unbelief became the movement of the apostles toward the Gentiles according to that word of Paul: 'It was necessary for you first to have the word of the Lord spoken, but since you cast it aside and do not judge yourselves worthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles' (Acts 13:46). For thus the Lord has commanded us. This, therefore, was the command, and toward the Gentiles was the apostleship.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Paul asks how they will hear without a preacher, and the prophecy of the beautiful feet shows that preachers of God's peace and good things are not lacking.
comments.comment: And because of this, Paul says, as if no one had been sent to them nor preached; how shall they hear without preaching? and how shall they preach if they are not sent? And the fact that they do not call upon the Lord fixed the matter from not having been sent to them as God's judgment, showing rather nothing of the judgment, but only himself remembering the economy; as it is written, 'How beautiful are the feet of those preaching peace', those preaching good things (Rom 10:15). For it is evident, he says, also from the prophecy, that it is not without those preaching, who indeed release a voice like something beautiful and extraordinary as from a mountain, who preach the peace of God and the good things, pleasing the ear with beauty and quieting the hearing with greatness
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Israel wrongly supposed the gospel among the Gentiles was foreign, for Moses foretold that God would honour a non-nation in place of the nation that took up vain idols.
comments.comment: But they suppose, he says, irrationally, as if the Gospel in the Gentiles were something foreign and without agreement (Rom 10:19); for it is not to say that this was kept silent from them or not foretold. Immediately, indeed, the Lawgiver Moses says that God will repay them in kind for the foolish nations' preference, which they themselves began toward God by the worship of vain idols, and as they deemed the non-God to be God instead of the true God, so God will honor the non-nation as a nation instead of the nation that was previously with him, calling the things that are not as though they were, that he might annul the things that are, … And the zeal which was stirred up in them through their association with demons will bring them forward to the nations through His own power which He has joined to them.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God's hands stretched out toward the people show the form of the cross.
comments.comment: It seems that through the falling away of the hands, the people calls to himself by stretching out the hands toward them, and through the same, he shows the form of the cross (Rom 10:21).
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Paul does not let hardened Israel despair but wins it with kind words, proving by his own case as an Israelite called to apostleship that God has not rejected his people.
comments.comment: “Has God rejected his people? By no means” (Romans 11:1). Paul acts wisely. Although Israel had suffered the darkening, he does not let it be hardened still further by utter despair, but he goes after it, as it were, with skill and with kind words. For just now he was accusing Israel of disobedience; yet he does not strip it of the hope that comes from above, nor does he say that it has been wholly thrust out of its closeness to God. And he makes the proof of the matter plain by setting himself forward as an Israelite and of the seed of Abraham (Romans 11:1). Most aptly, too, he still calls them God’s people, and he adds “By no means” to the words about being rejected. This was the act of one who, as it were, gently wins over those who had chosen to disobey, coming round them with coaxing words and bringing them to a devout and teachable habit of mind. If, then, it is evident that he himself has been called to apostleship, and has been appointed a minister of the sacred mysteries of the Saviour, a herald and apostle to the nations (1 Timothy 2:7), although he is from Israel, it is plain that “God has not rejected his people” (Romans 11:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul answers 'Has God rejected his people?' with himself as proof, and why he is so gentle.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul brings in Elijah as a picture of Israel's fall, since Israel acted outrageously to its own harm.
comments.comment: “Or do you not know what the Scripture says in the story of Elijah?” (Romans 11:2). Most fittingly he brings in the account of Elijah as a kind of picture of what had happened to Israel. For from the likeness of the events of that time one can easily see that Israel itself has acted outrageously, to its own harm. When Ahab reigned over Samaria, things carved by hand were worshipped by Israel beyond all bounds, and there were sacrifices and sacred precincts everywhere (1 Kings 16:29–33). Those who held fast to God were utterly afraid, …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Israel's apostasy, like that of Elijah's day, was not driven by God but chosen by Israel itself, so God has not rejected a people to whom he offered salvation in Christ.
comments.comment:
… at the time when Elijah himself fled into the deep wilderness and fell down before God, saying, “They have torn down your altars, they have killed your prophets, and I alone am left, and they seek my life” (Romans 11:3; 1 Kings 19:10). And at once he heard in answer to this, “I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal” (Romans 11:4; 1 Kings 19:18).

But just as then it was not God who drove Israel into such dreadful impieties, but they slipped down of themselves, following their own folly, so now again, when God the Father set before all the salvation that comes through Christ and thrust no one away at all, they slipped of their own will into apostasy, having pushed aside the Redeemer. So God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:2); for, as I said, he set before them the chance to share in the salvation that comes through Christ, if only they would choose it.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul speaks of a small remnant by election, as with Elijah's seven thousand, for grace shows the goodness of the giver while works demand wages by merit.
comments.comment: Having again feared that the abundance of the rejection of the Jews might produce a sect of disobedience, the apostle speaks of a small remnant of the election and of those who believed together with them (Romans 11:5). For he had previously said: 'For not all those who are of Israel are Israel, these are Israel' (Romans 9:6), and he noted that there were some being saved, even if not all (Romans 11:5); and again: 'whom he called not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles' (Romans 9:24). For a testimony of the remnant, he takes up the matters concerning Elijah, from which he shows him acknowledging that God was saving his people not in a great multitude, but in seventy thousand men (Romans 11:4); a remnant which indeed, in likeness, also went forth regarding the Savior, having received the promise by grace alone. For it has already been foretold that faith ended the law, while grace prevailed over works (Rom 11:6).
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: If anyone wins approval by works, grace becomes pointless, because a wage is owed and not given as grace.
comments.comment: “But if by grace, it is no longer from works,” and the rest (Romans 11:6). “But if by grace,” he says, “it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace.” Where, he says, someone supposes that he wins approval from works, there the name and the reality of grace will surely be pointless and superfluous; for, he says, “to the one who works, the wage is not counted as grace but as what is owed” (Romans 4:4). So if grace comes from works, it is no longer grace.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why grace and works exclude each other.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul meets the objection that God has rejected Israel by saying that Israel sought justification through the law's types and did not obtain it, while the elect who were ready to obey were justified by faith.
comments.comment: “What then? Israel did not obtain what it seeks” (Romans 11:7). He had said, “God has not rejected his people” (Romans 11:2). But since some were likely to rise up against this, putting forward, no doubt, this objection and saying, “Yet how has God not rejected his people, if Israel has slipped away, even if not entirely and completely, yet at least in part? For a remnant has been saved, and that by election” (Romans 11:5), he meets them again, and very wisely, and says, “What then?”, that is, what do I say to this? “Israel did not obtain what it seeks, but the elect obtained it, and the rest were hardened” (Romans 11:7). For Israel sought justification from the law; but how, he says, could it be justified, when the law had brought no one to perfection (Hebrews 7:19)? So Israel sought the justification that comes through the type, but did not obtain it; yet those who were picked out and set apart from the rest because of their readiness to obey did obtain it, for they have been justified through faith. But the rest have been hardened, that is, the stubborn and those who would not be corrected.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who 'the elect' and 'the rest' are, and why Israel did not obtain what it sought.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: All of Israel except the elect were hardened and so did not attain the promise of becoming sons and heirs of the world.
comments.comment: What then? he asks, what Israel seeks, it did not attain, but the election attained it; while the rest were hardened (Rom 11:7). All, he says, those of Israel were hardened except for the election; therefore they did not attain what they were seeking (Rom 11:7). And what were they seeking? The promise of becoming sons and heirs of the world (Rom 11:7).
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Scripture often credits God with what he only allows, for he lets each person follow his own choice rather than take away his freedom by force.
comments.comment: It is the custom of Scripture to refer matters concerning the forgiveness of God happening to men to the One who forgives (Rom 11:8). And God forgives according to each person's impulse to move toward what He wills, so that they might not seem to seize freedom by force. For he says such a thing: a spirit of stupor toward godliness He gave to them, but neither do they see nor do they hear.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Isaiah's spirit of stupor is the absence of the enlightening Spirit, which lets the house empty of divine power be filled by evil spirits, so God does not work evil.
comments.comment: The continuous word of the prophet Isaiah was taken up by the apostle according to his own knowledge from the Hebrew; for the version of the Seventy has, 'the Lord has given you to drink a spirit of stupor,' which Aquila's has more clearly as 'slumber,' but Symmachus's as 'torpor.' Then it proceeds: and it blinds their eyes, so that those seeing the hidden things and remaining beyond the ignorance of the prophetic words, appear to them as if they were a sealed book and as if they were unreadable writings. For the ambiguity, as if sealing the prophetic book and making reading unnecessary for those reading, makes it as if anyone were unable even to read. The ones having followed Christ had their minds opened to the understanding of the Scriptures, as the Gospel says, and the ones of those having followed, having heard, were led into knowledge, just as the eunuch was by Philip; but the others, in not happening to receive enlightenment, seem to be blind and deaf. For the Apostle also joined the matter of the deafness of the ears, having understood from another part of the prophecy 'they will hear with their ears and not understand'; for not understanding is equal to not hearing, according to what is written: 'let him who has ears hear.' And it is also said regarding those who heard heavily. The absence of the enlightening Spirit gives place to a spirit of stupor and insensibility, constantly increasing ignorances and darkening them; for God does not work evil, because 'out of the mouth of the Lord neither evil things nor good things shall come forth,' but the house desolate of divine power allows evil spirits to dwell within, as the Savior has said. And thus, he who did not give the spirit of enlightenment gave a spirit of stupor.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Paul confirms his point with two prophets, and Israel's table became a snare in the cruel welcome it gave Christ at his crucifixion, which darkened its mind.
comments.comment: “And David says, ‘Let their table become a snare,’” and the rest (Romans 11:9; Psalm 69:22). “Let their table become a snare,” he says, and what follows. To prove what he has said he also brings in a prophetic text, and that of not one prophet but two, to confirm it, “so that every word may be established by the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Matthew 18:16; Deuteronomy 19:15). For their table has become accursed, and quite rightly: that is, the cruel welcome and the savagery that they showed toward Christ at the time of his crucifixion; for when he was thirsty, they brought him vinegar mixed with gall (Psalm 69:21; Matthew 27:34). For this reason they were also darkened in mind (Romans 11:10) and are bent down, picturing only the things on the earth.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Israel did not fall beyond recovery, since its fall served the salvation of the Gentiles, its error was a slip owing to ignorance, and 'to fall' can mean a time of misfortune.
comments.comment: Is it an irrecoverable fall? Far from it; for they did not undergo the passion upon their own destruction, so that the event might be a corpse and a ruin, but upon the salvation of the Gentiles, so that they might be called envious of these things. Thus, the established error is a slip deserving forgiveness due to existing ignorance. Let us not pay much attention to the difference of names, but to the demonstration of realities; and what Paul presents through the words, having taken them, let us not prevent the words from meaning something else. Immediately: will he who falls not rise again? It declares the sense of 'to fall' not as an unrecoverable state, as in 'my enemy does not rejoice over me, because I have fallen and I shall rise' (Micah 7:8), but 'to fall' declares a certain time of misfortune.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The prophets speak both of Israel's fall and of its being planted again, because the prophet speaks of the Israel being destroyed and the apostle of the Israel being saved.
comments.comment:
Rather, it is worthy to seek the matter: would Paul disagree with the prophet, saying: 'The house of Israel has fallen, and it shall no longer add to rising' (Amos 5:2)? Otherwise the prophet himself would seem to disagree with himself in the following, saying other good things and the end: 'And I will plant them upon their own land, and they shall never again be uprooted from the land which I gave them, says the Lord' (Amos 9:15). But the prophet Isaiah clearly solves the question: the remnant of the people that shall be saved, and Israel being called by a wholly different name; for he says the remaining ones shall be removed like a grape-fragment in a cluster, to be filled with the good things from God, dividing them toward the people: 'Behold, those serving me shall eat, but you shall hunger' (Isaiah 65:13), and the following. After much such opposition he says: 'For your name shall be left as an oath to my chosen ones, but you the Lord will lift up' (Isaiah 65:15-16); and to those serving me another name shall be called, as the blessed shall be blessed in God having been made certain, and the one swearing in the land shall swear in God having been made certain. And these foreign things are according to the Aquila edition, to which the Jews pay attention. Therefore it is necessary also for them to confess that there shall be a change of those who are to be saved from among them into another mind and polity, as it is true to say concerning them, either that they are not Israel, or truly these are Israel of the Israel being destroyed according to the flesh.

The prophet has spoken of the one being destroyed, but the apostle of the one being saved, separating him from the one according to the flesh.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The nations were called not to make Israel fall away for good but to make it jealous, as a parent provokes a sulking child to turn back, and Paul will not let anyone despair of Israel.
comments.comment: …insisting that the nations were not called for this reason, that Israel, having stumbled against Christ as against a stone (Romans 9:32–33), should fall away altogether from its hope in God, but rather so that, moved to jealousy by those who had been received beyond all expectation (Romans 11:11), they might choose to unlearn their baser ways, think better than before, and so receive the Redeemer. A short example will make the point. Children who are small and not yet grown sometimes fall into the sulks that suit those who are still infants. Then they run a little way off from father or mother, pour tears from their eyes for no real cause, and grieve their parents not a little; for the law of natural affection brings them to this. And then the parents, skilfully drawing them away from their pettiness and childish folly, simply catch up any child who happens to be near and give it the marks of their own affection, so making their own child jealous and, as it were, provoking it to turn back and love them. Something of this kind, as I think, is what the inspired Paul said had been done, since he does not allow anyone to despair of Israel, though it has stumbled.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'to make Israel jealous' with the picture of a parent drawing back a sulking child.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The call of the nations began with Israel's fall, as the apostles' turning to the nations after Israel judged itself unworthy shows.
comments.comment: The call of the nations had its beginning from the fall of Israel. And the apostles, preaching to the synagogues of the Jews, say: 'To you the word of salvation was sent; since you judge yourselves unworthy, behold, we turn to the nations.' (Acts 13:46) And the apostle, knowing what he knows about these things, says: 'By their fall salvation has come to the nations, to make them jealous.' (Romans 11:11)
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Israel's transgression had a double economy, for the Gentiles were made equal sharers and Israel, made jealous by this, will turn back.
comments.comment: May it not be so, he says. For their transgression has a double economy; for the Gentiles have been made equal participants, and they themselves, having become jealous because of this, will turn back. Since before the law they deviated, and having received the law they were more burdened than they were benefited, and they were neither persuaded by threats nor by exhortations, but always remained disobedient; the Savior came to another economy, and the Gentiles are being saved through their transgression, so that even through the jealousy of the Gentiles they might be saved.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Because the Jews did not keep the law Christ's coming by grace was needed, and their transgression enriched the world while their own fullness would bring Jews and Gentiles together to perfect piety.
comments.comment: If the Jews did not keep the law, the arrival of Christ through grace was necessary (Rom 11:12); therefore our Lord, by grace, is forgiving transgressions. But not all Jews received Christ nor the grace from him, but the remnant; and the others, as if striving to never be saved, pushed the grace onto the Gentiles. And through their transgression they bestowed riches upon the world, that is, the multitude of the saving ones. If God enriched the Gentiles who turned back, how could there not be something greater and a most perfect wealth for the world, if the Jews, having recognized their lack, were given the fullness, so that both the Gentiles and the Jews might run together toward perfect piety?
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: If the world was enriched because Israel stumbled, Israel's acceptance would be nearly the undoing of death.
comments.comment: “Now if their trespass means riches for the world” (Romans 11:12). For if, he says, the world has been enriched with closeness to God because Israel stumbled, and the nations were received because Israel lacked a right mind, what then would their acceptance be, if not very nearly the undoing of death and life from the dead?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul glorifies his ministry not for empty honour but to make his own kin jealous so that they will seek justification by grace, and he binds Jewish and Gentile believers in one mind.
comments.comment: “If somehow I may make my flesh jealous” (Romans 11:14). So he draws the believers from the nations and from the Jews into one mind and peace, so that they may not be puffed up, but may offer their thanks to God, who freely granted the forgiveness of their trespasses and bore no grudge. He says that he glorifies his own ministry (Romans 11:13), not from a desire for empty glory, but, he says, “so that I may make my flesh jealous.” Here again he calls Israel his own flesh, that is, his kin according to the flesh. It is much as if he were to say: “I declare my apostleship to be glorious, worthy, and most dear to God, and most needful to all who live under the sun, not so that I might be seen crowning my own head with empty honours and outlandish boasting, but so that I might save my own kin according to the flesh.” He all but pricks them with jealousy as with a goad, and rouses them to resolve that they must be justified by the grace that comes through Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul magnifies his ministry to the Gentiles: to save his own kin.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Israel's unbelief has become the means of the world's closeness to God, so its acceptance would be life from the dead.
comments.comment: “For if their rejection means the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance mean but life from the dead?” (Romans 11:15). Since, then, there was no way to praise Israel for its faith or its conduct, he turned to the reasoning of the economy, and says that their unbelief has become for the world the means of its closeness to God. He tries to say that by the very things in which they stumbled they have perhaps even become benefactors of the world; and so he crowns the Jews, as it were, though they have fallen and lie on the ground. For he says that their acceptance is life from the dead, if indeed it is true that their rejection has become the reconciliation of the world.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Israel's rejection can be the world's gain and its acceptance life from the dead.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Patriarchs and prophets are the root; the nation, the branches.
comments.comment: The patriarchs, the lawgiver, and the prophets are indeed the firstfruits and the root; but the whole Jewish nation is the bud and the branches (Rom 11:16).
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Those saved from Israel are the firstfruit through which God sanctifies the whole remainder, so Israel has not fallen entirely like the Canaanites or Sodom.
comments.comment: And if, as he says, the saved ones are from Israel (Rom 11:16), those who have become partakers of sanctification toward salvation, God has received these as a firstfruit of the nation (Rom 11:16), and has sanctified the whole remainder through the one received, according to the gift given unto the whole world—for we know that the mass of dough is sanctified through the firstfruit (Rom 11:16)—this, however, is a proof that the nation has not fallen entirely, unlike the Canaanite nations devoted to destruction, of whom even one impious was saved because of the universal vote of God against them, and like Sodom which was handed over to the fire, from which even the race of the righteous stranger did not deserve salvation except through the grace toward him; but of Israel, we see many being saved. Let us not, however, count them together with the Canaanites and Sodoms, nor count them among the unclean, of whom the firstfruit is holy.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Paul sets Israel right and urges it to claim its own root through faith in Christ, while urging the nations honoured by God to stand firm or be cut off from the root.
comments.comment: For he sets Israel right, since it had fallen short of what was fitting, and he urges it toward what is to its profit, and to lay claim to its own root through faith in Christ. He also says that those from the nations have been honoured by God, and he urges them to stand firm in faith and godliness: for if you remain so, you remain a noble branch of the holy root; but if you disobey, you too will be outside the root (Romans 11:16–22).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those grafted in must not be proud but fear, since the natural branches were cut off through unbelief and the added ones must be worthy of grace.
comments.comment: But regarding those being grafted in instead of those who were cut off (Romans 11:20), he says, let it not be a cause of any pride, but let there be fear; for let it be considered that they were grafted in according to grace through faith (Romans 11:20). Those were shoots from the nature of the root, and yet through unbelief they have been cut off. But there is much in between that is according to grace and that which is according to nature. If even nature did not grant those who disobey to stability, how much more shall those of the addition benefit, unless they appear worthy of the grace that has been given?
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Israel's falls are read so that we may fear, for if God cut out those rooted in the patriarchs he will not spare us.
comments.comment: The things that happened to Israel are read, and the falls concerning that people. We ought to fear: 'if he did not spare the natural branches, how much more not you?' (Romans 11:21–22) If, not sparing those who boast to be a cultivated olive, those rooted into the root of the patriarchs Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, the God who is kind and also a lover of man cut them out, how much more will he not spare us?
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the broken-off branches are a warning to Gentile believers to fear.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The cultivated and wild olive show that all share one nature, and the grafting in the faith of Abraham, the root, gives life.
comments.comment: Having mentioned the cultivated and the wild (Rom 11:24), he showed that there is one nature for all, just as with the olive tree; not one choice, as with the wild and the cultivated; the wild one, having been uprooted, is ugly and useless to the master, but the cultivated one is fruit-bearing. And he calls the grafting 'being grafted in the faith of Abraham,' whom he names the root; and he says that the grafting provides life.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Natural branches perish through unbelief while wild ones are grafted in, which shames those who teach that nature alone decides salvation or ruin.
comments.comment: Again, upon these, those who revile the flesh should remember how much the generation according to the flesh has a deviation, even if it is preserved through unbelief. When even the branches of the olive tree according to nature remain in destruction through unbelief (Rom 11:24), and those of the wild olive tree are being grafted in from being contrary to nature into the good olive tree, how are those who bring in both salvation and destruction from nature not ashamed?
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Insensibility seizes Israel until the foreknown Gentiles have entered, and after that the true remnant of Israel shall be saved.
comments.comment: For you do not ignore, he says, the thing unrevealed by the providence of God, which is unknown because of the present unbelief of Israel (Rom 11:25): that until the entrance of all the foreknown ones of the Gentiles, an insensibility seizes Israel (Rom 11:25), but after this, the remnant of the nation, he who has truly followed Israel, shall be saved.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: As far as the One who called is concerned, the fullness of the nations has come in and all Israel is saved, and if some have slipped aside of their own will the Scripture is not false.
comments.comment: “Until the fullness of the nations has come in; and so all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:25–26). Look again at this and consider it closely. He said that the fullness of the nations would come in and all Israel would be saved. But suppose someone chose to answer this: “Yet many of the nations have died in unbelief; how, then, has the fullness of the nations come in? Nor will all Israel be saved, if it is true that the Jews will receive the son of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:3), having cast away their love for Christ. For He Himself said this: ‘I have come in My Father’s name, and you do not receive Me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive’ (John 5:43). And the most wise Paul says: ‘Because they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved, therefore God sends them a working of error, so that they believe the lie’ (2 Thessalonians 2:10–11).” What, then, shall we say to this? We say that, since God has set the grace that comes through faith before all without stint and shuts out no one at all, how has the fullness of the nations not come in, as far as the mind and purpose of the One who called is concerned? For if some have slipped aside of their own will and missed the gift, we shall not on that account find the word of Scripture to be false. For though they were free to share in the gifts once given, why did they choose of their own will to fall away? So, as far as the gentleness and love for mankind of the One who called is concerned, the fullness of the nations has come in, and all Israel too has been saved. But since they have become unbending, for that reason he says that a hardening has come upon them in part (Romans 11:25).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: All Israel will be saved in the way that the whole world of Gentiles is saved, namely those who approach by faith, not everyone without exception.
comments.comment: What is this, and thus all Israel will be saved (Rom 11:25-26)? Just as we say that the whole world and all the Gentiles are being saved because there are those approaching by faith from everywhere and from all the Gentiles, so also all Israel will be saved; 'all' does not mean everyone indiscriminately, but either those being overtaken by Elijah or those scattered throughout the whole world who are about to approach by faith.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'all Israel will be saved': all who come by faith, as 'the whole world' is said to be saved.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Israel's offences will be remitted when those called through faith have overthrown idolatry, which is what Paul meant by saying that all Israel will be saved when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in.
comments.comment: He also makes plain the time at which Jacob too will be free of his offenses. For when, he says, those called through faith to the knowledge of him who is truly God take the field against the ancient error; when altars and sacred precincts and the swarm of idols are taken out of the way; when they consume with fire the temples built with toil for lifeless idols; when they cut down their trees, and besides these the things made with hands, like a forest: then, then indeed God will remit their stumblings to those of Israel as well. And this, I think, is what the godlike Paul declared: “But when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:25–26).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul confirms by an oracle that rejected Israel will be saved in due time, called last after the nations.
comments.comment: “As it is written: ‘The Deliverer will come from Zion’” (Romans 11:26; Isaiah 59:20). He confirms the hope that even rejected Israel is to be saved in due time, by setting out a sacred oracle. For Israel will be saved in due time, called last, after the calling of those from the nations.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Israel is an enemy as regards the gospel but beloved for the fathers' sake.
comments.comment: “Enemies for your sake” (Romans 11:28). As far as the preaching of the gospel is concerned, they have become enemies, for they stumbled through their impiety toward Christ. But because of the nobility of the fathers, who were honoured as holy and dear to God, they may be reckoned beloved for the fathers’ sake. Yet they have become enemies so that a cause of jealousy might be set before those who disbelieved.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Israel can be both enemy and beloved.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The gospel reached the Gentiles through Israel's alienation, yet Israel is kept among survivors.
comments.comment: For the preaching of the gospel to you, brothers, had to come through their alienation (Rom 11:28), and because of this they were alienated; but let Israel also be kept among the survivors as one belonging to their fathers.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Gentiles' belief convicts the Jews who hardened their hearts as enemies of God, yet they remain beloved because of the fathers and will be shown kindness.
comments.comment: Thus it is, so that from the comparison toward you, the Jews are convicted to be enemies of God (Rom 11:28-29), because you, the Gentiles, believed, but those who owed to believe above all things hardened their heart; and according to this very reason they are enemies of God, but beloved because of the fathers, for whose sake He will show philanthropy toward their descendants, and He will consider those believing and having shown a citizenship to be beloved, able to save.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Both Israel and the nations stand under equal charges and have been healed by one grace.
comments.comment: “For just as you once disobeyed God,” and so on (Romans 11:30). He shows that the charges against both are equal, and that those from the nations and Israel alike have been healed by one grace. For Israel was called in its time through Moses and rescued from its misery in Egypt; …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The nations, pictured by the Egyptians, once disobeyed the mercy shown to Israel, but now receive mercy while Israel in turn disobeys the mercy shown to the nations so that it too may receive mercy in due time.
comments.comment: … [The nations,] whom we may understand as signified by the Egyptians, for a time disobeyed the mercy shown to those of Israel. For they did not believe the divine signs worked through Moses; they would not know the God of the Hebrews. The people of the Jews was sent out, though barely, to offer sacrifice in the wilderness, while the Egyptians held fast to their ancient error. But now they have received mercy, since Israel has stumbled; and Israel in turn has disobeyed the mercy shown to the nations, so that it too may receive mercy in due time (Romans 11:30–31).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Past disobedience does not shut the Jews out from repentance, and God shut all up to unbelief by allowing them to disobey, so that they would turn back and be saved by his mercy and not by works.
comments.comment: What is called such a thing is this (Rom 11:30-32): if the former disobedience did not hinder the faith of the Gentiles, then neither for the Jews is the power of exclusion from repentance being shut away regarding the future. … Just as God handed them over to sufferings of dishonor and God blinded the minds of the unbelievers, we do not receive the word as if God were doing evil, but as one permitting men to do what they want through the freedom of self-determination; so also now, what God shut all up to unbelief must be understood: that He allowed those wishing to disobey to continue disobeying, permitting through the whole man to do what he wants with what he has under his own power. Thus God shut all up to unbelief, that is, He continued to permit disobedience, not so that He might condemn those remaining in sins, but so that, perceiving through time those things of which they sin, and having recognized and turned back, He might have mercy on them. Or perhaps what He shut up to unbelief is instead of Him reproving the disobedient, and just as He closed off from them all defense, so that they might sense that they are saved not from works, but from the philanthropy and mercy of God (Romans 11:32).
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: God shut all up in disobedience not by willing that some disobey but by showing them guilty by the facts, so that they stood in need of mercy.
comments.comment: So, as I said, the charges against both are equal, and both alike have needed the help of the One who shows compassion. And he says that all have been shut up in disobedience by God, so that He may have mercy on all (Romans 11:32). Yet we shall by no means reckon it the work of the divine will that some disobeyed, so that, having fallen into this, they might also be pitied. Rather, He shut them up in disobedience by showing them to be liable to the charges of disobedience, and convicted, as it were, by the facts themselves; so that they had come at last to such misfortune that they all but stood in need of pity and mercy.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'God has shut up all in disobedience': he exposed their guilt, not caused it.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God shut up all in disobedience by reproving both Jews and Gentiles, since the Jews had tried to keep the nations from salvation and the nations had been called.
comments.comment: It also signifies something else, as it lies within the philosophy of Paul: 'God gave them all over to disobedience, so that He might have mercy on all' (Romans 11:32). And observe the sequence of the words: the Gentiles, having believed in the Savior, were descending into the fold from the Jews. And previously, again, the Jews prevented the nations from being called unto salvation; for they were saying, 'You are receiving into salvation those from the descendants of your cursed fathers, from idolaters, from many gods.' Therefore, He has made a confinement; He has reproved both.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's judgments are an abyss and his ways like footprints in the sea, so it is no wonder that men stumble over providence, since no one has shared his plan.
comments.comment: One marvels at the manifold wisdom and unsearchable to men; He judges and acts concerning us (Rom 11:33-36). This is a depth, saying according to the ancient scripture which says: 'Your judgments are a great abyss'; this is because the unreachable is as the ungraspable things of the depths; and the ways according to the administration of energy are such that it is not for man to understand, just as even the footprints of one walking through the sea are not seen, as also the Psalmist says: 'In the sea is your way, and your paths in many waters, and your footprints shall not be known' (Ps 77:19). For the human mind does not leave behind any grasp of the divine judgments, because of the manifold and much and by no means single-form kind, the divine wisdom being offered to each of the things appropriately and by imposition, teaching indeed manifold things, saying the wisdom of God. And the 14th Psalm also said according to: 'And your thoughts concerning us cannot be set forth.' Therefore it is no wonder that men stumble in the words concerning providence, for according to Isaiah the mind of God is unknown to everyone; for no one has indeed shared His scheme.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God is the beginning, support and end of all things, and himself comes from no one.
comments.comment: Our Paul, however, says, “From him and through him and to him are all things” (Romans 11:36), showing the beginning of the existence of all things in “from him”, their holding together in “through him”, and their end in “to him”. And in truth God is from no one.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'of him, through him, to him': God is the beginning, support and end of all things.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Testing what is good, pleasing and perfect is a knowing of God's will by a heart that is set toward God.
comments.comment:
To test you, He says, the differing things; what is the will of God, the good and pleasing and perfect (Rom 12:2).

This is according to the prophet the law written in the heart; for the heart being placed toward God in a god-like leisure becomes knowing of the differing things and of the good things and of the wills of God, remaining pleasing only to those in whom God is pleased.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The perfect will of God goes beyond abstaining from evil to doing good even to enemies, so that men become like the Father.
comments.comment:
The will of the good Father, being implanted with goodness, He wills and hastens all to do good, as the one constructing us toward the likeness of His own Father as a good son.

He says, 'Overcome your enemies and do good, and you shall be sons of the Most High, because He is kind toward the ungrateful and the evil.'

This is truly the perfect and pleasing will of God.

For it was also said, 'You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy,' even if God was not pleased by this, yet this alone was endured by those being brought up by the pedagogue; for such a practice did not yet possess goodness, but rather a prevention of evil, and the abstaining from evil becomes a progress toward the good.

But the good which is pleasing to God is the perfect, that which makes men like Him; 'You shall be perfect,' He says, 'just as your heavenly Father is perfect' (Matt 5:48). …
comments.selected_reason: Shows what 'the perfect will of God' means: doing good even to enemies, not only avoiding evil.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The world turns toward luxuries and pleasures; refuse its pattern and be changed into a new man.
comments.comment: The present state of the world is turned toward luxuries and pleasures (Rom 12:2), which anyone may refuse the pattern of, and will change himself into a transformed self and a foreign citizenship. As having become a new man from one to another.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul speaks of grace and humility because arrogance is a terrible disease, and the gifted may be puffed up by grace and fall from the gift.
comments.comment:
Lest anyone might think the word of the exhortation to be human, He showed that it is through grace, and He says and teaches. Since therefore arrogance, in which the Romans are most strongly held, is a most terrible disease, it is proposed to them to be moderate toward the best state of humility, following the teaching of the Spirit. He who, knowing the arrogance of the disciples' human nature, washed their feet, was training them to be humble, lest, having partaken of grace and performed signs, they be puffed up by grace and fall from the gift (Rom 12:3).

To each, He says, as God distributed a measure of faith, instead of saying as each He measured grace according to his faith (Rom 12:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul warns against thinking too highly of oneself: gifts come by grace and pride can lose them.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Pride is a frenzy, because no proud person is of sound mind.
comments.comment: Crushing pride as a frenzy of the mind, he set against this the state of being of sound mind, for no one feeling himself proud would be of sound mind (Rom 12:3).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Do not be saddened at a lesser gift, for even a small part is useful to the whole body, and we are members of one another.
comments.comment: … Having forewarned that God measures the measure of faith (Rom 12:3-8), he follows the preceding pattern and defends the one giving, persuading us not to be saddened if anyone has a lesser gift. … For just as if there were a cheap part in a body, it is useful for everything, and the large and the small are apportioned into one body; for it is an induction from the former that we are members of one another.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Each person has a different grace for his own ministry, and prophecy is the revelation of unseen things, whether coming, old or present.
comments.comment:
Whether prophecy, He says, according to the proportion of faith (Rom 12:6-8). This has been stated incompletely; for it is lacking in the saying 'whether prophecy' that we show the grace in prophecy so that it may be such: having diverse gifts, whether prophecy, whether service, whether teaching. Those having prophecy, we show the grace in prophecy; those having service, in service; those having teaching, in teaching; and each in the ministry in which he is entrusted.

Prophecy, then, is previously the revelation of unseen things, whether of those coming, or of the old, or of the present things.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Each gift has its rank: the prophet remembers the apostles' primacy, the deacon serves like hands under the head, teachers interpret what prophets see, and bodily help and mercy are joined with gladness.
comments.comment:
'Some have prophecy among you,' He says, a most precious gift after the apostles—for God placed in the church first apostles, second prophets—so let him think according to prophecy, knowing the primacy of the apostles,

and indeed the deacon, knowing this rule of the ministry, should be in a lower rank, like hands under the head (Romans 12:7).

Again, the teacher should remain under the prophet within the measures of teaching—for second are prophets, and third are teachers—for teachers are the interpreters of the words from prophecy, just like ears hearing and understanding what is seen by the eyes that see and being made manifest …

And these indeed are the spiritual things.

But let the things concerning the body also be joined, bountiful transfers, and diligent protections; for he who shows mercy brought forth a man-loving mercy in gladness.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Mercy needs cheerfulness so that we give out of love for mankind and not arrogance, and bodily service is also a gift accomplished in the Spirit's power.
comments.comment:
But it is necessary for hilarity with mercy, since it happens toward the lowly, so that we might not grieve by giving not out of arrogance, but let us rejoice out of philanthropy. If indeed the distributions, protections, and alms also bring rest concerning bodily things, they are nevertheless gifts being accomplished in the power of the Spirit, joining to the order of the feet the holy body of those who serve.

For not only if someone speaks as the words of God, as Peter says, but also if someone serves as from the strength which God supplies; and Paul names the service of the liturgy that fills up the deficiencies of the saints, being called a ministry in many ways, both bodily and spiritual.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Giving in simplicity means giving to all who ask, though over-precision often prevents our giving.
comments.comment: The one giving in simplicity—that is, what the Lord says: give to everyone asking you, not seeking either good or evil and to whom you give (Luke 6:30)—since this precision often prevents us from giving to those to whom it ought to be given, the suspicion in us having erred many times.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Simplicity in giving means the generosity of an extended hand, given for fellowship with the saints and as an offering to God, while mercy goes to anyone in need.
comments.comment:
Having said the spiritual things and the things concerning the body, he defines the distribution in simplicity, and, placing simplicity as being the same as the distribution itself. For the one distributing, he says, is in simplicity in the distribution, just as regarding the service, the one serving is in the service.

But generosity is called simplicity by the apostles from the extended hand, as in the Second Letter to the Corinthians: their poverty according to depth abounded into the wealth of their simplicity. Likewise, the protection is defined to be with zeal, and mercy with hilarity, separating it from the distribution.

For the one is for the sake of fellowship with the saints; for upon the simplicity, he says, of the fellowship into them, saying into the saints. Therefore also the generous giving is as an offering to God, and a service to Christ, and a lover of fellowship: for make, he says, friends from the mammon of unrighteousness and the following things. But mercy is for the sake of the needs of whoever they may be; for to everyone, he says, give to the one asking you for the sake of philanthropy.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Taking part in the remembrance of the saints means remembering them and having their life as a model.
comments.comment: Regarding the participation in the remembrance of the saints (Rom 12:13), he says, that which is ready for the mind is to understand the honor of the saints and to fulfill their remembrance according to the day of their perfection. And it is also possible to say that those adhering to virtue most appropriately participate in the memories of the saints, which is to remember them and to have their life as a model of lifestyle.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Scripture names God's punishment 'wrath' only to speak in terms men understand, so we are to yield vengeance to God and not take it ourselves.
comments.comment: Regarding 'he names as wrath the punishment from God' (Rom 12:19), he speaks not as a passion happening to God, but because men would not easily perceive vengeance happening from God, not having heard the common name of wrath; for since men turn toward those sinning against them in anger and wrath, the Scripture sets these things aside for God, so that it is possible for the many to hear and to understand. He therefore says, 'do not permit vengeance to yourselves,' but give place and yield the vengeance to the wrath of God, which is appointed to avenge the wronged.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Scripture speaks of God's wrath and why Christians leave vengeance to him.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Paul does not teach evil by the coals of fire but restrains the anger of the wronged, since doing good to those who wrong us surpasses even the law.
comments.comment:
[On heaping coals of fire:] For he does not introduce these things as a teacher of evils—may it never be!—but by skill and wisdom he restrains and moderates the intensity of the one being enraged.

For it is a great thing indeed not to do wrong, but it is greater to not defend oneself against having been wronged, but rather to quench a boiling anger in the manner of forbearance; and the law, by granting retaliation to those wronged, appears more gentle than mere authority; but to do good to those who have done wrong, this even surpasses the law and philosophy. Therefore, so that he might overcome the anger from having been wronged and, instead of defending himself, prepare to do good, he gives hope by showing what terrible things are happening to those who have done wrong as a result of his goodness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'coals of fire' as a way to quench anger and rise above the law's retaliation.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Kings should be obeyed, since they serve God.
comments.comment: It is worthy for those to be subject to kings who persevere in the service of the will of God (Rom 13:1) …
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul teaches obedience to rulers to exclude the imitation of Judas the Galilean, whose sect caused killings and rebellion against the rulers.
comments.comment:
Judas the Galilean in the days of the census, as Gamaliel says in the Acts, led a great people after him, preventing them from obeying the Roman command (Rom 13:1) and from being registered, as when Cyrenius was sent into Syria. And from this cause the Romans were standing against those being persuaded by Judas, under the pretext of not serving men but God alone. And they willingly endured all punishments, in anticipation of piety, for the sake of not acknowledging any man as master, and they caused division against those not thinking the same things and not being associated with them. …

Since, therefore, the sect of Judas became a cause of killings among kinsmen and of rebellion against the rulers to the harm of the nation, it seems to me now that the apostle excludes this imitation, as those who consider not obeying rulers to be piety toward God. Therefore he also makes much discourse about this, exposing the opinion that is erroneous.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Kings rule by God's plan, and Rome's rule was given for the Savior's coming, so not obeying authorities is impious and brings judgment.
comments.comment:
Regarding Romans 13:1, since many various authorities and established rulers exist among men, adding to the surpassing royal authorities, he showed: for kings come to rule not without the economy and will of God, as the Proverbs teach. Through me, he says, kings rule, and the potentates write out justice. And the rule of the Romans has happened by exception from God's economy; for since the Savior was about to appear to men, God, beforehand a little, offered the Roman rule for his own service, through which he established our life more peacefully than other men. Having freed them from wars against one another, he gave such leisure for the knowledge of himself: come, for he says, and see the works of God which he set as wonders upon the earth, opposing wars even to the ends of the earth. And he leads on: relax and know that I am God.

Therefore, God having removed the continuous wars and having given fellowship to both cities and nations through the proclamation of the godly commonwealth, the apostle saw the economy of God regarding the kingdoms and advised that they be subjected to the authorities; for since God has ordered them, not obeying is impious and, in the present life, it is dangerous to have folly. Romans 13:2: But those who resist, he says, shall receive judgment upon themselves, that is, those not obeying the king receive judgment and a tribunal.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says rulers are from God: their rule serves God's plan, so resisting them is resisting God.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: We obey the authorities not only for fear of the rulers but for conscience, and taxes test our submission to them as ministers of God.
comments.comment: Romans 13:5: It is necessary, he says, to obey the authorities not only because of the anger of the rulers, but also because of conscience, which is the reasonable thing regarding the matter. Or he even says this: you do not wish to be judged because of God, but those from without suspect that you are doing something evil to yourself and that your conscience has been struck. Romans 13:6: Taxes, he says, test the submission; it is therefore worthy to be subject to the kings, being ministers of God and persevering in the service of his will.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Love brings many advantages: the one who loves does not commit adultery or murder, and so fulfills the law.
comments.comment:
Such then being this love, it naturally bears many advantages in itself; for the one loving does not commit adultery, does not murder, does not do anything else of the forbidden things (Rom 13:9), so that the one having love thus through love fulfilled the law continuously.

Fulfill, he says, the work of love (Rom 13:10), knowing the time pressing and virtue requiring (Rom 13:11).
comments.selected_reason: Shows why love fulfills the law: the one who loves does none of the forbidden things.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The time presses, so those once ignorant of the truth and now enlightened must rise from the sleep of inaction and lay hold of good works.
comments.comment:
Knowing that the time is pressing and that virtue is required, those who formerly were ignorant of the truth and were passing through the night and darkness of error were appropriately like those sleeping in the inaction of good works; but those who have now been enlightened by the memory of the Savior and have come into the day owe it to themselves to rise from the laziness of sleep and to lay hold of good works.

For our salvation is now nearer to us than when we first believed, that is, when we knew those works which are most profitable; it has become easier for us to be saved than when we were being catechized on the word of faith, for we did not at once possess belief in Christ and the precise grasp of what must be practiced, nor was it previously manifest to us which deeds we should abstain from and which deeds were fitting to adopt (Romans 13:11).
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's 'salvation is nearer': believers now know the works to practice, so they must wake and act.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Night and darkness mean ignorance, and day and light mean the precise knowledge of pious truth, while this life is the time for works.
comments.comment: Night and darkness are called ignorance, which he says we were running through until we were made known to the practices (Rom 13:12), but day and light are the precise knowledge of pious truth. But the Savior, having said, 'Until it is day, work the works of light; night comes when no one is able to work' (John 9:4), urged the conduct in this life as providing us the time for works, but referred to the night as the things to come and the eternal, as when it is no longer possible to do anything, but as being in darkness in inaction, having lost the time for works.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's 'night' and 'day' as ignorance and knowledge of the truth, with this life as the time to work.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: To put on the Lord Jesus Christ is to show him in how we live, and so to refuse to provide for the flesh.
comments.comment: Instead of merely imitating him in what you do, 'put on the Lord Jesus Christ,' he says, and show him through you in how you live (Rom 13:14). How then would anyone imitate Christ? He showed this by saying, 'Do not provide for the flesh for the sake of lusts'; for he who is occupied with the flesh and fulfilling the pleasures of the flesh certainly neglects the soul.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'put on the Lord Jesus Christ' means: show him in how you live, not feeding the flesh.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Foods are indifferent in themselves, being sanctified by Christ, but not all are strengthened in faith, so love must not treat the neighbor as indifferent.
comments.comment: Concerning the indifferent, he discourses (Rom 14:1), which makes no difference whether it be done or not done, advising indifference regarding these things, but assuming that which in them belongs to love, to no longer regard the neighbor as indifferent. Every food is indeed indifferent for the sake of purity, being sanctified by the power of Christ. But not all are thus strengthened in faith; as to having no fear of defilement in such things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'weak in faith' on foods: food is indifferent, but the weak neighbor's conscience is not.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Paul's one who eats all things and the weak who eats herbs are, in Origen's reading, the perfect and the imperfect in God's words, and not bodily foods.
comments.comment: And I take even the 'One believes he may eat all things, but the weak eats herbs' (Romans 14:2) to be said by him principally not of bodily foods but of God's words that nourish the soul: the most faithful and most perfect can partake of all — whom he indicates through the 'One believes he may eat all things' — while the weaker and more imperfect begins with simpler lessons, which do not strongly impart vigor — whom, wishing to mark him, he calls 'the weak eats herbs.'
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We should not despise the brother who abstains out of excessive piety, lest God despise us as those convinced they are righteous.
comments.comment:
Likewise, he [Paul] spoke to the one treating with contempt the brother who is not eating, because of a lack of faith.

For to despise the evildoer is the mark of the man who will be saved, according to the Psalm; but one should not despise the one who does something out of excessive piety, lest we be despised by God like those who are convinced they are righteous and despise others.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ's household is a stranger to the law, so no one may judge it by the law, and both the one who fasts and the one who eats, giving thanks to the Lord, do well.
comments.comment:
'Who are you, you who judge another's household?' (Rom 14:4). The household of Christ, which Christ received, is a stranger to the law. Who then are you, judging from the law the one who is a stranger to the law? Now he speaks concerning fasting (Rom 14:6); he says that both the one fasting, consuming the day in thinking and seeking divine things for the Lord, and the one thinking on the Lord, does this by having his hopes upon him.

Likewise, he who wastes the day not on thinking but on the enjoyment of filth—and this one does not think toward the Lord, as his laziness and his laxity toward God become—this one is not even cast away; for he does not do this by abandoning or denying the Master, but by being bold in the philanthropy of God in whatever things he may be lazy or think to be lax. So, let him who eats give thanks to the Lord for those things of which he enjoys, and let him who does not eat glorify God rightly for the self-control which he has, strengthening him. Even if someone eats according to God, or fasts according to God, he will do well.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Christ died and rose to rule both the dead and the living; he was always Master by nature, but his presence under the flesh brought believers under God's lordship and made him the firstfruits of the resurrection.
comments.comment: For this, he says, Christ both died and rose and lived, so that he might rule both the dead and the living (Rom 14:7–9). What then? Was Christ not Lord of all before the passion? But he was. What then is the surplus from the humanization? Because in truth and by nature he was Master of the one who made the things made, but to the turning away of the ungodly he was not. Regarding those who worship the creation rather than the Creator, he was not considered to be ruling, but the things worshiped by them; so that his incarnate presence brought those who were with him and those who will be with him under the lordship of God, but his presence remaining until death, showing the economy by the departure of those who perished in ignorance of salvation, and he broke through the bonds of death, and became the firstfruits of the resurrection.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Since all stand before God's judgment, none who stands accused should judge his neighbor, and Christ's judgment seat is the judgment seat of God.
comments.comment:
Furthermore, the reasoning for not being extremely angry with one another is this: for all, he says, are under God's judgment, and just as we shall be presented before God as a judge; for it is not the one presented before the judge who judges the one standing present with him, for each must take care of the one giving an account.

And let us not judge our neighbor, but let us remember so that we ourselves may not be condemned.

It is evident that the Christ's judgment is the judgment seat of God; for the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, having given him judgment to perform as a human judge of men according to authority, because he is a son of man.

He did not reserve judgment to human nature, since the Son is not man by nature, but is also man by dispensation.

Therefore it remains God's, and thus the judgment and the tribunal belong to his wisdom and power, of the holy one who was incarnated for man.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Nothing that enters defiles but what goes out from the heart, so an unclean thought makes something deemed unclean common.
comments.comment:
I know, he says, through Christ's faith, that through Christ all things are clean, and nothing that enters defiles, but that which goes out from the heart (Rom 14:14).

Such also is the opinion concerning the unclean; just as an unclean thought from the heart regarding a harm immediately makes that which is deemed unclean to be common.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Paul is sure in the Lord Jesus that no food is common, since Christ taught that what enters the mouth does not defile and God blessed all he made.
comments.comment:
“I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus,” and so on (Romans 14:14). “I know and am persuaded,” he says, “in the Lord Jesus that nothing is common of itself,” and the rest. The witness who firmly declares that he knows and is persuaded is trustworthy. He adds “in the Lord Jesus” so that the truth may be established still more firmly, and so that his hearers may follow in faith without any hesitation. No doubt he remembers that Christ said, “It is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a man” (Matthew 15:11), and that all food passes into the stomach and is sent out into the drain (Matthew 15:17); this is its nature and its use. So, as far as their own nature goes, nothing that serves as food is common or profane, “for it is made holy by the word of God and prayer” (1 Timothy 4:5).

And we remember that when God had brought all things into being, He saw, it says, that they were “very good” (Genesis 1:31), and He blessed them (Genesis 1:22). Since God praised and indeed blessed His own creatures, who would dare to say that they cause defilement and profanation, and not thereby bring a charge against the very One who brought them into being? So nothing that has been made is common by nature at all.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul can be certain no food is unclean: Christ taught it and God blessed his creatures.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Many things are not unclean by nature but become unclean through a weak conscience, as bogeymen frighten only children.
comments.comment: For there are many things that are not unclean by nature, but become unclean from the weakness of the conscience. And just as with children, masks and other bogeymen are not frightening by nature, but seem frightening to children because of the weakness of their nature, so it is with the things I mentioned. For example, touching dead bodies is not unclean by nature, but when it takes hold of a weak conscience, it makes the one who touches unclean. That the thing is not unclean by nature, Moses himself—the very one who ordained these things—made clear, for he carried with himself the whole corpse of Joseph and remained clean. For this reason Paul, speaking to us about this uncleanness that does not come by nature but through weakness of conscience, says something like this: Nothing is common in itself, except to the one who considers something common (Romans 14:14).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'nothing is common in itself' with the example of a weak conscience that makes things unclean.
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: Through faith in Christ Jesus nothing is common or unclean.
comments.comment: I know and am persuaded, he says, that nothing is common through himself, that is, nothing is common and unclean through the faith received toward Christ Jesus (Rom 14:14).
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Foods are common for those whose mind still limps on the way to the truth.
comments.comment: … But for those who have not yet come to this judgment, these things are not yet clean, by what seems right to them; they are common, because their mind somehow limps on the way to the truth.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Do not stain a brother with a weak conscience by hastening to eat, since losing one for whom Christ died over trivial food breaks love.
comments.comment:
Watch out, he says, to bring a stain upon the brother who is being weakened in conscience (Rom 14:15).

For he also said this in the letter to the Corinthians, that the weak consciences are being stained by those eating as if eating idols.

Do not, he says, make the eating of such things a matter of haste; for if we do this without having reliability toward the grief of the brother, we surpass love by making the eating a pretext for the more necessary thing.

For the sake of a trivial food, let not the possession of Christ be lost, he who purchased life with death.

For he will perish, being severed from the union and deprived of love, or even compelled to eat without faith.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The kingdom of God is not defined by eating and drinking, so we should not stir up blasphemy over food.
comments.comment:
Let us not stir up blasphemy against the faith, by choosing profane eatings because of this.

It is sufficient to glorify what is necessary concerning foods.

It is not that if we eat, then God reigns in us; for it is not by eating and drinking that the kingdom of God is defined.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The worthy person does not let his good be spoken of as evil but stoops to the weakness of his weak brothers and abstains, as Paul blamed Peter not for abstaining but for leading the nations to think they must live by the law.
comments.comment:
“So do not let your good be spoken of as evil” (Romans 14:16). Let not the brilliance of those who are well approved lift itself up over the weak, nor let your good, that is, what is admirable in your faith, be spoken ill of by anyone. For the achievements of a life pleasing to God would not come about through eating (Romans 14:17), nor would such a person be worthy of the kingdom of heaven, as one who reveres God, if he eats without distinction whatever is set before him; rather, the one who is worthy is he who stoops to the weakness of his weak brothers and abstains.

For even if Paul blamed Peter for living like a Jew because of those who had come to Antioch from James (Galatians 2:11–14), he did not blame him for stooping to the weakness of those of the circumcision and abstaining from foods. He blamed him because, by the weight of his own standing, he was drawing the many believers from the nations into thinking that they had to live according to the law, and Paul’s preaching was in danger of coming to nothing; for he was the teacher of the nations.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the strong should give up foods for the weak: so their good is not spoken of as evil.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Uncleanness comes from the weakness of the reasoning, and eating to another's stumbling causes it.
comments.comment: Do you see that uncleanness comes not from the nature of the thing itself, but from the weakness of the reasoning? And again: All things are clean, but it is evil for the person who eats to another's stumbling (Romans 14:20). Do you see that it is not the eating, but the eating to another's stumbling, that causes uncleanness?
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: What makes things common is the unbeliever's little faith, not the things themselves.
comments.comment: …For all things are clean (Romans 14:20); what makes the unbeliever common is his little faith about certain things, and not at all the things themselves that he has supposed to be common.
comments.selected_reason: Explains that things are clean in themselves; the unbeliever's little faith makes them common.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Eating meat and drinking wine is lawful, but abstaining is useful for ourselves and much more for a brother, so that he may not stumble.
comments.comment: For it is lawful to eat meat and to drink wine, but freedom in these things is not altogether without harm (Romans 14:21). Abstaining is also useful, so that we do not fatten the flesh with soft living and make the passions within it rage wild against ourselves. If, then, we abstain from these things for our own sake, much more for our brother’s, so that he may not stumble, because of the saying, “You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18).
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's advice to abstain for a brother's sake: love of neighbor.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Abstain from meat if it scandalizes your brother, but eat if abstaining would make you a stumbling block.
comments.comment: It is good, he says, not to eat meat, if your brother is scandalized by this, thinking you to be a slave to the stomach (Rom 14:21). And from the opposite again: if not eating meat, you might seem to abstain from unclean things, eat so that you may not be found a stumbling block to others (Rom 14:21).
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: The one who wavers in faith and eats is condemned, so it is better for him to abstain than to strike his own conscience.
comments.comment: He who does not judge himself; this is the one touching the filth with faith, whom he also blesses as faithful, but the one having a soul irregular concerning faith and not being bold in himself but wavering, if he eats, he is condemned (Rom 14:22–23). So it is better for such a one to abstain, so that he may not strike his own conscience.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'whatever is not of faith is sin': a doubter who eats is condemned and does better to abstain.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: To please the neighbor for the good is no longer human-pleasing, which is doing something for men according to pleasure.
comments.comment: And having exhorted to please the neighbor, he necessarily added to the good; for this is no longer human-pleasing, since God scattered the bones of those pleasing men, and if he still pleased men, I would not be a slave of Christ; for human-pleasing is doing something for men according to pleasure.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ shows we should abstain for the brothers' benefit, and he stayed with the annoying ones and did not turn away.
comments.comment:
Christ did not say that he pleased himself as in pleasing men (Romans 15:3), but he shows what is present: for he exhorts us not to choose for ourselves a way of living that would bring us harm, but to abstain for the benefit of the brothers, which happens through not causing grief. …

Because of this, he did not please himself by passing away or turning away from the annoying ones, but remained saying: 'O faithless and stray generation, how long shall I be with you?' (Matthew 17:17).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ became flesh not to please himself but to bring the weak to godliness.
