comments.comment: He wishes to say that our Lord and Savior did not please himself, but incarnated so that he might have compassion on weak men and through the incarnate economy [God's plan of salvation] bring them to a firm godliness (Rom 15:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'Christ did not please himself': he became flesh out of compassion for the weak.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Christ bears, in his person toward the Father, the insults of those who insulted God, as when Israel made gods.
comments.comment: For indeed they compelled Aaron to make gods for themselves which would go before them, as an insult and a reproach to God. Therefore, as concerning the person of Christ toward the Father, the psalm is said, saying: 'the insults of those insulting you have fallen upon me' (Psalm 69:9).
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: The reproaches that fell on Christ refer to the cross, which he endured while despising the shame.
comments.comment: And if the Savior says this, he calls the cross a reproach; for this is what the apostle taught: 'The reproaches of those reproaching you have fallen upon me' (Romans 15:3). Again: 'Who, despising the shame, endured the cross instead of the joy set before him' (Hebrews 12:2). Reproach and shame are the same thing. And see how much it reached him, that joy was set before him, a man not having sin. Therefore he despised the shame, he trampled it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'the reproaches fell on me': Christ calls the cross a reproach and despised the shame.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ binds us into unity with the bonds of love, so we receive one another by being of the same mind, bearing burdens and sharing in one body.
comments.comment: “Therefore receive one another, as Christ also received you, for the glory of God” (Romans 15:7). We who are many are one body, and members of one another, as it is written (Romans 12:5), since Christ binds us together into unity with the bonds of love: “For He Himself is the one who made both one and broke down the dividing wall of partition, abolishing the law of commandments in ordinances” (Ephesians 2:14–15). So we must be of the same mind toward one another (Romans 12:16); and if one member suffers, all the members must suffer with it, and if one member is honoured, all the members must rejoice (1 Corinthians 12:26). That is why he says, “Receive one another, as Christ also received you, for the glory of God.” And we shall receive one another if we choose to be of the same mind, bear one another’s burdens (Galatians 6:2), …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God has received us in Christ, who was given as the price of our life, and by his death we obtained reconciliation and redemption.
comments.comment: … So too God has received us in Christ (Romans 15:7). For he spoke the truth who said that the world was so loved by God the Father that the Son Himself was given for us (John 3:16). For He was given as the price exchanged for the life of us all, and by death we have obtained reconciliation, and we have been redeemed from death and sin.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ became a servant of the circumcision to fulfil God's promise to the fathers, though he came not to be served but to serve.
comments.comment: And Paul makes clear the aim of the economy when he says that Christ became a servant of the circumcision for the sake of the truth, and the rest (Romans 15:8). For since God had promised beforehand to the fathers of the Jews that He would bless the offspring that was to come from them, and that it would be “like the stars of heaven in number” (Genesis 22:17), for this reason the Word, being God, appeared in the flesh and became man. He is the very one who holds all creation together in being and, as God, grants well-being to all that exists. He came into this world with flesh, yet, as He Himself says, not to be served, “but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many” (Matthew 20:28).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ is called a servant of the circumcision: to fulfil God's promise to the fathers.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ fulfilled the promise as seed of Abraham, and after him the Jews stopped worshiping idols and the nations turned to piety.
comments.comment: From the presence of Christ, neither did the Jews still worship idols, and the nations were turned toward piety. The Lord has become a servant of the promise and of the philanthropy of God (Rom 15:8). For he fulfilled the promise, having become from the seed of Abraham and subsequently receiving circumcision according to the race. …
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Christ became a mediator to confirm the promises given the fathers through faith, so the nations are justified as Abraham was.
comments.comment: For it is written that “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him unto righteousness,” (Genesis 15:6) and it was said to him that “in you all the tribes of the earth will be blessed.” (Genesis 12:3) And Paul made it clear for us, saying: “For the promise to Abraham or to his seed, that he should be heir of the world, was not through law, but through righteousness of faith,” (Romans 4:13) and again: “so that those from faith are blessed with faithful Abraham.” (Galatians 3:9) If therefore the promises have been given to the fathers from God through faith, Christ has become a servant—that is, a mediator—to confirm the promises given to the fathers from God, that is, the justification through faith. … For blessed Abraham was justified having believed toward God; so also the nations would be justified in him, having followed in his steps and believing in God—that is, in Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Christ became a servant to confirm the promises to the fathers and for mercy to the nations, since Israel's disobedience left few saved, and the prophecies foretold the nations' calling.
comments.comment:
So Paul does not speak falsely when he says that Christ became a servant from the circumcision to confirm the promises made to the fathers (Romans 15:8), and that besides this He was appointed by God the Father for mercy also to those from the nations, so that they too might glorify the Saviour and Redeemer as the Maker and Craftsman of all things (Romans 15:9).

For it was needful, truly needful, since the circumcision in its great disobedience insulted Him wickedly and would not accept the redemption He gave, that the unspeakable grace of God should not seem to have achieved nothing, when those from Israel who had believed and been saved were few, a bare handful. For this reason, as the calm that comes from above was spread wide, as it were, over all, the nations were received. And the mystery of the wisdom that is in Christ is seen not to have missed its aim, an aim set on kindness. For in place of those who had slipped, the whole world under heaven has been saved, because God had compassion.

And that the mystery had been proclaimed beforehand by the voice of holy men who foreknew in the Spirit what was to come, he establishes by setting out the prophecies most plainly (Romans 15:9–12).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The nations were called by God's philanthropy, not their righteousness.
comments.comment: Regarding the calling of the nations: for they were not called because of their own righteousness, but because of the philanthropy of the one calling.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: Paul's coming will be full of Christ's gifts.
comments.comment: He says to them that his presence will appear through apostolic grace, full of the good things from Christ (Romans 15:29).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Paul remembers each well-known person in his greeting according to worth, as each is written down by God in the invisible books of the Spirit.
comments.comment:
He makes a portion of remembrance of each well-known person in greeting and salutation (Rom 16:8), which is appropriate to his own doing of love and of speaking in his spirit, showing to us the Philanthropist and having each one remembered by him according to his worth, just as in the old writings there are lists of the generations and a memory according to the worth of each,

showing that each is written down by him according to worth in the invisible books of the Spirit.

Which indeed Daniel saw when opening the scroll that was set, upon the ancient of days, that is, upon the eternal God (Dan 7:9).

And the angel, foretelling concerning the end, said to him: 'In that time all your people shall be saved who are found written upon the book' (Dan 12:1).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Prudence keeps us from being wronged, and innocence keeps us from plotting against others.
comments.comment:
He says, 'But I want you to be wise toward the good, and innocent toward the evil' (Rom 16:19); this is to use prudence so as not to be wronged by others, and innocence so as not to plot against others.

And the Lord also commanded this, saying: 'Become prudent as serpents and innocent as doves' (Matt 10:16). For indeed innocence and simplicity without prudence is foolishness, …
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's 'wise toward the good, innocent toward evil': prudence guards us, innocence keeps us from harming others.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: The mystery once kept silent is now revealed to all the nations, who turned to Christ.
comments.comment: See how clearly he [Paul] says the gospel and the proclamation are of Jesus Christ; and that the mystery concerning him was hidden and kept silent for eternal times, but has now been revealed unto obedience of faith unto all the nations. For the nations, removed from the falsely named worship, turned to Christ and recognized him as God by nature and truly.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina
